### On the Sunday of the Resurrection of JESUS Christ from the Dead / Gospel of Mark, Chapter 16.

And when the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices <note>original: "Specerey." These were aromatic herbs and ointments used in Jewish burial customs to honor the deceased.</note>, that they might come and anoint Him. And very early in the morning, on the first day of the week <note>original: "an einem Sabbather." In the German Lutheran tradition, this phrasing refers to the day after the Sabbath, or Sunday.</note>, they came unto the sepulcher at the rising of the sun. And they said among themselves: Who shall roll us away the stone from the door of the sepulcher? And when they looked, they saw that the stone was rolled away: for it was very great. And entering into the sepulcher, they saw a young man <note>The "young man" described here is traditionally understood to be an angel.</note> sitting on the right side, clothed in a long white garment; and they were affrighted.

<margin>The 12 Articles of the 12 Apostles.</margin> <note>original Latin: "12. Articuli 12. Apostolorum." This refers to the Apostles' Creed, which tradition once claimed was composed by the twelve apostles together.</note>

Also / that the Holy Spirit / the third Person / enlightens the saints / that there is one Christian Church / a communion of saints / a forgiveness of sins / a resurrection of the flesh / and an eternal life / etc.

<margin>Principal Articles. The resurrection of the flesh is the principal article of faith. Necessary causes of that article.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Præcipui Articuli. Resurrectio carnis præcipuus articulus fidei. Causæ necessariæ illius articuli."</note>

<term>Body of Adam</term> — A theological term for the mortal, fallen physical nature inherited from the first human, which must be shed to achieve eternal life.

We come into heaven by way of inheritance.

But because we have a part in the first resurrection / that is / Christ’s body / in which the true resurrection is / so the second death <note>The "second death" is a biblical concept from Revelation referring to eternal separation from God after the final judgment.</note> has no power over us / for the dead body of Adam falls away from us / like an old garment / so now the rising from death / and hell / is of two kinds / the first from GOD the Father / the other from GOD the Son / so there must surely be two kinds of bodies / namely the body through the awakening from the graves / and the body of those condemned to eternal life. For the body / which GOD the Father created / the same passes entirely away with the elements <note>The elements refer to the physical matter of the world—earth, water, air, and fire—which the author believes will be dissolved at the end of time.</note> / there nothing of it remains living; But the body from Christ / the same remains and possesses the Kingdom of GOD. Therefore GOD regretted that He had made man / for the reason / that he fell from Paradise / and was sentenced to damnation / and through his fall was evicted and robbed of Heaven and Paradise; But through the Son / who has given man a new Body <note>original: "Corpus"</note> / a new creature has been made out of him / and yet the man / whom GOD himself created / remained man / (that is) in the form and essence of his father / but in a new flesh and blood / namely that which belongs to heaven / therefore we now come into heaven by way of inheritance / that is / just as heirs possess by way of inheritance. Because we are now from the earth / so we must now leave the earth / and not inherit it / but die / therefore we have another body from heaven out of the Bread / that descended from heaven <note>A reference to the Eucharist or Holy Communion, where Christ is described as the "bread of life."</note> / and died on the Cross / who has given the same to us. Thus we receive heaven / for just as we inherit the earth from Adam / and everything that is therein / and grows / because we are his blood and flesh / so follows now everyone / who will be in the judgment of GOD; If he is Adam’s heir / so he dies / but if he is Christ’s heir / so he remains / therefore Adam’s creature dies / but Christ’s creature becomes living in him. When Christ now / after the judgment is held / will say: Go hence, you blessed ones, into my Kingdom/

<margin>The first resurrection.</margin> The first resurrection, I understand it to mean that it begins in this life, when one walks in Christ and falls asleep <note>An archaic and gentle way of saying "to die in faith."</note> in Christ; there the soul departs into rest to await the Last Day; the body is buried in the earth, and because body and soul must be together (for both the good and the evil must rise), the believer is nonetheless not entirely separated from death until after the Judgment is held. Then the body of Adam <note>original: "Adæ"</note> will fall away from the Holy; that is death, the last enemy. And so, after the sentence is spoken, the believers will rise from the death-grave of their bodies to eternal life, which is the second resurrection. But whoever has a part in the first resurrection, over him the second death has no power. <margin>What is death? <note>original: "Mors quid?"</note></margin> Death is not a man outside of us, but he is the body of Adam <note>original: "Corpus Adæ"</note>, and is in Adam—that is, in Adam’s children. Also, the immortal soul is killed if it lives for the Adamic flesh; this death is not separated from the believers until after the Judgment is held; then, in the resurrection to life, the old Adamic body is cast off and passes away with the elements <note>The "elements" refer to the physical matter of the earthly world (earth, water, air, fire) which the author believes will be dissolved at the end of time.</note>. Death was entirely separated from Christ on the third day. He rose invisibly in a glorified body, but from us, death will be separated at the Last Judgment, for body and soul come together again before the Judgment.

### this book; but these are written so that you may believe that JESUS is the Christ, the Son of GOD, and that through faith you may have life in His Name. <note>The OCR reads "Rahmen" (frame), but the biblical text (John 20:31) and context confirm this is "Namen" (Name).</note>

IN this text, we wish to consider three small points together.

<margin>1.</margin> First, the certain testimony of the resurrection of the flesh: that Christ rose invisibly from the grave, and we shall come forth visibly in the flesh of Adam <note>The author uses "flesh of Adam" to refer to our natural, fallen human bodies.</note> for the Judgment—both the good and the evil—and after the Judgment is held, we must arise with glorified bodies.

<margin>2.</margin> Secondly, concerning the office of the Spirit: that those sent by God also bring the seal with them, namely the Holy Spirit, and shall have the power to loose and to bind <note>This refers to the "Power of the Keys," the authority to forgive or retain sins.</note> the believers and the unbelievers; also to communicate the Holy Spirit to the believers; and also that they speak what they know and testify to what they have heard. In contrast, those who are chosen and sent by men bring no Holy Spirit with them; their absolution and preaching are nothing; they speak and testify like a blind man speaks of color; they have neither heard nor seen it, nor experienced it in their hearts; they preach human doctrine and not Christ the Crucified.

<margin>3.</margin> Thirdly, that faith alone justifies, takes away sin, makes one blessed, and brings life. This is the preeminent point in this text, for faith is mentioned six times as doing everything; for where true faith is, there one observes the Lord’s Day <note>Original: *Dominica*. Latin for "The Lord’s Day" or the Sunday service.</note> and allows oneself to be baptized. Where faith is, there the absolution is valid. Faith is an experience through the Holy Spirit, where one sees, hears, and touches—no differently than how the disciples saw and touched Christ physically.

AND for the first point: today a certain testimony is once again presented to us that there is a resurrection from the dead. Christ is from heaven; therefore He rose from death on the third day invisibly and heavenly. His body was so clear and subtle <note>In historical theology, a "subtle" body refers to a resurrected body capable of passing through solid objects, like doors or rocks.</note> that He passed through rocks, and no mortal eye could see Him. Therefore, all people—good and evil—must arise from the grave and from the earth with visible bodies and see Christ with their natural eyes. We shall also know one another. We do not come to the Judgment in glorified bodies (as some think), but with the natural, elemental flesh; we are awakened from the earth visibly and bodily. Thus we have the account of the Article [of faith], "I believe in a resurrection of the dead," namely that the flesh of Christ, after the Judgment is held, shall arise from the deadly grave of Adam’s flesh into the Kingdom of GOD with Christ. However, first all people in the flesh of Adam <note>The author uses "Adam’s flesh" to refer to our mortal, fallen human nature.</note> must be awakened and arise from the grave for the Judgment—both evil and good, bodily and visibly—so that all people may be recognized as damnable within it. Should we leave it at that and continue preaching with our "Holy Spirit of the synagogues"? No, indeed. We should turn to GOD and ask Him that we may experience the truth in our own hearts through the Holy Spirit, not clinging to men or to great status. To gather the fallen, wandering people to Christ and lead them to the witness of the Spirit, so that they have the witness of Jesus within themselves. ### 2. The Hireling.

Hirelings, on the contrary, are all those false teachers who are not "good" from Christ, who do not love the little sheep but rather love themselves and pasture themselves. They preach for wages and have no conscience regarding whether people are converted or not. Such men love temporal goods and large incomes; they have a "trapped foot" <note>This likely means they are constrained or tied down by their worldly interests and obligations.</note>, preaching for pay and for the sake of their bellies. They rely on human teachings and human books—as unfortunately happens among us all—seeking only ourselves. Where there is a large income, there we gladly go; we preach as long as the sheep give wool and milk, or as long as the goose has feathers. A trade is made out of the Gospel.

Secondly, it is also the nature of hirelings that they are dark and blind in the knowledge of Christ. They recognize Him either only "according to the flesh" from Adam <note>That is, they understand Christ only as a historical human figure, rather than recognizing His divine nature.</note> and do not know from whence He comes. And because the first principle in theology <note>original: "primum principium in Teologia"</note> is not recognized, everything else is false and wrong. Thus, the little sheep cannot be led to the pasture, nor can the souls be refreshed with the heavenly water. Therefore, they cannot protect the sheep from the wolves—that is, from the heretics—who scatter the poor sheep and tear them into many parties away from the one Christ.

<margin>
The first principle in Theology.
</margin>

A hireling flees; that is, he cannot stand by them in the storm-wind. He is overturned along with the sheep—not physically, but spiritually. Namely, he leaves his listeners in uncertainty, so that they do not know what they should believe or upon whom they should rely.

A true shepherd instructs the listeners so that they have and find the witness of Jesus within them, even in the agonies of death, and so that Christ remains known to His own. Then no wolf or heretic may turn His people away from Christ; for where Christ remains, there they remain also, to which they were directed by a good preacher. But the hirelings themselves lack the witness of the Spirit, and they cannot...

And though they might remain bodily with them for the sake of their own bellies <note>A common 17th-century idiom for self-interest or financial gain.</note>, they certainly could not advise the poor, straying ones. ### 3. Little Sheep.

<margin>1.</margin>
Why are the faithful called "little soul-sheep"? First, because the Lamb of God, Christ, has redeemed them: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world" <note>original: "Ecce Agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi"</note>, etc. "The Lamb has redeemed the sheep" <note>original: "Agnus redemit Oves"</note>. The soul that You have redeemed, to her give, Lord Jesus, Your comfort.

<margin>2.</margin>
Afterward, they are also called little sheep because they follow the Lamb wherever He goes, washing their clothes in the blood of the Lamb <note>A reference to Revelation 7:14, symbolizing purification through Christ's sacrifice.</note>, and because they suffer injustice with patience, just as Christ, the patient Lamb, suffered. And finally, because the believers "taste" the pasture and perceive the Shepherd’s voice through the witness within themselves. This is the best quality of the sheep: that it can distinguish between what is good and what is evil. All believers are sealed to the extent that they can test the spirits <note>To "test the spirits" means to discern whether a teaching or impulse comes from God or another source.</note> and remain united in the holy assembly, while others, in several

<page-num>47</page-num>

several twenty sects and parties, must be divided. Such a thing is contrary to all the synagogues and "world-scholars" <note>A dismissive term for academics or theologians who rely on worldly intellect rather than spiritual experience.</note> who want to possess the Holy Spirit for themselves alone and deny the witness of Jesus—that is, the witness of the Spirit in all believers. They tell the listeners that they cannot test the spirits because they have not studied and can neither write nor read. O, you blind Pharisees! Is it the letter or the Spirit that does the work? Which is more? Christ says that all His little sheep know His voice and taste the pasture, and they may not be led astray nor scattered, for no one shall pluck them out of His hand.

<margin>9. The wolves and the high schools <note>Universities or academic institutions.</note>. 1.</margin>
Two points in this short text are well worth remembering against the wolves and hirelings, and against the high schools and world-scholars. Namely: that faithful teachers lead people to the witness of Jesus; that is, to the witness of the Spirit, where every believer has and knows as much as his preacher, and is as certain of his faith as the teacher. He finds within his soul that he is known by Christ, the Arch-Shepherd, and cannot be led astray by any man.

<margin>2.</margin>
The second point is that all simple, faithful little sheep can taste the pasture, know the voice, follow the Lamb, and test the spirits, so that they may be as certain of their faith as all teachers. This is the inner witness that surpasses everything; the inner witness overcomes the world. Even if a thousand stood against it and pointed or taught otherwise, such a little sheep could not be led astray. The desperate Pharisees deny and reject this, though everything depends upon it. They take the key of wisdom <note>A reference to Luke 11:52, where Jesus accuses religious experts of hindering others from entering heaven.</note> for themselves and yet do not enter heaven themselves.

# On the Sunday Jubilate / Gospel / John 16.
<note>Sunday Jubilate is the third Sunday after Easter, named after the Latin Introit "Jubilate Deo omnis terra" (Make a joyful noise unto God, all the earth).</note>

"A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I go to the Father." Then some of his disciples said to one another: "What is this that he says to us? 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me,' and 'that I go to the Father'?" They said: "What is this that he says, 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about." Then Jesus perceived that they wanted to ask him, and said to them: "Do you inquire among yourselves concerning this that I said, 'a little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and wail, but the world will rejoice;

but you will be sorrowful, yet your sorrow shall be turned into joy.

A woman, when she is in labor, has sorrow, for her hour has come. But when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers the anguish for the sake of the joy that a person is born into the world. And you now also have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no one shall take from you, and on that same day you will ask me nothing."

We read that there appeared in a vision to the Evangelist John a man who was like a Son of Man, girded with a golden belt, and his feet were like brass <note>original: "Messing"</note> that glows in the furnace, like pillars of fire, like a glowing ore. This man is Jesus Christ, God and Man, the Word of the Father in human nature. And that his feet were like a <term>glowing ore in the melting furnace</term><note>A "Schmelz-Ofen" or melting furnace refers to the process of refining metals; here it serves as a metaphor for the purifying power of suffering.</note> signifies that his entire life and conduct were ordained for the melting furnace of tribulation, of suffering, of the cross, and of death; and that through this melting furnace of the cross and death, he passed entirely unharmed through to the Father.

into his glory. Christ, in his assumed human nature, has redeemed us all through the Cross, suffering, and death, and has also shown thereby that all his followers must be tested in the <term>Smelting Furnace</term> <note>The "Schmelz-Ofen" or smelting furnace is a frequent metaphor in 17th-century devotional literature, representing the "refiner's fire" that purifies a soul’s faith by burning away earthly attachments.</note> of tribulation, of the Cross, and of death.

<margin>Smelting Furnace.</margin>

They shall be purified and swept clean, so that they may be found clear and pure on that day. In Daniel, chapter 3, we find a prefiguration showing that all believers shall pass through the smelting furnace of death uninjured and unharmed into life. When the three men were thrown into the glowing furnace by the king, the mighty flame of the fire could not harm them; indeed, one could not even smell the fire upon their clothes or hair. This serves as a testimony that all the <term>Newborn</term> <note>The "Newborn" (Neugebohrne) refers to those who have undergone spiritual rebirth or regeneration in the Christian tradition.</note> shall come before the face of God unharmed through the smelting furnace of tribulation and the Cross. Every soul has a twofold body: one from Adam, of the earth; the other from Christ, from heaven. The earthly body from the earth rots, decays, and becomes nothing; the worms, toads, and snakes eat it, yet it must rise for judgment. But the new body from heaven is not consumed by fire or water, just as the Apostle testifies: though our old body from the earth decays and comes to nothing, the <term>Inward Being</term> <note>The "Inward Being" (der Inwendige) refers to the spiritual self or the "inner man" described by St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 4:16.</note> is renewed daily. That is to say, the more the old body decays, is killed, and is crucified, the more the inner being is swept, purified, and renewed, and nothing may harm it. As a testimony to this, the three men in the fiery furnace of death were preserved even in their earthly bodies through the power of the inner body, which is invisible. If we were as closely related and similar to the new birth from Christ as we are similar to the outward, old man, the fire would not burn us, the water would not drown us, the sword would not cut us, and poison would not kill us, until the natural laying down of the old body—where one would reap where one had not sown. —denial and losing of oneself is a death of the **old man** <note>A Pauline concept (Romans 6:6) referring to the unregenerate human nature prone to sin.</note>, wherein one must renounce everything that hinders our access to the Father.

The first and easiest dying is when one detaches one's heart from all temporal goods and does not let the worry of food and sustenance keep one from the Kingdom of GOD. Rather than deny Christ, he would sooner let all his goods be taken from him; therefore, he does not litigate or quarrel over temporal things. When you receive temporal goods, you should not rejoice inordinately, and if temporal goods are taken, you should not be grieved. Such a person would be "dead" [to the world] and would have access to the Father. The first dying, wherein one detaches the heart from all temporal things.</margin>

Secondly, one has also "died" when he regards the world with its pleasure and joy as nothing, and when he flees all vice and sin to the highest degree. Thus he lives for GOD and has died to the sinful world; he has access to the Father. But he who has great pleasure and joy in worldly amusement, and great pain if he cannot live in **revelry** <note>original: "Sausse", meaning living in excess or riotous living.</note>, he has not yet died; he is "living dead." Thirdly, "dying" also refers to the laying aside of everything earthly, transitory, temporal, and bodily, as in death when soul and body separate from one another. There, everything that one has put on from nature in this time is stripped away, just as death is able to do. Such dying is common to both believers and unbelievers. However, the believers also cast off their **own will** as the worst hindrance; therefore, their dying is an entrance to the Father. But the godless retain their own will, and because they do not have Christ, they cannot come to the Father. Christ, by descending into the world, took upon himself human nature in the Virgin, such as sensitivity, eating, drinking, sleeping, waking, walking, standing, weeping, and speaking, exactly like any other human being. <margin>3. When everything earthly is laid aside in death. What Christ took upon Himself by descending into the world.</margin>

In this biblical context, it refers to the Holy Spirit making the world aware of its errors.</note> the world concerning three things, as was first seen in the Apostles when they were clothed with power from on high; they went out and preached repentance and the forgiveness of sins in the name of Christ. They convicted the world through the office of the Holy Spirit concerning sin, concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment.

<margin>Concerning sin: that is, concerning not believing. Rom. 14, Ephes. 2, John 3.</margin>
Concerning sin, concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment. Concerning sin: because they do not believe in Christ. Whatever does not proceed from faith or from the new birth is all sin, no matter how beautifully it may glitter <note>original: "gleisse," suggesting a deceptive outward appearance of virtue.</note>. Nothing is sin except for not believing in Christ—this unbelief from which all vices come, just as all good comes from faith. For the faith that brings salvation is God’s work within a person; through faith, a person has fallen away from themselves and become God’s own in Christ. Therefore, the newborn child <note>Refers to the "new creature" or the person reborn in Christ.</note> cannot sin. But unbelief is a human work, where a person remains their own master and walks according to the old creature, which is condemned to death. From this old creature nothing good proceeds; therefore, not believing is the greatest sin, which the Holy Spirit convicts and testifies to through the Apostles.

<margin>Concerning righteousness.</margin>
Thereafter, concerning righteousness: that Christ must go to the Father, moving from the state of his humiliation to the state of glory, where he can no longer be seen with mortal eyes. Only through Christ's death are we righteous by grace through faith, and we are a new creature; in the old birth, we are unrighteous and condemned.

<margin>Concerning judgment.</margin>
The Holy Spirit also convicts the world concerning judgment: that the prince of this world is judged. The whole world lies in wickedness under the devil; now the devil is bound with chains of darkness and is judged, only waiting to be cast into the abyss with the damned after the final judgment is held. If you cling to the world, then you are also already judged. Thus, in every believer dwells the Spirit of Christ, convicting unbelief so that it—

---

<page-num>63</page-num>
### Cantate Sunday.
<meta>catchword: we</meta>

—may be seen as the greatest sin; when one wants to be their own master and not remain God’s in Christ, that is the greatest evil. Likewise, that no righteousness is to be found except in Christ alone, who went to the Father for us; it cost him his life and earned for us eternal life, and he now sits at the right hand of the Father, etc. The Spirit also convicts us concerning judgment, so that we must confess: if we make ourselves equal to the world and wish to live according to worldly lusts, we would be already judged and bound, just as the devil is judged and bound. In short, the Holy Spirit convicts all people so that they might recognize and accept Christ. But those who give this Spirit no room or place can neither accept Christ nor understand the reason why the "second creation" through the Son is necessary. Such people remain servants and must be condemned.

3. Thirdly, that no one may understand Christ without the Spirit of God, nor read books with true understanding. "I have much more to say to you, but you cannot bear it now; but when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth."

<margin>1 John 2.</margin>
This is certain: we must be taught by the Holy Spirit, by the anointing <term>anointing: "Salbung," a reference to the inner teaching of the Spirit mentioned in 1 John 2:27.</term> within us; otherwise, everything that is taught or written outwardly is in vain. We must all be taught by God; knowledge must gush forth from the inside into the manifestation <note>original: "Gegenwurff," a term often used in mystical theology to describe the outward reflection or objectification of an internal reality.</note>, and not be carried into us from a book. For the latter does not hold up. We see well what those achieve in theology who deny the inner witness of the Holy Spirit in everyone, or who only want the "learned ones" to have the Holy Spirit, while the simple-hearted are expected to believe based on fine persuasion. It is the worst kind of seduction when the greatest thing is denied; it is like poking out someone’s eye and trying to persuade them that they should see with other people's eyes. Christ wants to give the Holy Spirit not only to the disciples, but to all believers.

There are indeed three kinds of worshippers; the **Beginners** pray with the mouth / and also to some extent with the heart / who often do not know what they are praying for: As some sick people pray for health / some poor people pray for wealth / and do not know / that they often pray for their own damnation / such worshippers often fall into great sin / and hinder their own prayer.

...has [fore]seen <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's thought about God's omniscience.</note> what has happened and what we need before we were even born. From this, it follows that you must not say your prayer as if God needed your storytelling, or as if God had to be woken up by your shouting. He has never slept; rather, you have fallen asleep through sin and blindness. You must wake up again through your persistent prayer. Oh, how many thousands of people there are who think nothing else but that God does not know it beforehand until they tell him first! But whoever takes this meditation to heart and confirms it with other testimonies of Scripture will come out of this darkness and blindness, so that he may know that God does not need our prayer. For Christ does not need anyone to ask him; rather, we need to do so, to cheer ourselves up and also to see how God is knowing of all things.

Secondly, although some confess that God indeed knows these things, they still hold the view that it matters little whether one prays or not; if God wants to give it, he will surely do so without prayer. Against such an obstacle, resolve to consider that God does not only see and know everything, but that he also commands that one should pray, giving a certain promise and assurance. As in Luke 18, Christ testifies that one should pray without ceasing, and in this text: "Truly I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name." "Ask, that your joy may be full." God commands such things, not because he needs our prayer or that he gains anything from it, but for our own use and benefit he drives us to prayer and promises us a certain hearing. Therefore, he is much more ready to give than we are to ask; indeed, he anticipates us with his gifts, and through prayer we become aware that this is so. Therefore, if one does not pray, one acts against the commandment of God and punishes oneself.

<margin>3.</margin>Thirdly, even if we recognize that God knows everything beforehand and that it is a commandment that one should pray, an obstacle sometimes arises where we think: such a commandment does not apply to all people; perhaps only some are chosen and some are not, and we are perhaps not part of the 

<column-break/>

predestined <note>original: "præstinirten"</note> crowd. Against such an obstacle, one should think: Now I know that God is no respecter of persons; <margin>Acts 10.</margin> He is minded the same toward everyone; he created them all equally; he sent Christ his Son for the whole world; he has given of his Spirit to us all.

<margin>4.</margin>Fourthly, another great obstacle follows that occurs to us: "Yes, it is all true, but I am a great sinner; if I were as holy and righteous as others, I would pray boldly." But one must neither pray based on one's own worthiness and piety, nor should one postpone prayer because of past sins, for both would be great sins. Thus, speak with David: Though there be many sins among us, with <margin>Ps. 139. <note>The text quoted here is actually from Martin Luther's hymn based on Psalm 130, not 139.</note></margin> God there is much more grace; his hand to help has no limit, however great the damage may be, etc. Where sin is powerful, there <margin>Rom. 5.</margin> God's grace is even more powerful. For it would be a blasphemy against the Son of God to act as if he had not done enough for the sins of the whole world, as if he were not the Lamb of God. He came for the sake of sinners and not for the righteous who do not need repentance. So that no one should pray for the sake of their own worthiness or piety, speak thus: With you, nothing counts <margin>Ps. 139.</margin> but grace and favor to forgive sin; it is in vain with our doing, even in the best life. All saints must say: "Forgive us <unclear>o</unclear>ur debt, LORD, do not enter into judgment with your servant."

<margin>5.</margin>Fifthly, one must also consider in what place and at what time one should pray, so that one does not think God hears at one time sooner than another, or that one place is closer to God than another. All places are one place before God, all times one time, and God is not bound to a place or time. He is in eternity and helps in an instant. However, the fact that we choose a heavenly place and a certain time happens for our own sake, so that we are less hindered. When you want to pray, go into your little chamber. <note>A reference to Matthew 6:6 regarding private prayer.</note>

->II.<-

<margin>Matthew 6.</margin> After this, let your **Lord's Prayer** <note>original: "Vater Unser"</note> follow, and then go about your **vocation**. But someone might say: "Should I contemplate so many things every morning and evening? It would require much time, and I would neglect my work; I will leave such things to the preachers." **Answer:** initially, it might require about an hour before one has put it into practice, but after diligent practice, it goes quickly. If we wish to be Christians, we must certainly venture something for it and seek the same through prayer. A Christian does not regret spending time on it. This is so that it may be understood how all good things are contained within the **seven petitions**, and that God anticipates us with His gifts before we even pray; and that Christ commanded and gave us this prayer to awaken us to these things, to see how God anticipates all people—both evil and good—with the sun, with daily bread, and with His kingdom. Yet, no one would notice, find, or rightly enjoy the gifts of God if he did not pray for them. That it may be understood, I say, how we must and should pray for that which God has already given us; it is also necessary that for some time one contemplates each petition individually, and especially one must acknowledge that everything was given before we even asked.

# Our Father, who art in heaven:

God is already a Father to all believers; but if you do not remind yourself through diligent prayer, you are not a child of God, but only a servant who does not belong in heaven. God is indeed his Creator, as He is of other creatures, but He is not his Father. Those who pray, however, are children of God in Christ, and God is their Father; they call out **"Abba, dear Father"** <note>original: "Abba lieber Vater"</note> through the Spirit of Christ. See, whoever neglects prayer does not know the **Trinity**: the Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father, through the Holy Spirit.

# Hallowed be Thy name.

This is also already present, for God's name is and remains holy even if you had never been born. But that it may now also be holy *to you*—that is, that it not be profaned in you—you pray for that which is already there. God has no name; He Himself is the name. To this belongs **praying in Christ's name**, which does not mean that I merely carry the name of Jesus in my mouth <note>The original German "Maul" is a blunt, almost derogatory term for a mouth, often used for animals, suggesting a hollow or disrespectful recitation.</note> and imagine that I pray in His name while I persist in sin. Christ is also the name itself, and His name is called **Amen** <note>original: "אמן Amen"</note>. Revelation 3, Isaiah 65. And according to the **Jewish Kabbalah** <note>The author refers to a traditional Jewish interpretation where the letters of "Amen" (A-M-N) stand for the phrase "El Melech Ne'eman," meaning "God is a faithful King."</note>, **Amen** means as much as: "The Lord is a truthful King." To pray in the name of Christ is to pray in His Spirit, to walk in His life, so that we remain in Christ and He in us; then one will pray in His name. For one then has daily repentance and sorrow over one's sin and blindness. Oh, how many there are who carry the name of Christ in their mouths and speak the Lord's Prayer, just as two once presumed to use the name of Christ over a possessed man and said: "I tell you in the name of Jesus Christ, come out!" Then the devil answered: "Jesus I know well, and Paul I know well, but who are you?" and he leaped upon them and wounded them. <margin>Acts 19.</margin> Matthew 7: Many will say, "Lord, have we not prophesied and preached in your name, etc.?" Then Christ will say: "I do not know you; depart from me." Therefore, praying in Christ's name means walking, living, and praying through true repentance in faith.

Whoever does not pray "Hallowed be Thy name" falls into the blasphemy of God's name and makes unholy that which always remains holy; but he who prays guards himself against such profanation.

# Thy kingdom come.

God's kingdom is already here; "it is within you," Christ said to the Pharisees in Luke 17. And it comes without our prayer, but it would not come *to us*—that is, we would not enter into it—as it is with us, if we...

...refuse to pray / just as if we do not seek or knock through prayer / we ask for that which we already have / the Kingdom of God is already here / the Holy Spirit is already here / yet we must still pray for it (as is testified in the little book *On Sursum Corda* <note>Latin: *Sursum Corda* means "Lift up your hearts," a reference to an ancient liturgical preface; the author is likely referring to one of his own devotional treatises</note>) so that we also enter into friendship with God and do not lose that which has been given to us.

## Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.

God’s will certainly happens even without our prayer / and has happened before we ask and before we were born / but what does it help me / if God’s will does not also happen in me / so that I am taken out of myself and surrendered to God / so that I remain not my own / but God’s. He who does not pray "thy will be done" lives for the day according to his own will and journeys toward damnation / and such a person cannot be helped. But he who prays, confesses that the will which is in him is not his own / but God’s. God has become the Will within him; man had become a thief of that will / therefore he should pray: "Lord, break my will, and let Thy will be done in me."

## Give us this day our daily bread.

This is also already provided before we pray / God gives daily bread to both the evil and the good / and no one can earn anything through their prayer / it is all poured out from grace in abundance upon the world. If we humans did not have daily bread before we had it through our praying / we would have died of hunger long ago.

Those who know how to pray "our daily bread" learn to recognize that God anticipates us with His gifts / and they receive it from His gentle hand / not for excess / but only for bare necessity / be it food, drink, or clothing / with gratitude. But those who do not pray "our daily bread" also do not recognize that it comes from God / they credit it to themselves / saying—

<column-break/>

<page-num>73</page-num>
<header>Sunday of Vocem Jucunditatis <note>Latin: "The Voice of Joy," the traditional name for the fifth Sunday after Easter, emphasizing the joy of the Resurrection and the power of prayer.</note></header>
<sig>[E]</sig>
<meta>catchword: At</meta>

—that these ten bones or fingers of ours <note>A metaphorical way of saying "our own hard work" or "the labor of our hands"</note> have brought it about. They cannot use it rightly, either. Wealth and poverty are both "daily bread" / whoever can truly pray in the name of Christ for our daily bread / he can also use both rightly. Christians do not ask for earthly things / but first they seek the Kingdom of God / the rest will be thrown to them <note>A reference to Matthew 6:33: "Seek first the kingdom of God... and all these things shall be added unto you."</note>. For they well know that it is not fitting to be anxious about an old pair of boots, clothes, shoes, food, or drink / God gives it to everyone alone / let one seek His Kingdom first.

## And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

Here too, God anticipates us with His mercy / with His gracious forgiveness / for through Christ’s death the sin of the whole world is taken away. What does it help me, if I do not become a partaker of it and remain so / namely through prayer in faith? If I do not also forgive my neighbor as a testimony / then I am also not a partaker of Divine forgiveness. But if I pray "forgive us our debts" / as we—and I—also forgive my neighbor / then I have the absolution in me and with me. God anticipates everyone / and such a petition is therefore ordained and commanded by Christ for me to pray: "forgive us our debts" / so that we are testified in our conscience, in the Holy Spirit / that God has accepted us out of grace in Christ Jesus as His children into His Kingdom and forgiven us all sin. Just as the forgiveness of sins is there, and yet no one finds it unless he also prays for it and forgives his neighbor / so it is also with the other petitions: "lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." A detailed explanation of the seven petitions can be found in the *Little Book on Prayer*.

Such "good intentions" killed all the prophets in the Old Testament, as well as Christ and His Apostles, and continue to do so until the Last Day. Look at Israel: was it not persecuted by the Egyptians and hated for God’s sake?

Later, this same people became rogues against God themselves and strangled all the prophets out of "divine zeal" and "good intentions." Their children afterward realized that their fathers had wronged the pious prophets; they decorated the prophets' graves and said: "If we had lived at that time, we would not have treated the dear prophets so poorly."

Furthermore, it came to Christ Himself, whom they killed as a deceiver. Finally, the world realized that He had been wronged and made pilgrimages to the Holy Sepulcher. They did the same to all the Apostles, strangling them for Christ’s sake out of "good intentions." Finally, this blind world realized that these Apostles had been wronged; they scolded their ancestors and said: "O, if we had lived then, we would not have acted so." Then the world ran to their graves and had compassion.

And as often as God awakens people who preach of the **new birth**—that is, of Christ—they must be hated, driven out, and killed. All of this is done out of "good intentions," which comes from a lack of faith, because they do not know Christ. If a prophet or apostle were to come now, they would be treated worse than those of old, regardless of the fact that we all cry out that our teaching is pure and clear and is the Apostolic Scripture. We pray every day, **thy kingdom come,** and yet understand little of what God’s kingdom is, or where it is. Many think it is to be sought and found somewhere outside of themselves, in certain places; and yet it is within us, otherwise the prayer would be in vain: **Thy kingdom come.** Were God’s kingdom not in us, we could never enter into it. If God did not first recognize us, we could never learn to recognize Him; if God did not first love us, we could never love God: **He even precedes us with all his gifts.** <note>Theologians call this "prevenient grace"—the idea that God's grace moves toward humans before they can even think to seek Him.</note> Thus He also precedes us with His kingdom, and bids us pray for it, so that we might also enter in and find it within ourselves. The Holy Spirit is already in us, yet we must still pray to God for the Holy Spirit; our daily bread is already there, and is even given to all evil people, yet the devout must pray for it. It is a seductive business when people think to fetch the Kingdom of God from the outside, out of the sacraments <note>The author is likely critiquing a "mechanical" view of the sacraments, arguing that the spiritual reality must be internal rather than just an external ritual.</note>.

Now, God Himself is love, and is Himself the Holy Spirit in us; He precedes us with His love, while we were yet His enemies, so that we might be awakened by His sweet love to love Him in return.

Do not let yourselves be seduced, you simple ones, into wanting to find God’s kingdom here or there with the Anti-Christ. It is within you. He certainly dwells in heaven, but He also dwells in us through His Spirit. God would gladly dwell, govern, and rule in us, if we would only grant Him such. Let everyone see to it, so that through unbelief he is not a dwelling of the devil, but rather a temple of God.

obedient, hungry, and poor hearts are God’s dwelling, even here in this time <note>meaning during our earthly lives</note>; thus God has His kingdom and dominion in the believers, for they are born of God. <margin>The ungodly <note>original: "Impio"</note> does not keep my word, etc.</margin>
<margin>1.</margin>
On the other hand, it must remain difficult and impossible for the one who does not love, as Christ says: "But whoever does not love me does not keep my words," etc. For the one who does not love does not allow the infused Spirit to break forth, and wishes to be no dwelling or temple of God, but rather of the evil spirit.

<margin>2.</margin>
Secondly, he is not born of God, but of the **Old Adam**, <note>A theological term referring to the fallen, sinful nature of humanity inherited from the biblical first man.</note> for whom it remains difficult and impossible.

<margin>3.</margin>
Thirdly, Christ does not dwell in him with His flesh and blood, and such a person does not eat and drink His flesh and blood; therefore, he cannot keep the commandments of God. <note>This likely refers to both the physical Sacrament of the Altar and a spiritual internalizing of Christ's life.</note>

<margin>4.</margin>
Fourthly, he remains his own master, of his own will and mind, and lacks the peace of Christ; he has no rest, and therefore the kingdom of God must remain impossible for such a person.

Finally, how one may come to such sweet and easy commandments of God, find the kingdom of God within oneself, and taste the peace of Christ. It often happens when we hear of God’s commandments—how they are sweet and easy—that we say: "Yes, it may well be so, and God’s kingdom may well be in me, but how do I reach the point that I also experience it, and that God’s gifts become sweet to me?" Truly, we cannot learn this of ourselves, nor can we obtain it by hearsay, nor are we able to read it out of books; otherwise, the scholars <note>original: "Schriftgelehrten," literally "those learned in the Scriptures" or Scribes</note> would have it best, and the unlearned worst. But hear how we may come to it, so that we also recognize the kingdom of God in us; we wish to set down three means for the beginning Christians, through which they may come to the inward treasure.

<margin>How we come to the kingdom of God.</margin>
<margin>1.</margin>
The first is teaching or instruction.

<margin>2.</margin>
The second is prayer.

It contrasts this with the "Old Adam" or the ungodly person, who finds the commandments impossible because they rely on their own will rather than the indwelling Christ.</summary>

<margin>3.</margin> The third is obedience or yieldedness <note>original: "Gelassenheit" — a key term in German mysticism referring to a state of letting go of self-will to be receptive to God</note>, and we take this from the text: **The Holy Spirit will teach you all things and remind you of everything that I have said to you.**

Secondly, **I go away and come back to you, so that one might pray: Thy kingdom come.**

Thirdly, **so that the world may recognize that I love the Father, and thus do as the Father has commanded me.**

First, you should let yourself be taught by the Spirit. If you cannot do this yet, then look for faithful guides who will lead you to the foundation. Let yourself be instructed in the most necessary parts of the faith; during such a report, the internal teacher <note>The Holy Spirit acting within the soul</note> must be present. He must do the best work, and He will teach us everything necessary for salvation [Seeligkeit] without any error. After that, learn to pray, seek, and knock: "Thy kingdom come." Pray also: "Ah LORD, Your kingdom is in me and has come into me; wake me up, so that I also may enter into it and learn to find it, and could taste the peace of Christ." For Christ goes from us, out of the state of His cross, and comes back to us in the heavenly essence, in the state of His glory.

But where Christ comes, there truly is God’s kingdom and all heavenly goods.

Thirdly, after your inward prayer, give yourself often into a silence <note>original: "Silentium"</note>; celebrate God and keep the Sabbath <note>Here meaning a spiritual rest or cessation of one's own works</note>. Let God possess you entirely, from within and without. Come into a forgetting of yourself, so that God finds place and <margin>Psalm 119.</margin> room to work and to enlighten you. There you will come from day to day to such a light that you will surpass all your teachers. There, God’s commandments will become sweeter to you than honey and the honeycomb. You will taste the kingdom of God within you, for there are two kinds of sweetness: a human sweetness and a Divine one.

---

<page-num>89</page-num>
<header>Pentecost.</header>
<sig>(m) On</sig>

<margin>Sweetness. Human. Divine.</margin> The human sweetness is active and creaturely, arising from reading, hearing, and praying, but it does not last long and has no roots. The Divine sweetness is passive <note>original: "leidlich" — in this context, it refers to the soul being acted upon by God rather than being active itself</note>, where a person waits for God in a stillness and, like David, hears what the Lord speaks within him. This brings forth roots and eternal power, and is a superhuman sweetness that one can never forget. In this way, one might become an inward person <note>original: "inwendiger Mensch"</note> and learn all things in the school of God without effort or toil, which Tauler <note>Johannes Tauler (c. 1300–1361), a famous Dominican mystic whose sermons emphasized the "birth of God in the soul"</note> used to treat in almost all his sermons. Is it not, however, without work or toil, when I alone in a quiet Sabbath come to the kingdom of God, to wait and listen to what God Himself works in me? It is an excellent thing that He commands us the very easiest and most lovely things; it is even greater that He Himself wants to do and work within us, provided only that we hold still for Him in a yielded serenity <margin>Yielded serenity.</margin> <note>original: "gelassenen Gelassenheit"</note>. God gives us beforehand what we ask for, and He anticipates us; afterward He tells us to pray for it, and then He tells us to seek it; for He has laid it down for us and tells us to knock. <margin>Matthew 7. John 3.</margin> God commands us to love; we should love Him and our neighbor. And that which He commands is He Himself; God is love, and He Himself wants to work that love within us, if only we could be silent, celebrate, and pause. We could not love God if He did not first love us; we could not know God if He did not first know us; we could not come into His kingdom if it were not first within us to be entered. To find such things belongs to the Sabbath, the silence <note>original: "Silentium"</note>, and the day of rest. All commandments are framed as prohibitions—that is, all works are forbidden to man—only the Sabbath is commanded, and also framed as a positive commandment: "You shall hallow the holy day." Man was made for the sake of the Sabbath <note>original: "Homo factus propter Sabbatum"</note>, so that God may find room to work Himself and to complete in man what HE has commanded.

<vocab>Yieldedness [Gelassenheit]: a state of humble surrendering of the will to God. Silence [Silentium]: intentional spiritual stillness. Sabbath: here used as a metaphor for the soul resting from its own efforts to allow God to act. Tauler: Johannes Tauler, a medieval mystic. Inward person: the spiritual self that communicates directly with the Divine. Pentecost: the feast celebrating the descent of the Holy Spirit. Salvation [Seeligkeit]: the state of spiritual blessedness.</vocab>

The author emphasizes that God's commandments are fulfilled by God Himself within the believer once they cease their own striving.</summary>

# On Whit Monday / Gospel / John 3.

Jesus spoke to Nicodemus: For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, so that all who believe in him should not perish, but have eternal life. <margin>Pillar of Cloud.</margin>In the ancient figure <note>A "figure" is an Old Testament event or object seen as a symbolic preview of New Testament truths.</note> of the Jews, there was a pillar of cloud by day at the Tabernacle, and a pillar of fire by night. When it rose, Israel moved forward by day; but when the pillar settled down, the people had to camp. They had to direct their moving and camping at all times according to the pillar of cloud; no one dared to set out before it.

<margin>Application.</margin>Thus, Christ, God and man, is our goal and predecessor; we should follow him and not run ahead of him as thieves and murderers. That is, preachers should not baptize before they are called by God, and should not preach before they are appointed <note>original: "gedinget," meaning hired or formally engaged for a task</note>; one should turn inward and first wait for the calling, and not run before the rising of the sun. That is, we should not preach unless we are taught and driven from within by the Spirit of Christ. *Those who are led by the Spirit of God, not those who lead [themselves], these are the true preachers.* <note>original Latin: "Qui aguntur Spiritu Dei, non qui agunt"</note>

Therefore, rebirth from above is now necessary; and whoever is not born again from above cannot see the Kingdom of God, let alone enter into it. Flesh and blood according to Adam may not possess the Kingdom of God; it belongs to death and remains in death. But the flesh that comes from above, out of Heaven—that alone enters into Heaven.

Now, two men come together here: one born of the earth through the seed of man, and the other from Heaven, not of the seed of man or of the flesh, but of the Holy Spirit alone. Namely, Nicodemus and Christ. These two converse with one another regarding the new creature, the rebirth, and the creation—each speaking of his own. Nicodemus speaks of the earth, for he is earthly, of flesh and blood, from the masculine seed. Christ speaks of Heaven as a Creator of the new creature, of the new heaven, and the new earth. Each defends his own and testifies to what he knows and hears. Nicodemus comes with good intentions and a desire for salvation, thinking he can enter Heaven with his old earthly body. Christ is to instruct him on how he might enter the Kingdom of God with spirit, soul, and body—specifically, not with the body of the old birth from the seed of man.

**born again** if he wishes to understand my speech and enter into eternal life. Nicodemus did not understand such a second birth from above. He imagined that the new birth, or second birth, proceeded from the body of Adam, from the earth—as if Adam's flesh and blood had to be born anew, and as if Adam's flesh entered into Heaven. *How can a man, when he is old, enter again into his mother's womb and be born?* He understood the second birth as coming from his mother and father, from flesh and blood, which is nonetheless subject to death and damnation and cannot enter into Heaven.

Whoever wishes to come into the Kingdom of God must not pay heed to his earthly father and mother—be it Adam, Abraham, Noah, Daniel, or Solomon—it is all nothing. This new birth requires another mother and another father. It is impossible for a natural man, through his own light, reason, or skill, to know or believe that he should take another body upon himself.

From these parents, we must be born from above with flesh and blood. Water is the mother and the Spirit is the father, just as Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit in flesh and blood within the Virgin Mary and born a Child of God; so also are all believers born of the Holy Spirit in the water with new heavenly flesh and blood, and can never die,

This is taken in bread and wine by believers in remembrance. No one goes to heaven except He who has come from heaven, namely the Son of Man, who is in heaven.

We wish, however, to consider several lessons from this text, and specifically:
<margin>1.</margin> First, that short-lived worldly pleasure and joy inherit eternal agony and martyrdom; whereas, in contrast, short-lived tribulation and poverty in Christ inherit eternal joy and delight.
<margin>2.</margin> Second, where we go after our death; namely, whether one be evil or good, each comes into his appointed <term>dwelling-place</term> <note>original: "Behältniß"; referring to the intermediate state or "receptacle" of the soul before the final judgment</note>, and why a period of waiting is to be believed.

<margin>4.</margin> Fourth, that everyone’s works follow them in death, and one is plagued by that in which he sought his pleasure.
<margin>5.</margin> Fifth, concerning the place of salvation and damnation, and the gulf between them.

And to the first: that all joy, pleasure, and delight of this world is small and brief, and that without any doubt, infinite agony and the martyrdom of hell follow it; whereas, in contrast, the cross, tribulation, and poverty of the believers is very brief and slight in this world, and that without any doubt, comfort and infinite joy follow it. <margin>Converting oneself.</margin>
He continued in this way until his time came to die. Then he began to "convert himself" (as all the world does), making his own repentance. He sent for his priest, confessed to him, and received from him the forgiveness of sins; for he believed the priest sat in God's place. He then took the <term>Sacrament</term> <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>, believing it blotted out all his sins. He had a Psalter read; the priest comforted him. He said: "Yes, he believes." And all these were human works, undertaken by human strength, for there was no true <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "Reu noch Leid"; literally "remorse nor sorrow." In this context, the author is critiquing an outward ritual that lacks internal change</note> or sorrow for his evil life. One would have seen this clearly had he recovered from his illness—what a human "repentance" or devilish "conversion" it would have been! For he would have lived exactly as before (if it had not become even worse). God will not stand still for someone who lives in sin and refuses to feel remorse or repent, only wanting to be converted by a priest during his illness. Let such a person watch where he is going; he is not in earnest. If he were healthy, he would be worse than before.

Now this rich man died and was buried. As he had lived, so he died. He lived honorably and praised before the world; thus, he died honorably and celebrated before the world. For he had confessed, received the Sacrament, and the priest had stayed with him, constantly shouting to him that he must believe. He was buried, and the funeral was just like his life—namely, laudable and glorious. An "honest ringing" of bells was ordered, for he could pay much money; they had to ring three pulses with all the bells. The whole city accompanied him, many priests were summoned, and the Bishop himself gave a funeral sermon. He praised him, saying what an honorable man he had been, how he had often used the Holy Sacrament in his life and taken it again in his hour of death, and thus passed away not alone, but in the presence of priests. # Gospel on the first

...not worthy of the glory which shall be revealed in you after a short time; only believe in Christ; he cannot lie.

### II.

Secondly, we learn from this text where we go after our temporal departure from this world. Namely, whether one be a believer or an unbeliever, each comes into his appointed <term>abode</term> <note>original: "Behältniß"; a place of keeping or a receptacle where the soul waits</note> and waits there for the Last Day. For it is certain that the blessed do not immediately fly from the mouth up to heaven, nor the damned into hell; rather, they go into death and darkness, pain and torment, which is a beginning of the second death. Afterward, death and hell will be thrown into the fiery lake that burns with sulfur, and that will be the eternal death and the eternal hell. Christ testifies to this with the rich man and Lazarus, who both, after their passing, went each into his abode: the rich man into darkness, which is the first death, where there is pain, agony, and torment, and where he must wait until the Last Day.

<margin>Abraham’s Bosom is Paradise. A blessed person is in 3 parts: Spirit, Body, Soul.</margin> Lazarus went into <term>Abraham's Bosom</term> <note>A biblical expression for the place of comfort for the righteous dead before the final resurrection</note>, which is Paradise, where he also waits for the Last Day. If it were not so, then the soul of the blessed would only be in heaven—but where would the body be? And as for the soul of the damned, the devil wants both body and soul in hell. But God wants the whole human being in heaven—with spirit, body, and soul—and not just a piece of a human. When a blessed person dies in the Lord, they are divided into three parts: the spirit goes back to the Lord, the body is buried in the earth, and the soul comes into Paradise or Abraham’s Bosom.

<margin>The 3 parts of the damned.</margin> When a damned person dies like this rich man, three parts are also separated from him: the spirit travels to the Lord <note>This likely refers to the "breath of life" returning to God the Creator (Ecclesiastes 12:7), rather than the person entering heaven</note>, the body is committed to the earth with great ceremony, ringing of bells, and preaching, but the soul travels to its abode—that is, into death and darkness, wherein it shall wait for the Judgment. Whoever denies this waiting and believes the blessed fly immediately to hea—

---

<page-num>125</page-num>
<header>Sunday after Trinity.</header>
<sig>(q) 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: III.</meta>

—ven and the damned into hell, denies the <term>Article</term> <note>Referring to the specific points of the Apostles' Creed</note> of the general Resurrection of the Dead. For the creation of the Father, from Adam until the very last human, must be called forth entirely, and not one shall remain behind. We must all be made manifest before the Judgment Seat of Jesus Christ in our flesh, in which we walked upon the earth. Such a resurrection of the flesh is denied [by those other views]. Furthermore, one also offends the Article of the Last Judgment of the wicked and the good. For if all the damned were already judged and all the blessed were already in heaven, then Christ would not need to hold a judgment, nor would he need to place the damned on the left and the blessed on the right. It would also be wrong for us to believe that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead. 

And if someone wished to overturn this truth by saying: "Yes, but the remaining living people on the Last Day will still be placed on the right and the left, so Christ does not need to judge those long-dead, for they are already judged, only those survivors whom the Last Day catches"—such interpreters are also against themselves. They hold that the Last Day will break in suddenly with fire and all people will be transformed in an instant, the believers to heaven and the unbelievers to hell. Just as those who died long ago supposedly flew from the mouth into heaven or hell, so too would those on the last day. Where then would be the Resurrection of the Flesh and the Last Judgment? Where would it be that "hell and death shall be cast into the fiery lake," which is the second death? 

Therefore, to keep these two articles pure—the Resurrection of the Flesh and the Last Judgment—we will believe that there is a waiting period for the blessed and the damned, so that after the Judgment is held, body, soul, and spirit may enter heaven into the eternal Kingdom of Christ; and that the body, spirit, and soul of the damned may be cast into the abyss, which shall be the second death without end.

<margin>That there is a waiting for the blessed and the damned.</margin>

### III.

Thirdly, that the damned depart from the mouth into a state of <term>damnable unrest</term> <note>original: "verdammliche Unruhe"; a state of agitation and lack of peace</note>, and the blessed soon enter into sweet rest. Although they do not immediately go entirely into Hell, but rather into their <term>abode</term> <note>original: "Behältniß"; a place of keeping</note> as if into the dark house of shadow, their misery, heartbreak, and hellish torment begin at once. This serves as a sign that, after the Judgment is held and they are placed on the left hand, they shall be cast into Hell itself.

While the damned are in the body, they have temporal pastimes; but as soon as they depart from the body, their hellish pain begins. It is the same for all believers: although they do not immediately ascend to heaven, they nonetheless enter into Paradise and have comfort and joy there. This is a sign that, after the Judgment is held, they shall occupy the eternal Kingdom of God with Christ. That this is indeed the case—that the wicked are soon tormented and the pious soon gladdened, or that the wicked enter into unrest and the blessed into eternal rest—can be seen from this text.

<margin>The wicked are soon tormented, and the pious soon gladdened.</margin>
The rich man in Hell and in torment receives agony, suffering in this flame. And Abraham says that Lazarus is comforted, which is to say, he is in sweet rest. Upon short worldly pleasure follows unending hellish martyrdom, whether it be in the first or the second death; and upon short temporal tribulation follows unending joy, whether it be in Paradise or in Heaven itself.

### IV.

<margin>As one lived, so his works follow him.</margin>
Fourthly, that the works of every damned person follow them, and they are tormented by the very things in which they sought their delight and pleasure on earth. Whoever will not take the time in their life to keep the <term>Sabbath</term> <note>The day of rest and worship</note>, so that they might learn therein of Jesus Christ—the highest treasure—and dies entirely in <term>impenitence</term> <note>original: "Unbußfertigkeit"; the state of not feeling regret for one's sins</note>, such a person must go from one unrest into another. Just as one who consumes his life with hunting and jousting,

He who dies in drunkenness, gambling, or whoredom will be so tormented in the next world that he will still wish to practice such works. Therefore, the proud are seen as they adorn and dress themselves; the drinkers as they drink; the gamblers as they play; the warriors as they wage war; the whoremongers as they sit with harlots. And this is not all pleasure and joy, as it was here in the world, but eternal pain, unrest, and hellish martyrdom. A thief who was hanged for his theft has a gallows with him; a murderer or manslayer who was <term>broken on the wheel</term> <note>original: "geradbrecht"; a brutal historical method of execution</note> has the wheel with him; and just as each one perished for his misdeed, so with those weapons shall he come before the Judgment, and is even now thus tormented in the darkness. # On the Second Sunday after Trinity: The Gospel, Luke 14.

There was a man who prepared a great supper and invited many guests. He sent his servant at the hour of the supper to say to those who were invited: "Come, for everything is now ready." And they all, one after another, began to make excuses. The first said to him: "I have bought a field and I must go out to see it; I ask you, please excuse me." And the second said: "I have bought five yoke of oxen and I am going now to examine them; I ask you, please excuse me." And the third said: "I have taken a wife, and therefore I cannot come."

And the servant returned and told this to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant:

### Gospel on the Second | Sunday after Trinity.

(r) 2

> *Go out into the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled. For I say to you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.*

The understanding of this text is not difficult in itself; nevertheless, we wish to look, first, upon the unspeakable goodness of God, in that He Himself invites us all to His supper and also calls us through the servant—we who were invited before the foundation of the world was laid.

Secondly, let us consider with sighs the great negligence of the invited guests, who, out of love for temporal goods and external pursuits, dare to refuse the great supper. They thus make themselves so unworthy of it that they shall never taste it again. Is it not a pitiable thing that Christ’s death and suffering should be in vain and lost upon so many people?

<margin>Detachment <note>original: "Gelaſſenheit"</note>, Luke 14.</margin>
Thirdly, let us also ponder the certain judgment of God upon His invited guests: namely, that it is true that those who persist in a lack of <term>detachment</term> <note>The German "Gelaſſenheit" is a central concept in Christian mysticism, referring to the state of letting go of one's own will and worldly attachments to be fully "yielded" to God.</note> shall never come to it or taste it in eternity. And this text focuses primarily on detachment, as can be seen in the words that follow.

Therefore the Lord says: *If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters, and yes, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.* One must venture such things for the sake of the Kingdom of God—namely, to leave oneself and all things behind, and to cling to nothing,

<column-break/>

not even to ceremonies, nor to hope for salvation through the sacraments alone. Therefore, let everyone sit down and calculate, reckoning the costs involved: this and that will cost so much; so much will be required for the building of the tower; so much must he expend—namely, to renounce himself. Otherwise, he might begin to build and then be unable to finish, and thus have to abandon it in shame. It will be a similar shame before all the chosen ones, who will say on that day: "Look, this man began to build a tower and could not complete it." There was a man who prepared a great supper and invited many; and he sent out his servant at the hour of the supper to say to those invited: "Come," etc. Although this speech of Christ refers to the Jews, who were gathered before all other nations as God's own property so that they might be children of the promise and should accept Christ—those who were there in a symbolic way—† they are not out in the streets, † nor are they out on the highways like the Gentiles, who were far from Christ (as the Apostle says). Yet even if this refers to the Jews, it applies to all people in the whole world.

<margin>Ephesians 2:3.</margin>
For God desires to save not only the Jews, but also the uncircumcised Gentiles. In this, His great and immeasurable goodness is praised, for He invites us all Himself (since we are all appointed to God by God) and also sends His servant to tell us who are invited that we should all come. Everything is ready; before God, it has already been ordered and accomplished. Christ has already come and has given Himself for us.

<margin>The only lack is that we do not want to come.</margin>
The only lack is that we do not want to come. The servant who was sent out—the Word of God—comes to everyone and skips no one. If it is not through the external office of preaching, then it is certainly internal; He calls and knocks always at the door and waits until we open. He wishes to enter into us and eat the supper with us. This Word, which is in our heart and mouth of the inner man, and which also became flesh and is Christ—this same Word is preached publicly in the world.

The third group is held back from entering by **taking a wife**. That is, out of love for blood-relations and relatives, many a man does not dare to become a Christian; he does not want to be considered a **heretic** by his own people, and therefore he stays outside. Oh, how many among the great and the small, among the high and the lowly, let themselves be held back by their friends and acquaintances so that they do not come to the knowledge of Christ! They have taken a wife—that is, they love their wife so much that they even forget God for her sake. They do not wish to anger their friends or fall into the disfavor of their parents, and so they abandon the treasure in heaven. Therefore, such a man cannot excuse himself, for he has esteemed and loved men more than Christ; he will not be worthy of Him and will nevermore taste the Supper. <margin>Concerning the conversion of man. A question.</margin>
Now follows the second part regarding the conversion of man: whether he should conduct himself physically passively, or effectively actively therein. That is, whether man can convert and find himself, or whether he is converted and found by God?

->If we consider these three parables: of the lost<-

Thus all <term>Synergists <note>A term for those who believed that the human will cooperates with divine grace in the process of conversion—a view the author here rejects.</note></term> are excluded, who think to perform penance and convert themselves by free will; yet nothing comes of it, for it is only human work. <meta>This page continues the sermon on the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15). The previous page ended with a question about whether a person's conversion to God is something they do themselves (active) or something God does to them (passive).</meta>

# Page 146
## Gospel on the Fourth [Sunday after Trinity]

<margin>Man does nothing toward his own conversion.</margin>
<margin>It is not of him who wills, but of God who shows mercy. <note>original: "Non est volentis, sed miserentis Dei," a reference to Romans 9:16.</note></margin>
A human being contributes as much to his own conversion as he did to his own existence before he was even conceived in his mother's womb—which is to say, he does nothing at all. He merely suffers it to happen and remains entirely <term>passive</term> <note>Receiving an action rather than performing it.</note>, and in no way <term>active</term> <note>Taking the lead or acting by one's own power.</note>. In this way, the glory remains with God. Man should take care that he does not simply continue safely in sin; it is not up to him when he wishes to be converted. Rather, it rests solely in the mercy of God, for which he must wait with fear and trembling.

Thirdly, regarding what "near" and "far" mean in this passage: the lost son traveled away from the father into a foreign land, squandered his inheritance, began to suffer want, and had to tend the pigs. The older son stayed home with the father, yet he was also out in the field and did not want to go in to see his brother; he could not return inside because he was too attached to his own righteousness.

<margin>The older son; that is, the Jews.</margin>
A man has two sons. God chose one son for himself in the world: Israel, or the Jews. Beyond that, he is also the God of the Gentiles. The Jews were "near" and therefore "at home," according to the symbol, because they kept themselves outwardly righteous according to the Law.

<margin>The younger son; that is, the Gentiles.</margin>
The younger son represents the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people.</note>, who were without God in the world. But God loved both the Jews and the Gentiles; he also allowed the Gentiles to share in the heavenly garment and had Christ sacrificed for them. Furthermore, in another sense, every person is either a younger or older son depending on whether they are found in faith or unbelief. If one walks in faith, he is near to God and remains "young"—he cannot grow old, for the inner man cannot age, die, or decay. But if he walks according to the outer man, he is "old," for that man ages, turns gray, dies, and is furthest from his origin. Yet it says here that the younger son traveled far across the land and swallowed up his goods with harlots; this is because only the inner man possesses the inheritance, not the outer man. The younger son alone has the goods; he may squander them or keep them and increase them through trade. Likewise, only the inner man is the sinner when he falls into sin, and not the outer man.

<column-break/>

# Page 147
## Sundays after Trinity.

<margin>Concerning the wandering of the soul.</margin>
This younger son demands his inheritance and travels far across the land; that is, the soul leaves the spirit and turns toward the flesh, seeking its pleasure there. This is a "far country," away from the internal home. The fatherland is inside the soul; but when the soul turns outward toward the flesh, it becomes a stranger to God and enters a truly foreign land where the goods are not its own, and it must suffer want.

<margin>In man there are three powers.</margin>
<margin>The mind or intellect.</margin>
<margin>Reason.</margin>
<margin>Sensuality.</margin>
There are three kinds of powers within a human being. The highest power is the mind, called the <term>Mind or Intellect</term> <note>original: "Mens seu intellectus."</note>. The second power is reason, called <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "Ratio."</note>. The third power is the senses, called <term>Sensuality</term> <note>original: "Sensualitas."</note>, which is the animal power shared with other livestock. When the soul, through divine action, turns into the mind or <term>Mentem</term> <note>The Latin term for the higher mind.</note>, it is attached to Christ through faith and stays at home with the Father. If, however, it turns into reason and busies itself with worldly cleverness, it begins to deviate from its fatherland and starts to be "far off." Finally, it is furthest from the Father when it plunges into the fleshly lusts of the world. There it consumes its goods with harlots—it "prostitutes" itself with these things; that is, it seeks pleasure and joy in fleeting things and becomes entirely a stranger to God. That is the "far country" into which almost all people travel with the lost son, may it be lamented to God. Yet the Father does not stop searching for the lost son through many different ways. Blessed is he who allows himself to be found! He will no longer eat with the pigs among the animalistic people outside, but will go inside and eat the bread of heaven with joy, and be clothed with the heavenly robe, and thus walk in the life of Christ.

<summary>This page interprets the Parable of the Prodigal Son as an allegory for the human soul's internal struggle, defining conversion as a passive act of God's mercy rather than a human effort. It maps the son's journey to three psychological powers: the mind (faith), reason (worldly wisdom), and sensuality (sin).</summary>
