# Gospel on the Fourth
## Sunday after Trinity.

[He] sets before us his heavenly Father as a mirror, showing that we should be as he is: Merciful, Peaceful, Patient, Long-suffering, gladly forgiving, gladly giving, and praying for his enemies. For this is what the Father in heaven does: he is impartial, like the sun; he lets his rain fall over the grateful and the ungrateful; he lets his sun shine upon the evil and the good; he gives daily bread to believers and unbelievers alike. He does not judge, does not condemn, and forgives us all our sins. He loved us while we were still his enemies. If he were to judge and condemn us, he would have had to strike us into the earth with a thunderclap long ago. If he were to kill and condemn us, he would have had to let the earth swallow many of us, or burn us with sulfur and fire from heaven, or drown us with water, or let us die a sudden death. In summary, the kind God and Father remains kind, and a lover of humanity and all his children. That is to say, all his believers follow after the Father; they are merciful as their Father is. Likewise, the unmerciful also follow after their father by judging, sentencing, condemning, chasing away, declaring others heretics <note>original: "Verkeßern," to brand someone a heretic</note>, killing, breaking on the wheel <term>Radebrechen: a brutal execution method where a person's limbs were shattered with a heavy wagon wheel</term>, beheading, and hanging; for their father is also a murderer, just as they are. But because we, out of weakness, cannot look clearly upon this mirror in the heavenly Father, the Son of God sets himself as a mirror, a pattern, and an example, so that we might follow him and be just as he is.

How then is Christ? He is merciful toward all sinners; he binds up the wounded and heals the sick, and makes alive that which was dead. He neither judges nor sentences anyone, condemns no one, chases away nor kills anyone, but forgives sin. He sets himself as an example for us, saying: The disciple is not above his master; if the disciple is like his master, then he is perfect. This is to say: I am your Master and Lord; you believers are all my followers and disciples. From this it follows that you should judge or sentence no one, just as I do; that you should kill, behead, or hang no one, just as I do; but rather you should recognize yourselves 

<column-break/>

to all be equal brothers, and have compassion for your fellow men. You all still carry the Adamic flesh <note>Refers to the fallen human nature inherited from Adam, prone to sin</note> upon you, and should overlook one another's failings, or brotherly rebuke your neighbor for their sin, and confess your sins to one another, so that you all may be forgiven. You help up the repentant sinners and do not kill anyone, for you well know your own weakness and the blindness that still sticks within you. Therefore, let no one judge another, so that you all remain together under me and do not set yourselves above me, as the unbelievers do, who kill, behead, hang, declare heretics, burn, or chase away their fellow men. They set themselves up as judges over their fellow men; thus they are not like me, they set themselves above me. They are blind—how can one blind man show the way to another? They must both fall into the pit.

<margin>This mirror concerns all believers.</margin>
Such a mirror of the heavenly Father and of Christ is only held before the believers—those who hear this speech—and not the un-Christians <note>original: "Unchristen," people who do not follow the spirit of Christ's teachings</note>, who understand nothing of it. They can even set themselves above Christ, as their works show through judging, killing, condemning, breaking on the wheel, and chasing away. They pass judgment on the Son of God in his speech, making a gloss <note>An interpretive note, often used here to imply a self-serving or twisted explanation</note> over it, saying: "We are not allowed to kill, judge, or condemn anyone. The authorities <note>original: "Obrigkeit," referring to the secular government or magistracy</note> have the sword; they should do it and punish evil." They deliver the sinners into the hands of the authorities with a report, as if they are doing right by it, just as if Christ had placed the sword over his Church, or as if God wanted to rule his believers through the devil. If the authority is an un-Christian, then they have no business over punishment; but if they are a Christian, then they know well what they should do: namely, to remain under Christ, under faith, just as their subjects do, and not set themselves above Christ or in the place of God. Far be it from the Apostolic foundation that we should teach with the Antichrist, as if God had placed the sword over the Church, as if man could punish sin, or as if the authorities should sit in Christ's place—all of that is nothing. Christ has not placed the Pope or the sword over his...

# Gospel on the Fourth

Church is not governed by the devil; he alone remains the Head, the Master, and the LORD over his Church. All pagan, unbelieving authority is not within the Church. Therefore, it can neither judge nor pass sentence [in spiritual matters], for it lacks the Spirit of GOD. And the Christian, believing authority, because it is within the Church, must also remain under Christ, just as the subjects do.

<margin>In matters of faith, no one should be coerced.</margin>
In such cases, no one is to command another in matters of faith; no one is to coerce another; each must stand for himself, whether he be the authority or the subject, for we are all one in Christ. There are three reasons in this text why the believers should follow after the Father in heaven and on earth—that is, why they should not judge nor condemn, but rather forgive and give, acting with mercy toward all people.

The first reason is the great, insurmountable benefit or harm that comes if they do or do not do this; namely, with the same measure you use to measure, it will be measured back to you. If we are merciful toward others and forgive gladly, and give to those who ask us without hope of repayment: then we also have mercy to expect from GOD and remain partakers of God’s grace. If we do not judge or condemn our brothers on earth for the sake of anyone’s error, then GOD does not judge us either. And as we act toward one another on earth, so GOD in heaven shows himself toward us. Conversely, if someone falls from faith and acts unmercifully toward his brother—whether he be a priest or a ruler—if he judges and condemns, if he sentences, beheads, hangs, brands as a heretic <note>original: "verketzert"</note>, or drives away, he sets himself above Christ and makes himself a judge over his neighbor. This text is abused and misunderstood in four ways: First, that everyone takes such a word of Christ for himself and directs it away from himself toward another, such as: "judge not, condemn not, be merciful, first pull the beam out of your own eye, then come and pull the splinter out of mine." However wicked a person may be, he appropriates the Scripture, imagining it stands on his side alone. In response, his opponent does the same and says: "Judge not, sentence not, condemn not, forgive, first pull the beam out of your eye, then come and master <note>original: "meistern"; to lecture or act as a teacher</note> me too." Everyone can wield the Scripture like the other; thus judging, sentencing, condemning, labeling as heretics, and driving away remains always in vogue, and precisely thereby we despise ourselves because we do not listen to Christ. <page-num>160</page-num>
<header>Gospel on the Fifth [Sunday after Trinity]</header>

In this text we hear how a great multitude of people pressed toward Christ to hear the Word of GOD; for among the scribes and Pharisees, the people had heard only human doctrine <note>original: "Menschen-Lehre"; refers to legalistic traditions added by men rather than divine scripture.</note>, the **dead letter**, a sermon without sap or strength. Therefore, they followed the one who was sent by GOD and preached GOD’s Word. Afterward, we hear how Peter, at the command of Christ, casts out his net and catches a magnificent multitude of fish; for Christ was with him in the ship as the true Light, as the Day. Whoever does not have Christ with them must fish in the night in vain.

Peter and his companions also recognize that such an unusual catch of fish was not accomplished by his own ability, but was a blessing from GOD. He thus attributes everything to Christ (as is right) and recognizes his own inability and unworthiness. Finally, James, John, and Peter are called to the **spiritual fishing trip**; they leave their nets and their father in the ship and follow Christ, thus becoming <term>fishers of men</term> <note>original: "Menschenfaher"; a reference to Jesus' promise to make his disciples "fishers of men" who gather souls instead of fish.</note>.

<margin>1.</margin>
In the first part, we have an admonition regarding the nature and quality of the **living Word**: what kind of listeners it has, and how it draws all those who so dearly wish to be saved, even though the majority of the listeners may be of a different mind.

<margin>2.</margin>
In the second, we have a teaching that all our doing is fruitless and in vain where Christ is not with us in the ship—where He is not found with us and in us, in our soul. ->### III.<-

Thirdly, when we grasp and feel God’s blessing in our labor, to whom should we attribute it but to Him alone, who works, makes, and gives all things? Should we keep it only for ourselves? That would be against the love of our neighbor. We should beckon to our fellow men and let others also enjoy God’s blessing. They caught a great multitude of fish, so that their net began to break; and they signaled to their partners to come and help them pull, and they came and filled both ships so full that they began to sink. When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus' knees and said: "Lord, depart from me, for I am a sinful man," for terror and fear had come over him and all who were with him at this catch of fish.

<margin>How one should apply wealth.</margin>
There are some people who, when wealth suddenly falls to them—perhaps from mining, the fruits of the field, or livestock—recognize to some extent that God has given it. However, their hearts do not cling to the Giver; instead, they invest their goods poorly in grand buildings, fine clothing, improper food, and pride. Such people overload their "ships" so that they must sink; they can no longer lift their hearts to God in heaven as they might have done in poverty. They are so burdened with temporal goods that they sink to the earth or fall into fleshly lusts, much like Peter's ship, laden with fish, began to sink into the sea. But Peter and his companions give us a fine lesson in how we should behave when God shares temporal gifts with us: namely, we should fall down before God

<sig>(v) 2</sig>

[...]ly piety according to the flesh; one must have a better piety or righteousness, namely, that of the Spirit, of the inner person through faith. But so that we may rightly understand Christ's meaning regarding these two types of righteousness, we must carefully note and consider what Pharisaic righteousness is, what it is called, and where it comes from. Then, we must consider what the "better" righteousness is and where it comes from. **Unless your righteousness is better than that of the Pharisees and scribes, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.** This is to say: the Jews and Pharisees present themselves as outwardly pious before men according to the Law, so that no man can find fault with them—living blamelessly—but inwardly in their hearts they are full of impurity and sin, which they refuse to acknowledge.

If you wish to enter the kingdom of GOD, you must have a better righteousness; for behold, you must have a purified heart and strive to be right before GOD in your conscience. Now, what is the righteousness of the Pharisees? It is an outward discipline and piety according to the old, outward man, forced by the Law, and is called <margin>Righteousness of the flesh. <note>original: "Justitia carnis"</note></margin> **Righteousness of the flesh**, a civic discipline and respectability, through which one expects to stand even before GOD—yet it cannot be. For GOD and his Christ have nothing to do with the outward man. Pharisaic righteousness is practiced and undertaken out of fear of punishment or hope of reward, and both of these displease GOD. For being pious out of fear of punishment belongs to servants, and not to children. All those who are pious out of fear of punishment, and guard themselves against outward deeds while still having the will and heart to do such evil, are servants; they belong in the Old Testament under Moses, and not in the New under Christ. They have no reward to expect from GOD. Worldly piety or Pharisaic righteousness comes from human strength, such that one outwardly refrains from murder, adul-

<column-break/>

tery, theft, usury, gluttony, or drunkenness according to the Law. If someone falls into an outward deed, we are there, wanting to punish the evil—hanging the thief, beheading the adulterer, killing the sinner—and we do not consider that we ourselves are guilty of all that for which we wish to judge our neighbor.

For it is not the body that is the sinner or the doer, but the inward man. And that is Pharisaic righteousness: when we force ourselves outwardly to piety out of fear of punishment or the world’s shame, but inwardly before GOD we are guilty of eternal damnation. But the righteousness of the Spirit and the inner man is the <margin>Righteousness of the Spirit. <note>original: "Justitia Spiritus"</note></margin> righteousness of which Christ speaks here, where one is reconciled through the death of Christ by grace and has peace with GOD the Father; <margin>Romans 5.</margin> where the heart is purified and sanctified through faith. There, one is obedient to the Law not out of fear of punishment or out of shame before men, but out of love without any compulsion. Even if no punishment or Law were given, all believers would still be obedient, even without hope of reward. For in the New Testament there are no day laborers, but children in the kingdom; that is, believers do not serve GOD for reward or out of fear of punishment, but do all things freely out of love. And if someone should perhaps be overtaken and fall into a sin, such as adultery or theft, the believers are there to heal the wounded and make the dead live again; for they well know that GOD does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he be converted in the body for the sake of the sins. For the body has not sinned, but the inner man has sinned; GOD Himself punishes that person with eternal damnation unless he is taken up through Christ's death. But He wishes to receive all sinners who simply convert through true repentance in faith. Therefore, there is a magnificent distinction between worldly piety (or Pharisaic righteousness) and Divine righteousness (or inward piety).

<header>Gospel on the sixth [Sunday after Trinity]</header>

1. That [Pharisaic] righteousness comes from the Law according to the letter.
2. It is according to the outward man in the sight of people.
3. It is according to the Old Testament under Moses.
4. It is undertaken and practiced out of human strengths.
5. It is done when one wishes to earn something, or at least intends to avoid physical punishment before the world.

->But spiritual righteousness<-

1. Flows from the Spirit and is practiced
2. According to the inner man before God in a pure conscience.
3. According to the nature of the New Testament under Christ.
4. Not out of one's own strengths, but through the ability that God provides.
5. Not out of hope for reward or fear of punishment, but out of voluntary love.

As far as heaven and earth are from each other, so far also is [true] righteousness from worldly piety. The Law only makes one worldly-pious out of fear of punishment, but faith makes one pious out of the fear of love <note>The "fear of love" refers to a reverent, filial devotion where one fears grieving the beloved (God) rather than fearing a penalty.</note>. It was said to the ancients, "You shall not kill"; but I say to you, whoever is angry, whoever says <term>Racha <note>original: "Racha." An Aramaic term of contempt meaning "empty-headed" or "worthless."</note></term>, whoever says "Fool," is guilty of damnation. The ancients in the Old Testament understood everything physically and literally; they believed it was enough if one abstained from outward murder, even while having anger and hatred in the heart, which men could not judge. But God, who looks upon the heart, is a judge of thoughts. Christ does not want such outward righteousness before men while the heart remains impure before God, and He says: "It was said to the ancients"—that is, to those who live according to the old, outward man and who are only pious out of fear of punishment—"But I say to you," that in the New Testament, anger or the internal consent to kill is murder, even if it is physically avoided out of fear of punishment. For in the New Testament, being merely outwardly pious does not count; God wants the heart. Therefore,

when you are offering [your gift], and you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first and be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

In the Old Testament, the sacrifice was undertaken to testify to outward purity, but in the New, it does not count; one must first purify the inward man before a good work can flow out. In our times, we also have an outward practice which the unbelieving consider the highest piety, such as going to confession, hearing the absolution, and receiving the Sacrament from the priests. <margin>Confession, Absolution, receiving the Sacrament.</margin> If someone wishes to confess and fetch the forgiveness of sins (as is commonly believed), he should first reconcile with his adversary and forgive him from the heart, and above all things confess to God in heaven—which is the right and most important confession. Afterward, one might go and perform the outward practice; otherwise, it is all in vain and brings damnation. But just as the sacrifice was completed among the Jews while the heart remained full of hate and envy, so it is now among the so-called Evangelicals <note>The author uses "vermeinten Evangelischen" (supposed Evangelicals/Protestants) to critique those who claim the name of the Reformation but rely on empty rituals like the Pharisees did.</note> regarding going to confession, hearing absolution, and taking the Sacrament. They expect such things to take away sin, yet nothing outward brings salvation; faith in the inner man alone must accomplish it, for that is what God alone requires and regards, and nothing else. It was said to the ancients, "You shall not commit adultery"; but I say to you, whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. Hereby both types of righteousness are depicted: the ancients only called it adultery if one physically touched a woman, and the inward consent to do evil was no adultery to them if it was avoided out of fear of punishment or hope of conversion. If someone among such "pious" people fell into the outward act, he was stoned or beheaded; they believe the sin is punished on the body with death, and

and he is not the sinner; rather, the **inner man** is the sinner, whom no one can punish except **GOD**; however, **GOD** desires conversion and not death. <note>The author distinguishes between the physical body, which carries out an action, and the "inner man" or soul, where the actual intent to sin resides.</note>

**Moses** in the Old Testament was but a man; he could not look upon the heart. He only protected outward piety and punished evil physically—not because that was [completely] right, but so that **Israel** would not be destroyed prematurely if external vices were allowed to run wild, and so that the Heathens would not be offended by them. But **Christ** is **GOD**; he looks upon the heart and is a creator of the **new creature**. He has nothing to do with the "old" [nature]; his people are also never confined to a specific land, as **Israel** was. Therefore he says: **But I say to you, whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already broken the marriage.** Here we should take note: there is no one among the **children of Adam** <note>A traditional way of saying "all of humanity."</note> on earth who could remain so free of thoughts that he would not be tempted by external objects. This is to say: no person on earth is without sin. But we should not *commit* sin; that is, we should not persist or continue in **consent**. Even if a desire or lust rises within you, if you do not consent to it, it does not harm you. But if you continue in your desire and would gladly proceed to the outward deed—only held back by worldly shame or the fear of punishment—then you are an adulterer before **GOD**. If you die in such consent, you will be damned; for you lacked nothing in your will, had you only been permitted to act without fear of worldly punishment and shame.

**For I say to you, unless your righteousness is better than that of the scribes and Pharisees.** Here the Gospel begins [this section]; **For I say to you** points back to the preceding words where he had said: **Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets, but to fulfill them; not one jot or letter of the law shall pass away. Whoever now dissolves one of these least commandments and teaches people so, he shall be the least in the King-**

**-dom of Heaven.** <note>The catchword from the previous page "melreich" completes "Himmelreich," or Kingdom of Heaven.</note> The **Pharisees** only paid attention to human laws, or to the law according to the **letter**, which is the smallest part. They only looked at the works of the body and punished sin only physically. They asked nothing of the **inner man** or the internal law, which belongs to **GOD** and the prophets. They wanted to become righteous and blessed through outward piety. Therefore **Christ** says: **For I say to you, you must be more righteous than the Pharisees,** who only look at physical works. You must walk according to the **inner man**, which is the greatest thing, upon which **GOD** alone gazes, and not upon physical works. Why does the world think **Christ** abolishes the law and the prophets? That is, why do the **scribes** <note>Scholars of the religious law.</note> imagine that true **faith** is against the law, against all good order and <term>policy <note>original: "Policey." In this era, this referred to the general organized administration and civil order of a community, not just the modern police force.</note></term>? For if one preaches the true faith, then one must not kill any sinner; **GOD** wants them converted and not killed. **GOD** does not punish sinners in the body, but in the inner man with eternal damnation, unless it is taken away through **Christ**. Why does one think **Christ** or **faith** abolishes the law?

**First:** Because the world regards the physical deed as sin and asks nothing of the true, great sin that is in the heart.

**Second:** Because the law is taken only according to the **letter**, and one thinks the law is [merely] physical and that outward piety is enough.

**Third:** Because **Christ** only looks at the **inner man**, toward whom the law is directed; it is spiritual.

**Fourth:** Because **Christ** asks nothing of the outward works of the body—whether they are good or evil—nor does he wish anyone to be physically killed for them. Instead, he punishes eternally in the inner man with damnation, if the person has not converted and done penance while in the body.

It explains that the Law is spiritual and that God seeks the conversion of the "inner man" rather than mere physical punishment or outward compliance.</summary>

# 182 Gospel on the seventh; Sunday after Trinity. 183

<margin>The true Heavenly Bread.</margin>
...they spoke more of the Manna through Moses than of Christ; therefore they said: "Our fathers ate Manna in the desert, what sign do you perform?" JESUS answered and said: "Your fathers ate Manna and died, for it was food for the belly." The feeding through Moses with Manna and the feeding through Christ with the seven loaves are almost the same; although the seven loaves were from the earth and the Manna from the invisible heaven, they were both mortal food for the mortal body, pleasant and agreeable to the natural man. The heavenly, supernatural part received nothing from it; but Christ's flesh and blood is the true Heavenly Bread for the heavenly man, and not for the earthly one.

<margin>3. Twofold food, twofold body.</margin>
Thirdly, that all believers in this world are not yet at home, but are in the desert as strangers, and are in need of twofold food because of the twofold body; for they have one from Adam, the other from Christ.

<margin>Christ feeds bodily from above.</margin>
If we rightly consider this miracle of Christ and its causes, we find that earthly feeding leads us to the heavenly. For precisely for this reason He took bread from the earth and satisfied the mortal body, so that He might testify that He Himself is the Bread from Heaven, and feeds the believers according to the inward new man, bodily from above. All believers have a twofold body; each comes from birth and is earthly and mortal; the body from Christ comes from the rebirth from heaven, is heavenly and immortal. And while believers dwell in the body, they are not yet at home in this world, but strangers in the desert; they are in need of food from the earth because of the natural body, and they are also in need of food from heaven because of the new birth; for every thing must be maintained and fed by that from which

it originates. Fish are from water and must be maintained in water; in the air they die. The tree grows from the earth, and the earth is its sustenance. The "New Creature" <note>This refers to the concept in 2 Corinthians 5:17 of a person being transformed through faith</note> is remarkably unknown in these times; the old one from the earth is prioritized, as if it should enter the Kingdom of God, yet it must die completely. The cause is that people do not want to know Christ as the Creator of the New Creature; hence all error comes concerning the flesh and blood of Christ, the Holy Supper <note>The Eucharist or Communion</note>, and His Ascension. The New Creature is the inward man with flesh and blood; this one is fed from heaven and also alone goes to heaven, and not the old creature from Adam.

Since all believers now have a twofold birth—the first from the earth through Adam, the second from heaven through Christ—they have a twofold body: a visible earthly one for the worms, and an invisible heavenly one for eternal life. Thus they require twofold food: an earthly food for the Adamite body, as the people ate of the seven loaves, and a heavenly one for the heavenly body, namely Christ.

He did not come to help the outward man; He has nothing to do with earthly things; He is not Moses, who had to handle only physical things. # On the 8th Sunday after Trinity
## Gospel / Matthew 8 <note>Although the source cites Matthew 8, the following text is actually the famous warning from the Sermon on the Mount found in Matthew 7:15–21.</note>

Watch out for false prophets who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; by their fruits you shall know them. Can one also gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree brings forth good fruit; but a rotten tree brings forth bad fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth bad fruit, and a rotten tree cannot bring forth good fruit. Every tree that does not bring forth good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire; therefore by their fruits you shall know them. Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but those who do the will of my Father in heaven.

# Gospel on the Eighth

[An ornate letter E decorated with flowers.]
> The Lord says: Enter through the narrow gate; for wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to damnation, and many are those who walk upon it; but the gate is narrow and the way is small that leads to life, and few are those who find it.

<margin>Matthew 7.</margin>
Two paths are found: a narrow and small one, leading to the Light and eternal life; and there is within us a broad and wide one, which leads away into error and into damnation. The narrow, small way to life within us is contained in these words: "Whatever you want people to do for you, you should also do for them; this is the Law and the Prophets." This <margin>Key to wisdom. <note>original: "Clavis ad sapientiam."</note></margin> is the key to wisdom; whoever lives according to it cannot be led astray by others. It is the innate light <note>The "innate light" (angebohrnes Liecht) refers to the "Inner Light" or "Spark of the Soul," a central concept in Christian mysticism suggesting that God placed a natural sense of right and wrong within every human heart.</note> within everyone, from which all knowledge flows, and it is in all of us. <margin>Matthew 5.</margin> Whoever walks in this light does not fall; he walks on the narrow, small path to life. But whoever acts against it and does not wish to have the light, but instead follows the teachings of men <note>The author distinguishes between "the teachings of men" (human dogma or external traditions) and the "innate light" of God’s direct guidance in the conscience.</note>, walks the broad path to damnation. For he must believe what others say—it is just as if I allowed my own eyes to be poked out and had to see with other people's eyes. We could not go astray nor do wrong if we walked according to this innate light, for we would avoid the broad way of men and walk the narrow way to eternal life. The Law of God and all the Prophets would be followed, for this very light which is in us also teaches the Law and the Prophets. Whoever follows this innate light remains in the Law of God and in all that the Prophets teach. Now, examine this narrow path within yourself—that is, the innate light. # Gospel on the Eighth
## Sunday after Trinity.

(aa) 3

...may be deceived; but Scripture is held in both fists <note>This "both fists" metaphor suggests that the Bible is often used as a weapon by opposing sides, each grabbing it for their own purposes.</note>; one can use it on both sides. No matter how wrong someone might be, they can still wield the Scripture against their opponent. From this, it is concluded once again that we must have the **inner testimony**; for look at the Pope and Dr. Luther, how one justifies himself against the other. The Pope says: "You are an Antichrist, a false prophet." The other says in turn against the Pope: "You are an Antichrist, the false prophet." Both use the Scripture against each other. In such a case, the **inner testimony** is truly required, so that one may know who is right or wrong, or if they are both right or wrong. Look at <margin>1 Kings 22 <note>original: "3. Reg. 22." In older German Bibles, the books of Kings were numbered differently.</note></margin> the story of Micaiah and the four hundred prophets. Micaiah says that they are liars; the four hundred also said that Micaiah was a liar. Whoever had stood there would have joined the great crowd if they had lacked the inner testimony. But he who has the Spirit of the Anointing <note>A reference to the "unction" or "anointing" mentioned in 1 John 2:27, which teaches the believer all things.</note> can soon see, recognize, and test who is right or wrong. Thus <margin>Touchstone.</margin> Christ says, "Beware of the Pharisees, they are false." The Pharisees say, "Beware of the Galilean <note>A common derogatory term used by religious authorities for Jesus.</note>, he is a liar." Both use the Scripture against each other. But whoever has the inner testimony within him can soon recognize who is right or wrong. Every sect does this against the others: they cite Scripture and regard the Scripture only on their own side, as if the sun shone only for them alone, and that with their opponent there is only error and darkness. The opponent does the same in return, being also in such a delusion. Since both parties use Scripture, and no one can know which is right or wrong—or if both parties with their Scripture are false—he must be in Christ and have the Spirit of Christ within him. Therefore the LORD says here: Watch out for <margin>John 15.</margin> **false prophets** <note>original: "à Pseudo-Prophetis"</note>. He means to say: You believers are sealed with my Spirit; you can test what is right or wrong. Indeed, the world will hate you, hunt you, kill you, and put you under the ban for my name’s sake. Both the righteous and the false use this speech and say: "We must suffer much for Christ's sake; blessed are those...

<column-break/>

...who suffer persecution." And yet it is only over some wretched priest's article <note>This likely refers to specific dogmatic points or "Articles of Faith" over which the established churches (Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed) were fighting during the 17th century.</note> that has never been rightly taught or understood. As it is in these days, where one despises, hunts, **imprisons** <note>original: "incarceriret"</note>, and even kills another—and it must all supposedly come from Christ and the Holy Spirit, even though it is sent from the Devil. Let every man take heed, then, if he is **branded a heretic** <note>original: "verketzert"</note> and persecuted, that his cause does not stand on a sandy foundation, but that his foundation is sealed by the inner testimony. Even if a thousand stood against him and said he was false, his conscience would testify the opposite in the Holy Spirit, and he could die joyfully upon it.

Now, because the faithful warning of Christ is not directed at the preachers alone, but also at all the listeners—for both should take care and test whether the spirits are false—the listeners should not rely solely on their pastors. He might be a liar and an Antichrist; every person should see with their own eyes. So we will now consider from the text the nature and character of the right preachers, teachers, and also listeners; for both must walk the narrow, small path to life and avoid the broad one. It is not enough that the preacher alone walks the narrow path while the listeners run the broad path; they must both have the inner testimony within them, and they must both recognize or test the spirits together. What the nature and character of right teachers <margin>1.</margin> and listeners are, we find from this text.

Firstly: A good tree cannot bring forth bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bring forth good fruit. One cannot gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles. That is: all believers are planted by GOD and are good trees; one recognizes them by their fruits. For they are of GOD and Christ and they follow Christ; they judge no one, they brand no one as a heretic, they do not hunt, kill, or **imprison** anyone in matters of faith.

Secondly: This is also a certain nature and <margin>2.</margin> character of the right teachers and listeners: that they have the testimony...

<margin>3. It is wrong to want to root out the heretics.</margin>
Thirdly, the nature and character of true teachers is that they are immovable and do not fear factions, sects, or heretics <note>The author argues here against the religious persecution common in the 16th and 17th centuries, suggesting that true faith does not need to use force to survive.</note>. No one can lead them astray; they remain constant like a rock. Therefore, it is a useless, "wooden" <note>Meaning stiff, hollow, or artificial.</note> concern that some want to "weed out the tares" <note>A reference to the Parable of the Tares in Matthew 13, where Jesus advises against pulling up weeds (heretics) before the harvest (the end of the world).</note> so that Christians are not led astray. We clearly hear the Lord saying that they are a rock; no one shall snatch them out of his hand. And so he says: "Whoever hears these words of mine and does them, I will liken him to a wise man who built his house on a rock. When a cloudburst fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against the house, it did not fall, for it was founded on a rock." All believers are immovable rocks; they do not need to fear the sects; they merely guard themselves against them. The narrow, small path is within them; they have the inner testimony and cannot be overwhelmed by the storm-winds.

<margin>Character of false teachers.</margin>
Therefore, the nature and character of false teachers is, first, that both together are not "good trees" from God, but from nature—from a spirit of dizziness <note>The author uses "dizziness" (schwindel Geiſt) to describe a state of spiritual confusion or erratic wandering away from the truth.</note>. They are thorns and thistles from which one cannot gather figs or grapes. They are the "evil tree" destined for the fire. They prick like thorns and thistles, helping to kill, incarcerate, banish, and subvert. Because they despise themselves enough <note>Likely meaning they have no self-respect or integrity.</note>, they want to root out the weeds before the time, though Christ did not command it of them. By their fruits, you shall know them.

Secondly, it is the nature and character of false preachers and listeners that they want to see through other people's eyes and believe based on smooth talk. For they learn from human doctrine—what this or that person has written—and they point out the "broad way." They know nothing of the narrow, small path or the inner testimony within themselves. Indeed, they deny it and stifle the Spirit. To them it is not said: "Beware, test [the spirits]" <note>original: "Cavete, probate".</note>, for they have no "eye" within them. They are robbed of the testimony of the Spirit and lack faith because they are taught by men out of nature.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring ornate floral patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>

In this parable of the rich man and his steward, we are all admonished by Christ that we should use the unrighteous mammon—that is, temporal goods—in faith, so that after this life we may also be received into the eternal dwellings—that is, into heaven. We are taught that we should follow the unjust steward not in his malice or injustice, but in his wisdom, or righteousness, shrewdness, foresight, or cleverness. We should take an example from the children of this world, who deal with temporal goods in such a way— <meta>catchword: deal/</meta>

<column-break/>

<header>Sunday after Trinity.</header>
<page-num>199</page-num>

<margin>Two types of goods entrusted to man.</margin>
—that they provide for themselves and make friends with them, so that they do not suffer want in this short life. How much more should the children of light—that is, the Christians—conduct themselves wisely, so that in faith they walk through temporal goods in such a way that they do not forfeit the eternal ones. There are two types of goods entrusted to every person by GOD: the earthly, perishable, bodily goods, which are called the unrighteous mammon and "foreign property" <note>original: "fremde Gut." This implies property that does not truly belong to the soul and must be left behind.</note>, because it is not our own and is commonly misused. We come into the world naked, and we depart naked; all things are only lent to us for a short time according to our necessity. We must leave them all behind, including ourselves; moreover, moths and grubs eat our clothes, the thief steals our money, fire burns our property, and war chases us from every possession. Finally, death takes everything away from us; nothing remains with us, all things stay behind us; therefore, they are foreign goods and are not our own. O, if people could consider such things, how could they then deceive and take advantage of their neighbor for the sake of such lowly, base goods? How could they be so unfaithful regarding these small, foreign goods?

<margin>The great eternal good, the Kingdom of God within us.</margin>
The other good entrusted to man by God is the great eternal good: the Kingdom of God within us. This is meant to be our own, which no thief can steal, no fire can burn, and which does not leave us even in death, if only we have recognized it in faith. O, how many people accept the lowly, small good in place of the eternal, infinite treasure! They take the shadow for the essence; we chase after and love that which cannot remain and must leave us in death, and the Eternal, which should be over us and can remain, we let slip away.

There lived a rich citizen in a city who had many goods and an outlying farm <term>outlying farm</term> <note>original: "Forwerck." A historical term for a manor farm or a secondary estate located outside the city walls.</note> outside the city; he hired a steward, a poor man who had nothing and, because of his poverty, would have had to go begging with his wife and children or else work for daily wages. When this man had managed the household for a time and had acted unfaithfully, he became notorious to his master for his evil intentions. The master said: "You can serve me no longer from now on, and I do not intend to have you on my farm any longer; you must leave." The steward thought to himself: "My master is dismissing me from service and wants to depose me; I cannot thresh, chop wood, or dig, and I am ashamed to beg. Well then, I will see where I shall stay; I will not have served for nothing." And he went and deceived his master in various ways, forgiving his master's debtors half their debt, and making favorable neighbors and friends for himself with someone else's property. Thus, when he was deposed, they took him into their homes, and he was provided for with his wife and child for his whole life and had no want.

<margin>GOD is the rich man.</margin>
This is how it goes in the world with the children of the world, who provide for themselves through unrighteous dealings so that they have enough for a little time, even though they lose what is eternal and must suffer deprivation, hunger, and want in eternity. But the children of light—that is, the Christians—should be prudent in their own way and use temporal goods without harming their neighbor, so that they may be received into the eternal dwellings after they have been deposed in this time. A marketplace is where one must buy or fetch the forgiveness of sins, etc. Thus, the Temple signifies every individual believing person; the city of Jerusalem refers to the entire assembly of those who dwell within the <term>walled-church</term> <note>original: "Mauer-Kirchen." A term often used by mystical or radical reformers to describe the visible, institutional church structure as opposed to the internal, spiritual "living" church.</note> without Christ. Christ takes a whip of cords and drives more than a hundred people out of the Temple, which caused great astonishment among the **Scribes**, who also asked by what authority He did this. They do not know the <term>new birth</term> from heaven; they attribute it to the mortal flesh of Adam. Therefore, they were not worthy for Christ to give them an account when they asked by what authority He did such things. Man is the Temple himself; as soon as Christ enters, all contrary things are chased out of the heart. Buying and selling are abandoned; one immediately understands that the inner Temple is no marketplace, and that those in the walled-church are against Christ—those who buy, fetch, or sell <term>absolution</term> <note>The formal release from guilt or punishment for sin, often associated here with the Roman Catholic or institutional Lutheran practice of the time.</note> or the forgiveness of sins. # Gospel on the Eleventh [Sunday after Trinity]

summarized together: prayer, faith, repentance, and sorrow over sin; for no one can pray without faith, and no one believes without praying, and no one prays without penance, without repentance and sorrow over sin. For he who has no repentance and sorrow over his sin, and performs no penance, cannot pray; and he who does not pray has no faith; and he who cannot believe is not converted, but remains in impenitence.

Right praying does not happen according to human order or with the mouth, but through true praying—the sighing of the Spirit. Praying means leading a penitent life, turning away from sins, and surrendering oneself to God, humbling oneself before Him, and attending to one's salvation with fear and trembling. From this it follows that those who use many words and pray in front of people do not pray at all; but those who walk in a penitent life pray at all times, and pray rightly. Christ said that one should pray without ceasing; some have misunderstood this poorly and therefore gave rules, statutes, and laws, and created orders regarding how and at what time one should pray. Some even abandoned all their daily work and prayed constantly without ceasing, day and night, in the sight of the people. These people were 

<margin>It is not right to leave one's calling.</margin>

called **EUCHITES** <note>original: "EUCHETES." This refers to a 4th-century sect, also known as Messalians, who believed that only constant prayer could cast out the demon inherent in every person, leading them to reject work and traditional church sacraments.</note> or "Prayers." This is not right, nor was it the meaning of Christ, that a person should leave his calling or station and sing all the psalms, or read, or speak many words. Rather, this is the right interpretation of Christ’s word: that we should walk without ceasing in faith—that is, in a penitent life and in the fear of God. In this way, we will pray without ceasing so that no person sees or knows it, but God will see it. Now, when the Lord had told this 

<margin>Matthew 6.</margin>

parable about praying and faith—that one could not pray without faith, and could not believe without praying—then he said: "Do you think that the Son of Man will find faith on earth?" <note>Luke 18:8</note> That is: do you think that I will be found among people in penance, in repentance and sorrow over sin, or in prayer?

<sig>(ee)</sig>

When he had said that no one could pray without faith, and no one could have faith without prayer, without repentance and sorrow, there were some standing by who considered themselves believers. They imagined they could well pray without repentance or sorrow over sin, without improvement of life, and without humility. They held themselves to be pious and despised others; they were proud, and even held that Christ was wrong to group prayer and faith together, as if faith could not exist without prayer, and prayer could be performed without faith. They calculated it according to the "outer man" <note>The physical or superficial self that performs actions for show.</note>, where one can pray with the mouth in front of people without faith and without improvement of life. Therefore, Christ proves to such proud, impenitent people that their praying is nothing, since it is undertaken without confession, without faith, and without humility. He says: Wait, I will tell you what praying is, and that one may not pray without faith. "Two men went up into the Temple to pray; one a Pharisee, the other a tax collector. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted." From these two persons we see that praying and faith, sorrow and regret over sin, and confession belong together, and one may not be without the other. This is seen in the tax collector when he said, "God be merciful to me, a sinner." That came out of regret, out of penance, and out of faith; it was his confession and his prayer, which God heard. # Gospel on the Eleventh [Sunday after Trinity]

was rejected. From this must follow the second part, regarding the twofold nature of faith, prayer, confession, penance, conversion, and justification. The world-scholars in the high schools <note>The author refers to the universities and academic theologians of his day.</note>, however, do not want these things to be thrown together in such a way. Instead, they want to separate them through artificial logic <note>original: "Dialectice"</note> so that they might better teach people in matters of faith. They pay no attention to "rightly dividing" <note>original: ὀρθοτομεῖν, *recte secare verbum*</note> the Word properly. Therefore, they do not follow Christ, but rather human reason. They describe faith and speak much about it, yet they have none; they say what penance is, they say what justification is, yet they remain in their unrighteousness. They also dispute much concerning Christ and his flesh, yet they have never truly known him. They divide one thing from the other, as if faith were one thing, prayer another, confession another, and conversion, penance, and so on were something else entirely. According to the "letter" <note>The literal or outward meaning as opposed to the spirit.</note> and the outward person, it may seem so; but what does that matter to Christians, who live and accomplish all things according to the Spirit and true faith, without ceremonies, without temples, without mouth-clattering <note>A dismissive term for repetitive, heartless prayer.</note>, and without priests?

### II.

That there are two kinds of faith, prayer, or conversion, no one can deny: one through one's own power and will, and a divine conversion through God's working and will. One man, the Pharisee, thought himself a believer without any regret; he prayed over his sin, justified himself, and was well-pleased with himself for the sake of his own piety. He remained in pride and despised others. By this, we recognize the false faith in the world, where people make themselves into "believers," and want to perform penance by themselves and convert themselves. From this comes false praying and confessing. One knows such trees by their fruits; whatever God does not plant is nothing, and whatever God does not work Himself does not please Him, no matter how much it may glisten before the eyes of people. Here belongs the saying: "Everything that does not proceed from faith is sin." <note>A reference to Romans 14:23.</note>

<meta>catchword: sin /</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>221</page-num>
<header>Sunday after Trinity.</header>

sin. Whether one prays, confesses, or fasts, it is merely a human work—a sin—in which God has as little pleasure as He had in the Pharisee. The greatest multitude in the world wants to save itself and thus drives itself into damnation. The beginning of their faith comes from free will and human strength; in the middle of it, one finds nothing divine at all; and at the end, there is no comfort and no peace of Christ in the heart. Thus they travel into darkness, and no one believes that such human works are false or against God. They live in arrogance and pride and die within them.

<margin>True repentance. <note>original: "Vera poenitentia"</note></margin>

The other conversion or true faith is a pure, unadulterated gift of God, a work of the Holy Spirit in a humble, hungry, and surrendered <term>gelassenen</term> <note>A central term in German mysticism meaning "letting go" or being "resigned" to God's will.</note> heart. In such a state, a person recognizes themselves as so unworthy that they hardly dare to lift their eyes toward heaven. They recognize their own nothingness, blindness, and lack of strength. They do not make many words before people but comfort themselves with the great mercy of God in Christ, saying: "Oh, be merciful to me, a sinner!" They stop sinning and judge or condemn no one but themselves. We see this in the tax collector <note>original: "Zöllner"</note> whom God converted and made a believer. In this tax collector, confession, prayer, faith, and justification were all joined together because it proceeded from the depths of the heart, from the inner man. He did not need to confess to a priest; his praying happened according to the inner man, where no priest or cleric can reach and where none is necessary. In the Pharisee, confession, prayer, and justification were divided after the fashion of the synagogues and practiced only with the mouth. Therefore, he possessed none of these, for he remained in pride and arrogance, considering himself unworthy of no gift of God and holding himself to be pious—which was a lie. The tax collector, through the working of God, held himself to be unworthy, sinful, and unjust—which was a truth. As long as lies remain in a person, they cannot truly confess, pray, or believe. It is a lie when a person does not confess their sin, when they remain in pride, despise others, and "convert" themselves. "To lie is to go against the mind" <note>original: *Mentiri est contra mentem ire*</note>; it is called lying when one acts against their own heart and conscience...

# Gospel on the Eleventh [Sunday after Trinity]

<margin>We cannot convert ourselves when we wish.</margin>
This is called speaking more than what is truly there, when one claims a thing for oneself that is not his own; when one takes the glory from God and attributes it to himself. Thus, the creature is nothing and should not recognize itself, nor cling or stick to itself, nor please itself. Nor does the Pharisee do this out of unbelief; therefore he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. For he does not confess his great sins to the priests <note>original: "Pfaffen," a term often used dismissively for clergy who relied on outward ritual.</note>, but to God: 
"Ah, be merciful to me, a poor sinner! Ah, I am not worthy that the air should blow upon me, or the sun shine on me," etc. And that is the truth, not a lie, as God Himself has worked it within the human being. From all this, we should conclude and remember that saving faith or conversion does not reside in human powers, such that someone could make themselves a believer or convert whenever they wished, without needing God for it. From such a belief follows a bold, secure, and godless life among the so-called Evangelicals <note>In this context, "Evangelicals" refers to the mainstream Protestant reformers (Lutherans or Reformed) whom the author critiques for a perceived lack of inward transformation.</note>.
<margin>It rests with God alone.</margin>
It does not rest with us to become believers; it rests with God alone. Therefore, it is our duty to wait upon God in fear and trembling, and to keep ourselves still before Him. He always goes before us with His flowing grace and passes no one by, whether it be day or night. If someone remains an unbeliever or unconverted, it is his own fault and not God’s. It is his own fault—either trying to make himself a believer and convert (from which absolutely nothing can come in all eternity), or failing to follow the drawing of the Father at all times; we could not properly keep ourselves still before God in the Sabbath <note>The "Sabbath" here refers to spiritual rest—ceasing from one’s own works so that God can work within the soul.</note>. If God’s Spirit is to work, we must not convert ourselves or make ourselves believers; if God is to work, the human being must suffer <note>In the sense of "submitting to" or "undergoing" God's action.</note> and wait upon God, or pray. Those who are desperate call this prayer "Enthusiasm" <note>original: "Enthusiasterey," a derogatory term for those who believed in direct revelation or inward spiritual experience.</note> or "Schwenkfeldianism" <note>original: "Schwenckfelderey." The followers of Caspar Schwenckfeld von Ossig emphasized the "Inner Word" and spiritual transformation over outward sacraments.</note>. They want to convert themselves or co-operate, and thus they remain here and there in darkness, and cannot be helped; they themselves are guilty of their own 
<margin>In the Old Testament.</margin>
damnation. In the Old Testament, among the Jews, all things were divided: prayer was one thing, sacrifice was another; the person was one thing, the temple was another. Therefore,
<meta>catchword: they went</meta>

<column-break/>

# Sunday after Trinity.

they went up into the Temple to pray in certain places. But <margin>In the New Testament.</margin> in the New Testament, it is not so, for the person himself is the temple. And his praying, confessing, believing, and his sacrifice all occur in the inward person <note>original: "äussersten Menschen," though contextually referring to the most essential or deep part of the person as opposed to mere outward show.</note>, who remains in Christ and believes. He who believes also prays, and he who prays also sacrifices, and does such things not before the people, but in his little chamber, in secret. He who wishes to pray without regret and repentance for his sins cannot be without humility. Therefore, praying, believing, confessing, sacrificing, and repenting belong together in the New Testament, and one can never be accomplished without the other. If someone wishes to pray, he must be a believer; he must confess not before the priest, but before God. For it would be Old Testament-like (as often happens) that "Mouth-Christians" <note>original: "Maul-Christen," those whose Christianity is only in their speech, not their hearts.</note> can confess before the priest without faith, without repentance, and without improvement of life. This is Jewish, Heathen, Devilish, and not Christian or New Testament-like. This Tax Collector acts according to the New Testament: he prayed, he believed, he confessed, he sacrificed himself, and did everything at once, undivided. But the Pharisee could pray without confessing, without repentance, and without conversion; therefore he was not accepted.

<margin>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'A' featuring interlaced scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>
**A**ll the miracles of Christ, which he performed physically upon people, can and should be applied to the **inner person**, for whose sake alone He came into the world, and not for the sake of the outer person, whom He neither saves nor condemns. For the outer man is from the earth, but Christ is entirely from heaven, and he creates a **new heavenly creature** <note>In this context, "creature" refers to a "new creation" or a person reborn through spirit rather than a biological animal.</note>, so that the old may entirely perish and die. And although he asks nothing of the outer man, nor was he sent for his sake, he nevertheless helped many people physically, making the lame walk,

<meta>the</meta>

***

# Sunday after Trinity.

the blind see, the mute speak, the deaf hear, and even raised the dead, and made many sick people healthy. All of this he did to witness that He was the **Messiah**, the Creator of the **new creature**, and so that people would be awakened to recognize him and also believe in him, so that all believers through him would be justified and saved. Since this miracle now speaks to the inward person, we are instructed by it in the following points:

->I.<-

First, that we are all **deaf and mute by nature** in Divine things, so that we are unwilling to hear and speak of Divine matters.

Second, that we, as deaf and mute people, may be brought to Christ through the **vocal office of preaching**, being guided according to the spirit or the inner ground.

Third, that all preaching is in vain and to no purpose, unless we are led by Christ **privately** away from the crowd, and enlightened from above.

Fourth, that in our enlightenment, conversion, justification, etc., we can work nothing nor help toward it in any way; it does not reside in our will or working, but only in the mercy of God. For just as little as this mute and deaf man worked or helped toward his physical healing, just as little may a person work or do anything toward their **enlightenment** or **justification**. A person must wait, suffer, and hold still solely in the **Sabbath** <note>The author uses "Sabbath" here metaphorically to mean a state of spiritual stillness or "rest" where the human will is quiet so God can act.</note>; God alone must work. **Our justification is purely passive** <note>original: "Justificatio nostra habet se pure passive." This is a central theological claim that humans are the passive recipients of God's grace, like a canvas being painted upon.</note>. Thus, no one can convert themselves or make themselves a believer whenever they wish. In this way, the glory remains God’s alone, and the person should, for their own part, take heed in fear and trembling, following the drawing of the Father willingly, and always giving room and place to the knocking Holy Spirit.

Fifth, that all believers and godly scholars must confess with wonder that God alone makes all things well.

# Gospel on the Twelfth Sunday after Trinity.

[...he] makes the deaf hear and the speechless speak. For truly, if anyone is to hear God’s Word or Christ, God must work it and no human being. If anyone is to preach Christ rightly and speak of Him fundamentally, God must work it.

From this, it is concluded sixthly that there are two kinds of office <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> <note>original: "2. Cor. 3."</note>, that of the Letter and that of the Spirit, of which Saint Paul treats. The office of the Letter kills and lets one remain dead; the preacher and the listener both remain mute and deaf, for the inner speaking is not there. But the office of the Spirit gives the Spirit and makes one alive—that is, both the preacher and the listener are enlightened, for the inner testimony of Jesus is present. But so that we simple folk may learn and retain something from this passage, we want to divide the text into three persons.

<margin>Division of the Text</margin> <note>original: "Divisio Textus"</note>
<margin>1. The Person of those leading to Christ</margin> <note>original: "1. Persona deducentium ad Christum"</note> First, the person of the **leaders**, who bring the poor person to Christ and beg Him that He would have mercy and help him physically, for they cannot do it themselves.

<margin>2. The Person of the mute</margin> <note>original: "2. Persona muti"</note> Secondly, the person of the **deaf and mute man**, what he signifies, and how he conducts himself during his healing.

<margin>3. The Person of Christ</margin> <note>original: "3. Persona Christi"</note> Thirdly, the person of **Christ**, who leads him away from the people privately, sighs toward heaven, touches him with His finger, and makes him well.

->I.<-

<margin>The Ministry</margin> <note>original: "Ministerium"</note> And as He went out again from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, they brought to Him a deaf man who was mute and begged Him. There were some pious people who had compassion and mercy for this deaf and mute man; they led him to Christ and begged that He would make him physically well, since He, as a physician, had helped so many others. They begged Him that Christ would do it, for they could not do it themselves. By this "leading to Him" is understood the **oral office of preaching**, through which people are to be brought under obedience to God. However, the preaching office is of two kinds: the office of the Letter and the office of the Spirit, of which the Apostle

acts and says: **The letter kills, but the spirit makes alive.** <margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin> <note>original: "2. Cor. 3."</note> There are two kinds of preachers in the world. This literalist crowd <term>literalist crowd (Buchstäbischer Hauffe): those who interpret scripture only by its surface meaning without spiritual insight</term> holds that the Son of God is of Adam’s stock and blood, and redeems the flesh of Adam from death, but knows nothing of the flesh and blood of Christ, in which the new birth from heaven is contained. They preach of Christ according to the letter while suppressing and erasing the Spirit. The letter is a dead thing; it does not make alive but lets one remain dead. Such an office of the Spirit leads to Christ without error and prays for the poor deaf and mute person, that Christ would help from above.

## II.

<margin>God desires the inner person / and not the outer.</margin>
The deaf and mute man / who is led to Christ / signifies the entire human race following the first, old, sinful birth from Adam / meaning that we are all, as a group, deaf and mute before our rebirth. For we do not like to hear talk of Christ / because He demands the surrender of ourselves / and the putting to death of our flesh <note>The author uses "flesh" in the Pauline sense: the fallen, self-centered human nature.</note>. We all wish to live according to our own will; the ears of the inner person are thus plugged / so that they perceive nothing of divine things / even if we hear them with our physical ears. And truly / if God did not touch the inner person / it would be impossible for us to accept Christ’s word. Furthermore, we are all so mute / that we do not like to speak of Christ / nor do we wish to preach of Him / unless the bond of the tongue is loosened. I speak of the tongues of the inward person / for the outer person can chatter enough / and is talkative enough / according to the rules of rhetoric and logic <note>original: "Rhetorica, Dialectica"</note> / as we see in those preachers who follow only the "letter" of the law. But God desires the inner person / and not the outer. But how do we reach this state / or how can we help ourselves / so that we are made to hear and see through Christ? Just as much as this poor man did for his own physical health / that is exactly how much we contribute to our own conversion, enlightenment, or justification—which is to say, nothing at all. This mute man allows himself to be led / guided / and brought to Christ. He also submitted himself to Christ entirely / kept still / let Christ do with him as He pleased / resisted nothing / and performed no work of his own / but only received his physical health from Christ. In the same way, every person must do the same / namely, let themselves be led, guided, and brought under the power of Christ / and there wait upon Him to perform all the work during the "Sabbath" <term>Sabbath: here used to mean a state of spiritual stillness and resting from one's own works to allow God to act</term> / keeping still in fear and trembling for one's salvation. One can help and work toward their own enlightenment or conversion just as little / as one helped or worked in their own natural <unclear>conception</unclear>

->I.<-

That true faith in Jesus Christ alone makes one blessed, pious, and righteous before God is taken from this speech of Christ, where He says: "Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, for I say to you, many prophets and kings wanted to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it."
<margin>Romans 10.</margin> From these words (I say) we should not only learn that faith alone makes one blessed, but we also learn to rightly understand the saying 
<margin>Twofold hearing:</margin> of Paul, *faith comes from hearing* <note>original Latin: "fides ex auditu." A reference to Romans 10:17.</note>, and that one must necessarily admit there is a twofold 
<margin>Twofold word:</margin> hearing and a twofold word—namely, the inner testimony and 
<margin>The inner and outer testimony.</margin> the outer testimony. This is a necessary point against the literalist theologians <note>The author is likely criticizing "scholastic" or "orthodox" Lutherans who emphasized the "means of grace" (the physical Word and Sacraments) over the "inner light" or direct inspiration of the Spirit.</note> who deny the anointing <note>The "anointing" (Salbung) refers to the internal teaching of the Holy Spirit, as mentioned in 1 John 2:27.</note> and quench the Spirit, rejecting the inner word, which alone makes one blessed.
<margin>The inner [word] alone makes one blessed.</margin> First, although Christ praises His disciples as blessed because of what they see and hear outwardly, He does not make them blessed for that reason alone. Rather, with this blessing, He gives us an instruction: that His disciples, being enlightened and taught by the Father, can now also see Christ with physical eyes and hear Him through faith. Thus, they have a double testimony: from within through the Spirit, and from without through Christ’s physical presence. This did not happen for many patriarchs, prophets, and kings, for they saw Christ only in the Spirit and not in the flesh. To be sure, many Jews and scribes heard Christ with physical ears, saw Him with eyes, and touched Him with hands—Judas, Caiaphas, Annas, and Herod also saw Him—but He does not praise their eyes and ears as blessed. The reason is that they were not enlightened or taught by the Father, and they did not have that inner hearing or inner seeing. From this, it is incontrovertibly concluded that true faith in Jesus Christ alone makes one righteous, pious, and blessed, and nothing external; for many hear and see Christ and yet remain unblessed and damned. This speech of Christ ex-

explains to us that saying of Paul, *faith comes from hearing*, with which the literalists shield themselves against the inner word or inner hearing. They say flatly that no one can have saving faith without external hearing; therefore, no one is a Christian or a member of the Christian Church who does not have the external preached word. But Christ says to the disciples: "Blessed are your eyes and ears that you see and hear"—namely, because of the inner seeing and hearing, upon which everything depends. Otherwise, Christ would not have left it at that; He would have praised all the others as blessed who see and hear Him in the same way as the disciples. In this way, Paul’s saying must also be understood when he says "faith comes from hearing."
<margin>Faith from hearing: how is it to be understood?</margin> Whoever does not hear it is not a believer. That is to say: whoever is touched by God’s preceding grace, so that he hungers for the Kingdom of God and longs for the eternal, and a preacher comes who proclaims Christ the Crucified and thus opens to him the way to salvation—such a person cannot help himself; he must run and hear, and give witness to the heard, preached word. Indeed, he will be awakened more and more in faith and come more and more to the obedience of faith. Thus, faith comes from hearing only when the external hearing is received as a testimony. Whoever despises the oral office of preaching, or does not find the witness in his heart, would not be a believer, and for him, faith would not come from hearing. Now, however, it is taught and held that saving faith is necessarily bound to external hearing, and is fetched from there, and cannot come from within through the drawing of the Father. This is a great deception, which makes faith into nothing more than a human work. If it were so—
<margin>Faith is not [merely] hearing preaching.</margin> that faith came only from external hearing without the internal, and if there were no internal hearing yet, then all children would have to be unbelieving and damned, as well as all the prophets and patriarchs; for who [preached] to them?

Therefore Christ says to the Samaritan, who returned: Has no one else been found who turned back and gave GOTT the glory, except this stranger? Christ had quickly granted their request, for as they were going to the priest, one among them noticed that they had become clean; and that was a Samaritan, who turned back and praised GOTT with a loud voice, and fell on his face at his feet and thanked him. Such was the true **thank-offering**, which GOTT requires of all those who have obtained a benefit; for thereby he confesses that it comes not from the creature, but from GOTT alone. There, glory is shown to GOTT, and not to the priest or the sacrifice. 

That the ten lepers had to show themselves to the priest happened so that the custom of the land would be kept according to the **Law of Moses**, and so that they would be publicly declared clean before the people; also to testify that they had been made clean neither by the priest nor by the sacrifice, but by Christ alone through faith. For Christ says clearly: *Your faith has helped you.* And the other nine were also cleansed through their faith, and not through their sacrifices, nor through the priest. 

Why then did they not return and give Christ the glory, offering themselves up to him with the Samaritan? **Answer:** If the **saving faith** <note>The author distinguishes between "saving faith" (Seeligmachende Glaube), which leads to eternal salvation, and "natural faith," which only expects physical miracles.</note> had been in them, or if they had become healthy through that faith, they could not have helped it; for all believers remain with the one they believe in. Therefore, it was the natural, innate faith; for they hoped in Christ the Physician, that he would help them, and it happened so. Their faith or hope was placed on bodily help, and Christ helped them bodily; or rather, their own faith made them healthy, which they had toward Christ. Thus, many people can often "believe themselves healthy" through their natural faith, for it is of a mighty power; it transforms natural things and throws mountains into the sea. And Christ let them become healthy through their own faith, helping them bodily, so that they, together with the Samaritan,

---

<page-num>247</page-num>
<header>Sunday after Trinity.</header>
<meta>catchword: as</meta>

should come to the **saving faith**, which is the true sacrifice and can give GOTT the glory. The other nine were satisfied with the bodily help and remained in unbelief with the priest and the sacrifice; they could not return and give GOTT the glory, for [natural] faith does not honor GOTT; it does not recognize the gifts of GOTT and remains unthankful.

### II.

**S**econdly, to consider the text according to the **New Testament** and the inner man: it shows itself that distress also teaches one to pray, if only one recognizes it; and that GOTT hears us in prayer—yes, even before we begin to pray—and that all believers offer a well-pleasing sacrifice:

> Call upon me in the time of distress / so will I rescue you / so shall you praise me. <note>original: Psalm 50:15</note>

Bodily leprosy <term>Aussatz</term> <note>In the early modern period, leprosy was used as a powerful metaphor for sin because it physically isolated the sufferer from the community, just as sin was thought to isolate the soul from God.</note> is a terrible plague, an incurable disease according to common medicine, and it separates one from the community of men. However, it signifies **spiritual leprosy**, namely, sin, for the sake of which a person is excluded from the Holy Christian Church if he persists in it against his conscience. Yes, just as the Jews on earth who were leprous were rejected and excluded from the entire community, so we are excluded from the New Testament and the spiritual assembly before GOTT because of sin, even if we are physically among a crowd where there is preaching, confession, etc.

In that faith you may go and receive the true body and true blood of Christ in His remembrance.

<margin>1. Distinguishing between the world and Christ.</margin>
First, the faithful teaching of Christ is so foreign, so hard, and so difficult for us because we think and hold that Christ is at one with the world, and that His teaching and life are not against the world, nor that Christ is against the **old man** <note>A theological term for human nature in its fallen, unredeemed state, as opposed to the "new man" redeemed by grace.</note>. The whole world lives in greed, and not in [spiritual] property, but in the care of nourishment. The world lives according to the old man of the earth; Christ lives according to the new man of heaven, and all of this is against each other. Few wish to understand this, but rather they think that Christ and His teaching might well agree with the world.

<margin>2. It is the lack of faith.</margin>
The second cause why the medicinal speech of Christ seems so foreign, so difficult, and so hard—that we should not worry about eating, drinking, or clothing—is the lack of faith, for so little faith is found on earth among all the children of men. For whoever believes in Christ believes everything that He has spoken, taught, promised, and done; for what He teaches, He also lives, and whoever accepts Him, accepts His life. But since so few people believe the Lord Christ—that one should not worry about eating, drinking, or clothing—the whole faith and Christ Himself are rejected by them. Thus, the lack of faith is a primary cause why such speech of Christ seems so hard and difficult to us, though it is light and mild to all believers.

<margin>3. Praying the Our Father.</margin>

The Lord's Prayer.</note>: "Give us this day our daily bread." Children can pray, "Our Father, You alone shall care, and we shall be obedient to You." Children ask for daily bread, not out of greed or anxiousness for the future time like the unbelievers, who also pray that God would grant them a stockpile. ### Gospel on the fifteenth [Sunday after Trinity]

A person should work diligently and be careful in their office, station, or calling, and should work daily; yet they should not worry for the coming day—what they shall eat and drink, or what they shall wear. For such worry is heathen, even idolatrous, and moreover entirely useless and in vain. For even if a person of short and small stature were to sit down and worry without ceasing, they still could not become a single cubit <note>original: *Elle*; a traditional unit of measurement roughly the length of a forearm</note> taller or shorter than they already are. Likewise, we could not place a single grain more upon a stalk than has already grown there; everything grows without our skill or cleverness while we lie and sleep. Our bread grows for us from the straw; wool grows on the sheep without our worry or effort; wine grows from the wood <note>referring to the grapevine</note> without our skill or help. Since God now gives bread from the straw for our hunger, wool from the sheep for our coat, and wine from the wood for our drink—all without our wisdom or help, even while we sleep—why then do we want to worry and interfere with our Father’s office? He alone cares for us as His children and nourishes us. Therefore, only apply the labor of our sweat; God will provide the rest, which comes to us more easily than it does to the birds. Let us look at the birds, whom God nourishes as a Creator; if He gives the birds their nourishment—who do not work for it—how much more will He give us humans food and drink for our necessity, we who work for it.

But this is no longer the case because of sin; therefore, we must be clothed. If God now clothes the lilies, which neither sew nor spin, how much more will He do for us with necessary clothing—we who work for it by sewing, spinning, and weaving.
