-lies their body and beauty, the gemstones their beauty, the pearls their beauty; so also Adam and Eve had their beauty in Paradise before the Fall. <margin>Solomon borrowed clothes.</margin> But now, even Solomon himself must not be so beautifully clothed as a lily in the field. The reason: he wears nothing but borrowed clothes—velvet from worms <note>referring to silkworms</note>, pearls from the water, gold from the mountains, a coat from the sheep, trousers from the goats, shoes from the oxen, etc. And each thing has its own beauty for itself: gold its beauty, the garment its beauty. Everything one sees on Solomon is borrowed; naked he was born, and naked he departs again. Since nothing we wear or have is our own—even the body itself belongs to the worms—only that which is in the inner person through faith remains eternally. In such seeking, we must earnestly turn from everything external to the internal; and the internal thing will be far more powerful and mighty than food or clothing. For clothing would be of no use to you if you did not have life and a body; no house or clothing would be of use to you if you did not have the body; therefore, the body and life are more than food and clothing. Likewise, the body would be of no use to you if the soul were not there; therefore, the soul is more than the body, for no one can kill it. The soul would be of no use without God's Spirit; therefore, God and His Spirit are more than the soul, for no one can take the Kingdom of God from you, even if all external goods and even your body are taken away. <margin>Goods <note>meaning spiritual goods</note> may not be taken away.</margin> Thus we should also let ourselves be led from the temporal to the inner eternal, from the external to the internal, and from bodily goods to internal eternal goods. That is what creates true courage, in which I also remain; I risk goods and body, and may God help me overcome. Amen.

Three things we have to consider in this text: The first is the craftiness or malice of the scribes from the synagogues, who lie in wait for Christ; the second is the great blindness and ignorance of the scribes from the synagogues regarding Christ and his kingdom, or the distinction between the Law of Moses and Christ; the third is their great pride <term>Hoffarth; an archaic term for excessive pride or haughtiness</term>, that they seat themselves at the top, indeed, sit in God's place, therefore they shall be humbled with Lucifer down into the abyss of hell, for there they must be cast down from their throne with eternal shame.

This refers to the theological idea that faith fulfills the true intent of the law even when ritual rules are broken.</note>. Through faith, we both set aside the Law and keep it through faith, as we see in Christ: that by not keeping the Law, he actually satisfied the Law; for what else does God’s Law <margin>Reason.</margin> want but love, which is the fulfillment of all laws?

And first, concerning the malice of the synagogue-dwellers, scribes, and Pharisees, who set a trap for Christ so that they might catch him in words and deeds: they invite him as a guest on a Sabbath and placed before him a man with dropsy <note>original: "waſſerſüchtigen"; a condition where the body swells with fluid, often used in sermons as a metaphor for spiritual greed or bloating pride.</note> and watched what he would do. It would have been against his teaching if he had not helped the poor sick man. But if he makes him healthy, then he has broken the Sabbath according to the opinion of the synagogue, and thus they have a case against him. But the Lord sees their malicious plot and notices their thoughts very well. Therefore, it stands in the text: JESUS answered and said to the scribes: "Is it also right to heal on the Sabbath?" For in that they placed the man with dropsy there for Christ on the Sabbath, it is a question, as if they wanted to ask the Lord whether it were right or wrong to heal on the Sabbath. For had they said, "Yes, it is right, one should heal the sick, for love of one's neighbor requires this; necessity knows no law <note>original: "die Noth hat kein Gebot," a common legal and theological maxim meaning urgent need overrides ritual laws</note>; illness does not take a holiday; death keeps no Sabbath; one must help in time of need," then they would have spoken against themselves with such an answer. Why do you act so cunningly with me and invite me as a guest?" Therefore, it was safer for those of the synagogue to remain silent than to speak. Here is revealed the cunning, evil heart of the scribes against Christ, whom they waylaid, seeking how they might trap him.

Secondly, their great blindness is also revealed, in that they neither understand nor know the distinction of the Law, of the letter and the spirit, or the distinction between the Old and New Testaments. For the Old is against the New according to the letter, and yet they are one in spirit and in divine understanding. They thought no differently than that the Law was trespassed and broken if one plucked ears of grain for hunger on the Sabbath, or if one made a sick man healthy on that same day. Now, to better recognize such malice and blindness, we must speak of two kinds of Sabbath: namely, the Sabbath of the Jews under Moses externally, and the Sabbath of the believers under Christ, which is internal. The Jewish Sabbath was a specifically named day in the land of Israel, and that was Saturday, or the seventh day of the week, just as we have among us the eighth day <note>The "eighth day" refers to Sunday, signifying the day of Resurrection and the start of a new creation</note>. On that same day, one was not permitted to do or practice any physical manual labor or other work—not to gather wood, not to light a fire, not to cook anything, not to lift or carry anything, not to walk more than a quarter mile, but to stay at home. It was a hard, strict law, such that violators were punished in the body

and put to death, as we read in Moses that a man was stoned because he had gathered wood <note>A reference to Numbers 15:32-36</note>. On the Sabbath, all feast days and works of the Law rest; they are ordained for the sake of the outward person, either to keep them under restraint or to obey the Law out of love without violating the conscience. As indeed many of the believing Jews in the Old Testament, who understood the intent of the Law, were obedient to the outward Law and remained imprisoned under the heavy yoke according to the outward person, yet without the burden or imprisonment of their conscience. Just as circumcision was a work of the Law that concerned the outward person and had to be kept—for whoever was not circumcised had to be separated from the people of **God** and be circumcised—so also the sacrifice, the Passover lamb, etc., and other ceremonies had to be observed. Such an external Sabbath with all the works of the Law, although it had to be strictly kept according to the outward person, did not bind the conscience; it depended more on the understanding of the conscience than on the letter, which was a heavy, servile yoke.

That He exercised such compulsion of the Law through Moses by physical punishments had its reason and its time, so that they remained under the servile yoke according to the outward person until Christ. ## after Trinity.

...are not difficult. The *scholars* <note>original: "Literati"</note>, who in the universities very diligently study the Scripture through the arts and languages for a long time even until death, and become *Doctors* <note>Teachers/scholars</note> and masters of the Scripture, yet die in pride. The reason is this: they do not seek him who is the Scripture’s origin, root, and kernel. Namely, they do not ask after the crucified Christ; they imagine they can learn and understand the Divine Law without the crucifixion, without faith in Jesus Christ, who is both God and man. One sees this in the way they cast aside the main book of the Scripture, namely the *Revelation* <note>original: "Apocalypsin"</note>, in which Jesus Christ, the crucified Lord, is meant to be revealed to us. They say it is an unnecessary book for the understanding of Scripture, just as their predecessor *Luther* <note>original: "Lutherus"</note>, along with many others, judged this book to be unfit. Now, where the *Revelation* is not used or understood, there Christ also cannot be used or understood in the Holy Scripture. If he is lost, then our studying is false and damnable. They may well know in a human way, like the *scholarly theologians* <note>original: "literatis Theologis"</note>, the greatest commandment, and even preach it to others, but they do not touch it with their finger. They remain in darkness and blindness, and begin to dispute against one another *concerning the Law of God: what is the Law? What is the Gospel?* <note>original: "de lege DEI, quid est lex, quid est Evangelium?"</note> One distinguishes them without understanding; the other confuses them without understanding. And although on one side they are not right in these things, they still err on the other side; for they chew on and search the Scripture, but not for Him who is the Gospel and the Law Himself. They deal with the dead letter without the Spirit; the others deal with the Spirit without the letter. Neither is right. If they found Jesus Christ the Crucified, they would recognize the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "A und O"</note>, accept the *Revelation*, reconcile the *contradictions* <note>original: "Contraria"</note> of Scripture, and take the letter and Spirit together—the end and the beginning. In this way, they would attain a whole, perfect understanding of the Holy Scripture, and moreover have the power to walk in the Law of God, to love God and their neighbor, and cease from disputing, quarreling, and warring over the

<column-break/>

Holy Spirit, whom they do not have, and over the Gospel, which they do not understand. But because they remain in pride, seeking mastery in the Scripture and accepting *doctorates*, they bear witness against themselves that they do not know whose son Christ is. They say freely that he is David’s son according to the flesh, and God’s son according to the spirit—that is, that Christ took on Adam-like flesh from the Virgin Mary—as can be clearly seen here with these Scribes from the Synagogue, that they understand and know nothing of the *incarnation of the eternal Word* <note>original: "incarnation verbi æterni"</note>.

Therefore, mark the third important question: While the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them and said: "What do you think of Christ? Whose son is he?" They said, "David’s." Christ refutes them from the 110th Psalm and says: "If he is David’s son, how then does David in the Spirit call him a Lord, when he says: *The Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool?*" <note>Psalm 110:1</note> If David then calls him a Lord, how is he his son? And no one could give him an answer. For they did not know the foundation of the *incarnation of the eternal Word* <note>original: "incarnationis verbi æterni"</note>. They thought God had taken on Adam’s flesh and blood, died in it, and taken that same flesh into Heaven with him—just as our scholars still say today, that Adam’s flesh and blood from the earth possesses Heaven. They do not ask after Paul’s teaching, who says: *Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.* <note>1 Corinthians 15:50</note> The Lord asks them: "What do you think of Christ? Whose son is he?" As if he wanted to say: "You have given me a question as to which is the greatest commandment in the Law; I have told you how it is in itself. They answer him: he is David’s son, as the Scripture states; according to the flesh, he is held to be a son of David by the promise, not that he was of the flesh and blood of Joseph, or David, or Abraham, or Adam. For the *incarnation* <note>original: "incarnatio"; the act of God becoming human</note> comes from the Holy Spirit; he is the bread from heaven. They do not understand this; they say he is David’s son, that he is of Adam’s flesh and blood and not from the Holy Spirit. Christ rightly refutes this as a point against the Old and New Testament, and says: how can Christ be David’s son, how can he be born of Adam’s flesh and blood, if David calls him a Lord in the Spirit? It is not customary for a father to call his son a Lord. In the 110th Psalm, David says to God the Father—or about God the Father and God the Son: The Lord (that is, God the Father) said to my Lord (that is, to the Son, who is my Lord), sit at my right hand. That is: descend and become man, redeem the human race in an assumed human nature in customs and behavior, like a man from Adam, until I bring all your enemies under your power, even death itself, which is the last enemy.

<margin>Christ according to the flesh a Lord of David.</margin>
By this, Christ proves to them that the Messiah is also a Lord of David according to the flesh. Our scholars <note>Likely referring to Lutheran or Catholic university theologians</note> also interpret it to mean that Christ is a Lord of David according to the spirit, and a son of David according to the flesh. They do not rightly understand Paul where he 
<margin>Romans 1.</margin>
speaks: Born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and powerfully proven to be a Son of God according to the spirit. Namely, according to the promised "seed of the woman," he is called a son of David. The Apostle, along with the whole Scripture, speaks of the flesh according to the promise—the *flesh of the promise* <note>original: "carnem promissionis"</note>. God did not promise Adam’s flesh from the earth; it would not have been useful to us. Rather, he promised the seed of the woman <note>A reference to the first prophecy of the Messiah in Genesis 3:15</note>; that is, the flesh incarnated from the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin, not from the woman. ...was. And they said to him: Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him. Then the father realized that it was at the same hour in which **JESUS** had said to him: Your son lives. And he believed with his whole house. This is now the second sign that **JESUS** performed when he came from Judea into Galilee.

In this history or story, we see that the **royal official** <note>original: "Hofmann der Königische" — a nobleman or courtier serving under King Herod Antipas.</note> at Herod’s court is converted to the Christian faith; from an uncircumcised heathen he becomes a Christian, and from an unbeliever he becomes a person of faith. To this end, three things urged him: First, **necessity** <note>original: "Noth"</note>, the great concern, the **household cross** <note>original: "Hauß-Creutze" — an early modern term for domestic suffering or family burdens</note> that he had to witness alongside his wife; namely, the great misery regarding his son, who lay deathly ill. After that, having endured Christ’s **words of rebuke** and **admonitions** <note>original: "Schelt-Worten, Straff-Reden"</note>, he surrendered himself to the Word of Christ. For when he begged **Jesus** to come and make his son well, he had to hear from Him that he was an unbelieving man and had no faith, saying: *Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe.* This is to say: if you are not drawn by the Spirit of the Father, you do not come to the Son; if you are not plunged into necessity, anxiety, and adversity, you do not come to faith. You do not ask for Christ, the **helper in times of need** <note>original: "Nothelffer"</note>. But as he persisted in his distress and said: *Lord, come quickly before my child dies,* and Christ then said: *Go your way, your son lives,* he surrendered himself to Christ’s word; the man believed the word that **JESUS** spoke and went on his way.

<column-break/>

And finally, so that he might be confirmed, his servants met him on the road; they strengthened him when he inquired of them the hour in which **Jesus** had said to him: *Go your way, your son lives.* These are the three pieces that lead him to faith: First, his **necessity** and his concern, which drove him to Christ. Second, that he patiently allowed himself to be rebuked and surrendered himself to Christ's Word, believing His powerful speech. Finally, that he allowed himself to be confirmed by others on the road and at home; when he arrived, he found the matter to be exactly so. Thereupon he became a believer with his whole household. He sought something small and found something great; he sought bodily health and received the salvation of the soul—for the child, for himself, and for his whole house—and he became a believer.

<margin>**No one is faithful without the cross.** <note>original: "Sine cruce nemo fidelis."</note></margin>
Necessity and adversity drive us to the Physician and testify to us that we were unbelieving people in the good days. **No one is faithful without the cross.** <note>original: "sine cruce nemo fidelis"</note> A human being is like a seed; if it is not sown, it does not grow and brings no fruit. Necessity, or **Christ’s Cross**, is the fertile field in which we must be sown; we must be baptized with Christ so that we grow into a tree that brings forth fruit for eternal life. **God’s Word** is so strong and powerful that whoever submits to it with patience experiences wonders within themselves; they are lifted out of themselves and transplanted into Christ. Faith—or a person in faith—once it has a beginning, must grow and increase. To him who has, more will be given, and things will get better with him daily. But he who has no faith must lose even what he thinks he has; it always gets worse for unbelieving people. The unbeliever increases in ignorance and malice. Therefore, we should gladly allow ourselves to be rebuked and submit ourselves in all patience to the **Gospel**, the Word of Christ, surrendering ourselves entirely. Then we would have the right way before us to come out of the kingdom of darkness into the kingdom of light and righteousness.

## On the 22nd Sunday after Trinity
### Gospel / Matthew 18

Therefore the kingdom of heaven is compared to a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he began to settle them, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand pounds <note>original: "Pfund" — In many English Bibles, this is translated as "talents." In the 16th and 17th centuries, "Pfund" (pound) was used to denote a very large unit of currency. Ten thousand talents was an astronomically large sum, intended to represent an unpayable debt.</note>. Since he did not have the means to pay, the lord commanded that he be sold, along with his wife and his children and all that he had, to make payment. Then the servant fell down and worshiped him <note>In this context, to "worship" (anbeten) implies a gesture of extreme reverence or prostration before a superior.</note>, saying: "Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay you everything." Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, released him, and also forgave him the debt.

But that same servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred groschen <note>original: "Groschen" — a small silver coin. While the first servant owed millions, this debt is a tiny fraction of that amount, roughly equivalent to a few months' wages.</note>. And he seized him and choked him, saying: "Pay me what you owe." <meta>catchword: fi-</meta>

**D** <note>The ornamental initial 'D' begins the German word 'Die' (The).</note>he summarized teaching of this Gospel parable—concerning the King who wished to settle accounts with his servants, and one came before him who owed him **ten thousand pounds** <note>original: "zehen tausend Pfund" — an astronomical sum representing humanity's debt of sin to God.</note> and had no way to pay, yet the king completely released him from his debt upon his humble plea; likewise, how this servant forgot such goodness and mercy, went out, and found one of his fellow servants who owed him only **a hundred groschen**, and he would have no patience with him but had him thrown into prison, for which he was finally called back and had to suffer the same fate.

To rightly and thoroughly understand such a parable (I say), the conclusion of today’s text shall serve us, where Christ says: **So will Christ also do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother’s failings.** Namely, just as the King did to the unmerciful servant—whom he had released from all debt, but who then forgot this and would show no mercy to his fellow servant, and so had to be thrown into prison until he paid everything—therefore the Lord concludes with such a closing statement: **So will my heavenly Father also do to you, etc.**

It is as if he wanted to say: My heavenly Father forgives everyone their great debt out of grace, for the sake of his son Christ, those who ask him with a repentant heart and do penance, no matter how great the sin may be. But if you choose to forget such goodness, grace, and mercy, and contend and fight with your fellow man over a small, minor debt, then everything shall be in vain; even the suffering and death of the Son of God shall be lost and useless to you, if you do not forgive your brother his failings. Such summarized teaching and the content of this parable are also contained in the **5th petition of the Our Father**, where we say: *Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.* Whoever understands this

**fifth** petition <note>The text continues from the catchword "fe" (fünffte) on the previous page.</note> understands this parable as well, and requires no human interpretation for it; the Holy Spirit explains it enough within his heart. *Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors*; this means: "O gracious Lord and Father, all my debt, which is great, and all my sin, which is much, you have forgiven me out of grace, because I confess to you alone and acknowledge my sin; help me that I may also forgive my neighbor and my enemies, so that I may remain sealed in my heart, knowing how you through your great goodness have forgiven all my sins."

Or, in such a way we should understand the fifth petition as an interpretation of the parable: "Lord, if I do not forgive my neighbor his failings, then all your gracious forgiveness toward me is in vain and lost; for you have indeed forgiven me everything, for which reason you sent Christ to me, who has become a sufficient sacrifice for my sin—this I know, this I believe, therefore I was baptized and have put on Christ. But thereafter, if I do not forgive my neighbor, then your forgiveness toward me is also nothing; for as I measure to my brother, so shall you measure back to me."

With this petition, we are all strongly exhorted that the **key of loosing and binding** <term>original: "Löse- und Binde-Schlüssel" — referring to the "Power of the Keys" (Matthew 16:19), the authority to forgive or retain sins.</term> stands in every person's hand, so that we do not make an error and nullify the Divine forgiveness toward us by being unwilling to forgive our brother on earth the minor sin he has committed against us. Beicht-Vater" — the physical seat of confession and the priest who hears it.</note>. Both high and low, great and small, have come to this mindset: that no one can be pronounced free or absolved of sins unless he fetches it from the priest; but they do not only want to fetch forgiveness of sins, but also to take from the **Sacrament** <note>referring to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>...

The third reason that moved them to present such a cunning and deceitful question to the **Lord Christ** was the income of the Temple, which was being given to the foreign Roman soldiery; this seemed wrong to them, that one should take it from **God** and give it to the foreign soldiery. It had a fine appearance of piety; with such talk, they intended to trap **Christ** in his speech. But human wit, wisdom, and cleverness are put to shame. He did not say, "Yes, one should give the tribute penny <note>original: "Zinß-Groschen"; the coin used for the Roman poll tax</note> to the Emperor," otherwise the people would have taken cause to complain against him, saying he was against the Temple and against **God's** laws by approving of unjust things. He also did not say, "No, one should leave the money to the Temple and give nothing to the Roman Emperor," so that **Herod's** servants would not notice this and write to King **Herod** and the Roman Emperor that a man had arisen who forbade giving tribute to the Emperor.

Finally, he did not remain silent in response to the question either; otherwise, they would have accused him of being a fawning flatterer <note>original: "Fuchsschwäntzer"; literally a "fox-tailer," someone who uses sycophancy or deceit to please others</note> who did not want to speak the truth out of fear of men, and that he feared men more than **God** in heaven. **I**t is presented to us in this text two beautiful, glorious miracles: one concerning the ruler’s deceased daughter, who is raised from death; the other concerning the woman who for twelve years could not be cured of her sickness, abandoned by all physicians; she is made healthy through faith by merely touching the hem of **Christ’s** garment.

In these miracles, we have three useful lessons to learn and retain. Firstly, how distress and concerns in adversity or the **Cross** <note>In this context, the "Cross" refers to the personal trials, sufferings, and burdens that believers must carry as a testament to their faith.</note> entice, drive, and lead us to **Christ**, the faithful physician, so that we may feel and find his goodness, love, and faithfulness toward us; so that it may be true as he says: *Come here to me, all you who are weary and burdened, I will refresh you; learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart; here you will find rest for your souls; my yoke is easy, my burden is light.* Without the **Cross** and concerns, we could never taste, recognize, or become aware of what a treasure we have in our helper-in-need **Jesus Christ**. Therefore, we should thank **God** that he sends us the **Cross**, so that we may come to his dear Son **Jesus Christ** and learn to believe in him, just as we see in this ruler of the synagogue <term>Archi-synagogos; the administrative head of a Jewish house of worship</term>, that he came to **Christ** through distress and concern; likewise, this woman was also driven by her distress and sickness to seek the right physician, and she found him too.

**W**ith this text, we wish to look at three small points at this time:

**First**, to speak of the <term>abomination of desolation</term> <note>original: "Greuel der Verwüstung." A prophetic term from the book of Daniel referring to a sacrilegious act that ruins a holy place, often associated by reformers with the corruption of the church.</note> in the holy place, and what it might be.

**Secondly**, how one should flee from this abomination of desolation and no longer remain with it.

**Thirdly**, that Christ’s kingdom is to be sought only in faith and spirit, and in no physical place; in addition, we shall speak of the eagle and the carcass <note>A reference to Matthew 24:28; here interpreted as believers (eagles) gathering wherever the true Word of Christ (the body) is found.</note>.

And for the **First** point regarding the abomination of desolation in the holy place, and what it is, so that one may flee from it: it is to be known that it is the <term>Antichrist</term> <note>Literally "Against Christ." In this period, it was a common polemical term for the Papacy or any spiritual authority seen as usurping Christ's role.</note> in the hearts of men. Of him, Paul says that he shall be revealed before the <term>Last Day</term> <note>The Day of Judgment at the end of the world.</note>, and says: Christ does not come unless the <term>apostasy</term> <note>original: "Abfall." A falling away or desertion from the true faith.</note> comes first, and the man of sin is revealed, the child of perdition, who is an adversary and exalts himself above all that is called God or worship, so that he sits in the temple of God as a God and pretends that he is a God. In these words, the abomination of desolation is described—that is, the Antichrist, who sits in the holy place. To speak precisely, this abomination of desolation, the Antichrist, is nothing other than when the heart is possessed and ruled by <term>man-made teaching</term> <note>original: "Menschen-Lehre." Doctrines created by human authority rather than derived from the Bible.</note>. For the holy city is not the temple in Jerusalem, nor otherwise a heap of stones or a church made of walls; rather, according to the nature of the New Testament, it is the person themselves: *you are a temple of God*, and you are holy in the inner depths of the soul. There, Christ wishes to live, rule, and dwell, and no human being should rule over it. When you now shall see the abomination of desolation standing in the

holy place, of which Daniel spoke, then it is time to flee; and one should let nothing delay them. the six <term>works of mercy</term> <note>original: "sechs Werck der Barmhertzigkeit"; referring to Matthew 25:35-36: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, welcoming the stranger, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and visiting the imprisoned.</note> and thereby
earned eternal life. I say no; had these righteous ones earned

Father, the stone is too heavy." So the father comes and carries
the stone himself, and says: "My son, just come here, I will
buy you a coat, for you have carried this stone over there."
God does the same: He gives us faith and the six
works of mercy. Now, it is naturally impossible for all people
to believe and love; thus, when we recognize our weakness and 
inability, God comes and works faith.
From faith flows the love of one's neighbor—that is, the six
works of mercy—so that the believing person, who is now
no longer their own, cannot do otherwise than love, or
rather, God loves through them. Then God says, "We have
done it," even though God the Lord Himself did everything in us,

and with us as a <term>yielded instrument</term> <note>original: "gelassenem Werckzeug"; from the concept of "Gelassenheit," meaning a state of surrender or letting God act through oneself.</note>. He has done everything in us;
the reason: God rewards and crowns nothing but His own
work. Therefore, those others are rejected because they claimed to have

summary, this discourse on faith and works all leads to this: 
that we are taken away from ourselves and given to God as His

When we have fully surrendered ourselves and left ourselves to God,

afterwards says: "We have done it," because we were 
obedient to His working grace and remained under Him. We 
can do nothing without God, and God does nothing 
without us; we both together, neither without the other. The hand
can do nothing without the person; the person nothing without the hand;
neither without the other; rather they both together. The person
works everything through the hand, and may say: "You, hand,
you have done it." Thus, Christ works everything through the
believers and says: "You have practiced the six works of 
mercy." He who begins the good work also completes
it, provided only that we keep still and remain an obedient tool;
and here the rhyme applies:

> I can do nothing without You / You will do nothing without me /
> we both together / neither without the other / the axe cannot

> nothing without the axe / these two together / neither without the other /

a comfort that is! What a certainty of salvation that is,
that all believers find the sweet work of God within them!

<column-break/>

der-working faith, the power from the Father. This faith is
the creature's work and its own, as a proper inheritance; and
through this faith many people have become healthy.
Of this it is said: "Your faith has helped you"
physically, but it has not yet made you saved; for no one is
saved through their own will, workings, or powers. It must be
another faith that creates new creatures and makes them saved—
namely, Christ dwelling, governing, reigning,

God's, as His entire property; where we have entirely 
withdrawn from ourselves and have been left to God, in death
and also in life. The natural faith of the <term>old birth</term> <note>original: "alten Geburt"; referring to the fallen human nature inherited from Adam, as opposed to the "new birth" in Christ.</note>
lets a person remain their own master and seeks only their own

and only God works this, and it is not our own work,
but God’s in us. What then is our own work, if neither
faith nor works are ours? Answer: Although 
saving faith is not our own work (for
no one can make themselves a believer) and the works also
are not ours, but God's in us, they are nevertheless
credited to us for the sake of the <term>experience</term> <note>original: "Befinden"; a crucial term in this period's theology meaning the internal, sensible perception or state of the soul's relationship with God.</note> or for the sake of 
inheritance. Namely, the physical, sweet experience is our own—
that we feel and recognize that God wants to govern, dwell, and 
reign in us, and we have the peace of Christ in us. And according to this,
the kingdom of heaven is our own: "Come, you blessed of 
my Father, inherit the kingdom which is prepared for you from 
the beginning of the world." God works it; we feel and experience it.
The work is God's; the sweet experience is ours. We have 
it and inherit it out of grace, and no stranger does; therefore it is ours.
And in this way, the works may also be credited
to us—namely, for the sake of the experience that God [works] such things in [us].

In these words from Revelation 22, we are shown the place of all believers after their death and after the Last Day, and the place of all the damned after their death—and the place of all the damned after their death <note>The original German text repeats this phrase, likely a printing error in the source manuscript.</note> and after the judgment has been held. ...and walk in the commandments of God; this very same thing is presented to us in today’s text through the parable of the five wise virgins and the five foolish ones: that we should watch, walk carefully, keep the oil in our lamps, and not spill it. Therefore, we are faithfully warned through the Gospel that we become careful and watchfully wait for the bridegroom, going to meet him with our lamps along with the oil; for whoever neglects it here has neglected eternity. For such oil <note>The "oil" is traditionally interpreted in Lutheran theology as faith or the Holy Spirit dwelling in the heart.</note> cannot be bought from the merchants, is not paid for with any money, and may not be borrowed or lent from anyone; each must have it for themselves and keep it for themselves. Just as little as a careless, foolish virgin, once she has lost her crown of virginity <note>original: "Kranz der Jungfrauschafft." In early modern German culture, the bridal wreath or crown was a physical symbol of a woman's purity and social honor.</note>, may borrow, buy, or lease her honor from a chaste virgin—no pious person would do so, nor is she able to—likewise it goes with this spilled oil: it is neither sold nor borrowed from others.

They may consider the reasons why the five wise virgins were prepared to enter with their bridegroom into the holy city of God, which God Himself has built. And first: how and why the five wise virgins waited rightly, went out to meet the bridegroom, and were worthy and fit to enter into the holy city of God, is found in the words of the text: that they had three <insert>means</insert>

means or ways before them, and these three are one thing in the eyes of God, flowing out of one fountain, though they may be divided into three. For the sake of instruction, they may be divided into three, showing how each person should prepare themselves here in this time, so that they also may be made fit to enter the holy city.

The **first** and most principal thing by which they were made ready and fit to go out to meet their bridegroom was the **oil** in their lamps; for the text reads: *the wise took oil in their lamps.* What is this oil other than the spirit of faith in Jesus Christ, as the "anointing" <note>A reference to 1 John 2:27: "But the anointing which you have received from Him abides in you..."</note> teaches you. And as David says: *You anoint my head with oil* <note>Psalm 23:5.</note>—not with linseed oil, nor with laurel oil, but with the Holy Spirit, with the spirit of faith. With this, all believers are anointed in their "vessel"—that is, in their hearts, inwardly in the soul. And in the "lamps" it is seen by other people—that is, through the life of Christ in the outward man.

From this oil flows the **second** means: namely, praying, confessing, acknowledging, and being absolved through the <term>Key</term> <note>The "Power of the Keys" (Matthew 16:19) refers to the authority to forgive or retain sins. The author argues here that the believer holds this key internally through faith.</note> within themselves. For they were made so wise and prudent by this oil in their vessels that they kept the key to the holy city of God with them in their hearts and in their hands. In their confession or prayer to God, they could say: "Forgive us our debts," and they did not need to buy or fetch the key to the kingdom of God from the **merchants**. These "merchants"—that is, the "absolvers" or sin-forgivers—are the buyers and sellers who set themselves up in the holy place and say: "Come here to us, the choice is with us, with us you will find the key." The five wise, prudent virgins understood such falsehood well; they kept the key within themselves and did not need to look to the hands of any merchant. Oh, what a precious, excellent treasure that is!

From this arose for them the **third** thing, by which they remained in a state of readiness: namely, the <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>A difficult term to translate, meaning "yieldedness," "devout detachment," or "letting go" of worldly attachments to rely solely on God.</note> of three things...

for the holy oil, together with the keys, necessarily brings with it the granting of the release—or the loss—of three things. First, they lost the world with its lusts: pride, [worldly] spirit, usury, gluttony, drunkenness, gambling, sorcery, cursing, injustice, hatred, anger, etc. Secondly, out of great love for their Bridegroom, they left behind father, mother, brother, sister, wife, child, etc. They did not allow themselves to be hindered or held back by such people. For many a person might well reach the City of God if the love of their neighbor were not in the way; human teaching <note>The author distinguishes between "human teaching"—outward religious rules—and the internal guidance of the Holy Spirit.</note> does not want to be despised by the world, wants to believe only to please its own people, wants to follow the "great crowd" and look toward the masses, and thus forfeits the Eternal. Such a person makes for himself earthly fathers and thus loses the true Father in Heaven; he gives the key out of his hand and tries to fetch it from the outside through another’s mouth or hand. He is deceived, reckless, and foolish. This does not happen to the wise and cautious ones who take the oil with them, for they allow themselves to be taught; their anointing remains undeceived. Thirdly, they left not only the world and all outward hindrances, but also themselves. They loved their lives even unto death; they were redeemed from the earth by the blood of the Lamb; their conduct was in heaven, in the holy city.

Thus they remain at all hours ready and prepared to go out to meet the Bridegroom, to wait for his joyful future. They could not fail; they could not lack oil. They did not need to fetch it from anyone else, for they had it within themselves. From all of this, one can also well understand the reasons why the five foolish virgins were unready and unprepared for the coming of the Bridegroom, and why they had to remain outside in the darkness. For it was only fair: they had kept their treasure locked away in the darkness and had walked in the darkness without the oil. Therefore, the gates were closed to them, and they had to remain outside. For as we walk in [this] time, so shall we be found at the end.

<page-num>381</page-num>
<header>Sunday after Trinity. 381</header>

As we are found, so must we remain there. We carry heaven within us—the kingdom of Christ, the holy city. If we walk within it during this time and are found within it at the end, then we shall also enter with our Bridegroom. Conversely, we carry hell or darkness within us; if we walk in the works of darkness during this time and are seized by death while in them, where else should we go but into the darkness? For we would not have practiced <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>Original: "Gelassenheit." A central concept in German mysticism meaning "yieldedness," "surrender," or "letting go" of one's own will to God.</note>. He who could not let go of things from within and without must remain forever outside. In considering the causes of the foolish virgins' failure, the text first reports that they indeed took their lamps, but they took no oil with them. That was the first, greatest, and most prominent fault: namely, the lack of oil—that is, of the Spirit and of faith in Jesus Christ. The anointing was lost on them; the oil was spilled. From this arose the other darkness: that they could not pray, "forgive us our debts." They could not confess, do penance, or be absolved within themselves. They did not have the key to the City of God. They ran to the "merchants"—that is, those who [claim to] forgive sins, the absolvers in the confessional chair. They made their confession and fetched their "solution" <note>Referring to the "Absolution" or formal pronouncement of forgiveness by a priest.</note> from the confessional chair, seeking enlightenment from the blinded and salvation from the damned. And even if they went to confession and the Sacrament every half-year, every Ember week, or every four weeks, they still remained always in their old nature. Nothing better came of them. They were sleepy and lazy in waiting for the Bridegroom; they remained unprepared and unready. In their whole lives, they had never had any earnest regret or repentance for their sins. When the Bridegroom finally came, he found them unready—that is, death overtook them unexpectedly. They sent for the "merchant" so that he might "oil" them <note>A reference to Extreme Unction or the "Last Rites" given to the dying.</note>, but nothing came of it; it was in vain. They had waited too long, and the doors were closed. Thus, such a thing always comes to a sinner at the most inconvenient time, precisely when he least expects it and thinks he will, in the quiet-

It warns that death reveals one's true internal state—be it heaven or hell—and that last-minute rituals cannot replace a lifetime of spiritual preparation.</summary>

# Gospel on the first Sunday

<margin>3. Advent.</margin>
The third Advent, or coming of Christ to us humans, is when he remains with the faithful after his Ascension until the end of the world—when Christ dwells, rules, lives, and governs within us. (Ephesians 3, Colossians 1, 1 Corinthians 6).

<margin>This coming is the most necessary.</margin>
Everything depends on this coming; it is the most necessary. Namely, that we be in him and he remain in us. For even though he was born as a man from the Virgin, it would be of no use to us without this indwelling within us. And though he rode into Jerusalem and entered the Temple, it is of no use to us if he is not also within us. Indeed, all his suffering and death would be lost on us if he did not dwell within us.

<margin>4. Advent.</margin>
The fourth Advent, or coming of Christ, is when he shall come on the Last Day to judge the living and the dead in his majesty and glory, etc.

<margin>Proposition 1. Regarding the visible coming.</margin>
We wish now, however, to deal with the visible Advent—the entry into the city of Jerusalem and into the Temple—and why he rode in in such a manner.

<margin>2. Regarding the invisible coming within us.</margin>
Secondly, we will speak of the invisible Advent to us and in us, where he dwells in his temple; this is what will be of greatest importance to us.

<margin>1.</margin>
And first: concerning Christ’s entry on the donkey into the city of Jerusalem, where he comes in his assumed human nature and thereby enters the Temple. This happened first so that the Scripture would be fulfilled which was spoken of him: <term>Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, humble, sitting upon a donkey.</term> <note>original Latin: "Dicite filiæ Syon: Ecce rex tuus veniet tibi mansuetus sedens super Asinam"</note>

<margin>2.</margin>
Next, it was so that he might come one last time into the city of Jerusa-

### Gospel on the first Sunday of Advent.

...the teaching and the life of the highly-learned is against Christ: Indeed, they could not bear to have a thorough, pure teacher appear among them. Therefore, these places are nothing but **dens of murderers**; <note>original: *Mördergruben*. This is a reference to Matthew 21:13, where Jesus cleanses the Temple, calling it a "den of thieves." The author is applying this critique to the religious institutions of his own time.</note> whoever has eyes to see, let him see, and depart from them in time, so that he does not cling to their teachings and be thrown with them into the fiery pool.

The reason Christ drives all commerce out of the temple—desiring the Temple to be a house of prayer and not a den of murderers—is to show that in the New Testament, the true Temple of God is no walled church, nor a heap of stones. Rather, the **human being themselves** shall be the temple. This internal temple is often greatly defiled by blasphemy and the great errors of false teaching. However, as soon as Christ is let inside, everything contrary shall depart, including all vices and human doctrines. For through human doctrine, this temple is poisoned and defiled, and the person is spiritually murdered by it. But Christ wishes to cleanse it, sanctify it, and dwell within it. That is to say, the believing person will be a dwelling and a Temple of God (1 Corinthians; Ephesians 3). They will no longer need to run here or there to pray, as happened in the Old Testament, for the night has passed and the day has arrived. This means Moses, with his **walled churches** <note>The author uses "walled churches" (*Mauer-Kirchen*) to symbolize external, ritualistic religion, which he believes is superseded by the "internal" church of the spirit.</note> which belonged to the external man and served as a foreshadowing, has now passed away. Christ has come and established a new, eternal temple through himself—that is, through his flesh and blood which he gives to us, so that we may grow out of him. We are taken from his side, just as the woman (Eve) was taken from the man (Adam), and not he from us. That is to say, not his

<column-break/>

flesh from our flesh, but we from his flesh. When Christ thus dwells and rules in faith, his Advent or his "coming" has occurred within us. Only then can one truly pray:
-> **Thy kingdom come** <-
For that is God's kingdom: where Christ dwells in us with all his peace, which overcomes the world. There, God reaches or governs through Christ within us. O, blessed and forever happy are those who find this Advent of Christ within themselves!

For them, his suffering, death, and resurrection are of use, and it is to their benefit that he will come on that final day to judge the living and the dead.

If we are to enjoy the Kingdom of God, it must not be outside of us, but within us, as it is written in Luke 17. This is why we also pray, "Thy kingdom come." # Gospel on the first Sunday

<margin>Everything depends upon the invisible Advent.</margin>
...the severed grapevine have sap and life, if it does not remain on the vine. Thus, how could a person be saved, if Christ were not in him, and he in turn in Christ? Therefore, everything depends upon this **invisible Advent** of Christ to and within us. Everything else would otherwise be in vain and useless; his incarnation, birth, cross, death, resurrection, and his final return <note>The "final return" refers to the Second Coming of Christ at the end of time.</note> would be of no benefit to us, if this invisible yet perceptible arrival were not within us; our conscience testifies to this in the Holy Spirit.

<margin>How does the Advent of Christ happen in us? The Anabaptists teach thus, yet it is nonetheless the truth.</margin>
How may we then come to this, or how might the Advent of Christ happen within us? **Answer:** Much human work is not necessary for this, but rather a **quiet waiting upon GOD**, with fear and trembling. Yet the simple-hearted may be led to it in these three ways. First, Christ sends out two disciples, who untie the tethered donkey and the colt and bring them to him, so that he himself <margin>I. How must Christ's coming happen?</margin> sits upon it and thus rides into the city of Jerusalem. The donkey, however, lets itself be tied and led; it is willing and carries Christ. So God gladly sends out two disciples or witnesses: the Old and New Testament, or the outer and the inner <note>The "outer and inner" refers to the written Word of Scripture versus the "Inner Word" or Holy Spirit speaking to the soul.</note>, etc. These testify and instruct us that we humans are tied up outside the city, and that we are conceived in sin and born into death. Thus, a good report is necessary for the simple-hearted through the **oral preaching office**, so that he may yet learn to recognize his misery and wretchedness. No one should despise this faithful guidance; and God has ordained the preaching office through Christ. Where that is not present, his Word is nonetheless available, which knocks at the door of all people.

# Gospel on the Second Sunday

<margin>Four Advents.
1.
2.</margin>
Eight days ago, we encouraged one another regarding the four types of Advents <note>The word "Advent" comes from the Latin *adventus*, meaning "arrival." In this period, preachers often categorized the "comings" of Christ into four distinct events to help the congregation understand his role in history and the soul.</note>: the first was when Christ came into the world by taking on human nature in the Virgin. The second coming or Advent was when he rode in upon a donkey to his suffering and death in the city of Jerusalem, and also drove the sellers and buyers out of the temple. <margin>The true coming. <note>original: "Verus adventus."</note></margin> The third Advent of Christ is when he comes to every believer, dwelling in them, ruling, living, and reigning, so that God’s Kingdom is found in the heart; then everything is driven out of the inner temple that is not God or Godly, and one can rightly pray: "thy Kingdom come." <margin>4.</margin> The fourth Advent is when he will come at the end of the world, not in his weakness or scorn, not upon a donkey toward the cross and suffering, but in the clouds with great power and glory—as we then together confess and say in our faith: from thence he shall come to judge the living and the dead.

Christ speaks here in the text of this, his glorious coming; but because the day of such a coming is hidden from all people and angels, and no one can know the hour, he announced the precursors or preceding signs to the believers in Matthew 24, 25 and in Luke 21. By these they may perceive that the last day is not far off, just as one can perceive from the fig tree that summer is near. <margin>To Christians, the day of the Lord is joyful.</margin> However, the day of Christ is not only joyful and pleasant to the believers, but all preceding signs are also comforting to them; with joy they lift up their heads when these things begin to happen, for their redemption draws near; they are
sober

<margin>

Here a Christian eye may look around.

<margin>
Man himself is the abomination, the cause of discord. <note>original Latin: "Homo ipse ist der Greuel Causa discordiæ."</note>
</margin>

The first and most prominent sign is the "abomination of desolation" in the holy places, as mentioned in Matthew 24. This is the source of all error, deception, quarreling, the fear of war, despair, and more. And this abomination is not a physical idol of Caesar in the temple <note>original Latin: "Idolum Cæsaris in templo." A historical reference to the statues of Roman Emperors that were placed in the Jerusalem Temple, which Jews and early Christians viewed as a supreme sacrilege.</note> at Jerusalem; rather, in the New Testament, the human person is the temple where the abomination of desolation is found. It is found when not only the heart is corrupted with false teaching, but also when the land and its people are devastated. This happens when human teachings occupy the heart instead of Christ, and when people cling to teachers who claim that one must seek forgiveness of sins from them—as if they sit in God's place—and that sins are erased through the sacraments <note>The preacher is likely critiquing the Roman Catholic view of the priesthood and sacraments from a Lutheran perspective, emphasizing that only Christ, not human "teachers" or rituals alone, can forgive sins.</note>, along with many other erroneous articles of faith. Whoever accepts such human teachings, defends them, and clings to this person or that while letting go of Christ, will inevitably go astray, become fearful, and cause war, strife, and division.

<margin>
Darknesses are not signs of the Last Day.
</margin>

The second sign concerns the sun, moon, and stars. For through human teachings, the heart is darkened and confused, and people fall into great sins and vices. Following this, God allows signs to appear in the heavens as heralds of the final day. These are signs that go beyond nature, not following the natural course of the heavens. They are not the eclipses of the sun and moon that an astronomer <note>original: "Astronomus"</note> can calculate using the tables of Ptolemy <note>original Latin: "tabulis Ptolomæi." Claudius Ptolemy was an ancient Greek-Egyptian astronomer whose mathematical charts were used for centuries to predict the movements of celestial bodies.</note> or others many years in advance. Such things have occurred throughout time and have been understood by students of nature. These cannot be the signs of the Last Day, for God has not written that day upon the face of the sky <note>original Latin: "ad faciem cœli"</note>, nor has He commanded the natural course of the heavens to reveal that day, which remains hidden even from the angels—

2. Supernatural signs.

—angels in heaven, but here we understand the signs of the Sun, Moon, and Stars <note>The original text uses the symbols ☉, ☽, and ***.</note> that sweep in across nature and appear against all natural movement, so that no master of nature can know when they are coming. By such supernatural signs, the godly realize that God sends them as a warning and an awakening of hearts for the Last Day.

The third sign is gluttony, drunkenness, and anxiety over food and sustenance. People live in great excess <note>The original German "Füllerey" refers to a state of being "over-full" or constant over-indulgence.</note> and no longer consider it a sin. It is said of such a person: "He is a poor fellow; he won't even drink a jug of beer with an honest man." Noble and commoner, citizen and peasant, high and low are despised and mocked by the world if they do not want to lie under the table <note>The original phrase "unten und oben liegen" implies being so drunk that one doesn't know which way is up or down.</note> or be "drinking buddies." All of this is caused by false preachers who drink and gamble just like the most prominent citizens. Self-interest, greed, usury <note>The practice of lending money at high interest rates, often condemned as exploitative.</note>, the oppression of the poor, and similar sins rule among us; let each person reflect on this for themselves.

# Gospel on the Fourth Sunday
<meta>catchword: none</meta>

In this text we find a different delegation <note>original: "legation"</note> than the one from eight days ago; this one is not dispatched from an obscure place or by a man in prison. Instead, it comes from a famous and praiseworthy place—namely, from the capital of Judea, from Jerusalem itself, and from the Synagogue. Those sent are not lowly or common people, like the servants of John, but learned, respectable, and high-ranking men: priests, Levites, and Pharisees. This delegation of the Jews was sent to John not so that Christ might be revealed or made known—for they were his enemies and bore him a grudge—but so that he might remain unknown and obscured. However, the more they wished to suppress Christ and the knowledge of him, the more John confesses and explains him. He says: "I am not Christ <note>original: "Christus"</note>, who bears the sins of the world; you must not attribute such honor to me. I was not born from the tribe of Judah, but from the tribe of Levi <note>In Jewish tradition, the Messiah was expected to come from the royal line of Judah, whereas John's father was a priest from the line of Levi.</note>. I was not conceived by the Holy Spirit like Christ, but from the seed of Adam—though beyond or against the laws of nature <note>John refers to his parents, Elizabeth and Zechariah, being past child-bearing age when he was conceived.</note>. Christ was born of the Virgin, but I was born of a daughter of Eve, from Elizabeth. I am a witness and a voice crying in the wilderness: 'Make straight the way of the Lord!' I preach repentance so that people may confess their sins—not to me, but to GOD—and so that through this crying voice, everyone might prepare the way for the Lord. Therefore, I baptized with water; I am not a forgiver of others' sins as Christ is, who takes away all sin. I do not seat myself in his place, but I am his servant, and I am not worthy to untie his shoelaces. My baptizing is only water; it has no—

---

# of Advent.

—no effect or power, and I have come solely to baptize with water so that he might be revealed in Israel.

<margin>Proposition: 3 Parts.</margin>
So that we simple folk might retain something from this text, we shall consider three small points:

<margin>1.</margin>
The first: the thorough confession regarding Christ, by which John distinguishes himself from Christ and gladly acknowledges his own unworthiness.

<margin>2.</margin>
The second: concerning the crying voice in the wilderness, through which the way is prepared for the Lord.

<margin>3.</margin>
The third: concerning the baptism of John and of Christ, in which is somewhat revealed the "child of perdition"—who is the Adversary and the Antichrist <note>A term used here to describe one who usurps God's authority, particularly regarding the forgiveness of sins.</note>—who claims divine honor or power for himself by forgiving sins and wishes to seat himself in God’s place.

### The First Part.

<margin>1. Difference between the parents of John and Christ. 2. Tribe.</margin>
The Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to question him—that is, to suppress Christ and exalt John. But he confessed and did not deny it, saying: "I am not Christ." It was as if he were saying: "You surely know my parents, the elderly Elizabeth and Zechariah, and that I am born from the priestly tribe of Levi. The Messiah <note>original: "Messias"</note>, however, must not come from Levi, but from the tribe of Judah, and be born of a virgin. Therefore, you must not think that I am the Messiah who is to come; I am not he." He means to say that there is a great difference between the one born of the Holy Spirit without any male seed and from a virgin, and the one born of the earth from a married couple of Adam’s seed. Furthermore, the tribe also distinguishes us, as said above. "I am not Christ; I also do not have the power to bear or forgive the sins of the world, nor do I sit in his place. Indeed, I am not worthy—"

worthy that I should untie his sandal-straps. Moreover, I am not Elijah, who came in the Old Testament with fire; I come as a forerunner of the New Testament and come to baptize with water, so that he who was before me and comes after me might be revealed in Israel. He was before me according to the state of his exaltation and divinity; he comes after me in the state of his humiliation and office, for after my death he will enter into his office and perform the work for which he was sent. Furthermore, I am not a prophet in the old sense, for all of them have now ceased, having only prophesied of Christ with words; but I point to him as one present with my fingers. They saw him only in spirit, but I see him with physical eyes in his assumed human nature.

->This is the confession of John concerning Christ before the delegates from the Synagogue, whereby he distinguishes himself from the person of Christ in terms of his arrival, birth, office, effect, and power. He recognizes himself as humble and unworthy, and does not presume any divine power, nor does he set himself in Christ’s place.<-

<margin>John's confession is a prophecy in the New Testament <note>original: "Confessio Johann est Prophetia in N. They will not merely exercise this presumed power, but will defend and confirm it with Scripture.

### Secondly

**Secondly**, John says: I am a calling voice in the wilderness; prepare the way of the Lord, etc. Here is understood the office of a faithful teacher, and also the manner in which the way of the Lord should be prepared. <margin>Preparing the way.</margin> Everything depends on the knowledge of Christ—that Christ may come and find the way prepared, for where the way is unprepared, he does not enter. To this preparation of the way belongs a crying voice in the wilderness: first in the teachers, then in the listeners. John saw that all the people in Judea were misled by the Pharisees and priests; therefore his spirit cried out to God in his heart, considering such distress. Afterward, he preached repentance to the people and told them to go into the wilderness of their hearts and there consider their many and various sins, to confess them to God and not to a priest. <margin>What is the confession of sins?</margin> The confession of sins occurs when we fall away from ourselves, when all our reason, senses, thoughts, wit, and cunning are dead within us, and when all...

The wilderness or desert is not a place somewhere in the forest, but it is in the body, where the body renounces all the world’s pleasures and does not merely flourish in fleshly lusts, but withers; where also all human teachings and idolatry are cast out of the heart; where all our reason, cleverness, art, skill, wisdom, and human discretion are dead. In such death, <margin>The crying voice of the Spirit.</margin> the Spirit cries out in the wilderness. Such a crying voice of the Spirit in the heart prepares the way for the Lord so that He may come, enter in, and dwell in the heart. There, the person becomes new and believing; upon this, one may be baptized. And John did this: first, he made his own body a wilderness and let his spirit call and cry out over the great blindness and darkness of the people. This was followed in many listeners by them also having the crying voice in their hearts. In this way, the path for Christ the Lord was paved, leveled, and prepared:

### The Third Point.

**Thirdly, concerning the baptism of John and of Christ.** It is proper for a faithful teacher to make a distinction between these two baptisms—even though Christ did not baptize [physically]—namely, because when they are mixed together and considered the same, a great error arises: that people bind faith, the forgiveness of sins, or salvation to the act of baptism itself. John says: I baptize with water, but He has stepped into your midst whom you do not know. He is the one who will come after me, who was before me, of whom I am not worthy to untie his sandal-straps. Likewise: therefore I have come to baptize with water so that He might be revealed in Israel. With these

# Gospel on the Fourth Sunday
<header>of Advent.</header>

On the other hand, there are now some who completely despise Holy Baptism as a worthless thing, saying: "Since you are not Christ, why then do you baptize?" That is: since faith in **Jesus** alone makes one blessed, what does baptism, the Sacrament, help me? Answer: Although the water has no power, works nothing, nor takes away sin, we should look to Him who instituted and commanded baptism. He is the Creator of the <term>new creature</term> <note>In Lutheran theology, the "new creature" is the person spiritually reborn through God's grace.</note>, the Son of **God** Himself. We are of the earth and understand nothing of heavenly things, *John 3.* Therefore Christ takes water and adds the Word to it: "In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." With this water He wishes to lead us to the heavenly body, so that we must have a new flesh and blood from heaven and kill or subdue the old flesh of Adam <note>The "old flesh of Adam" refers to human nature in its fallen, sinful state.</note>. It is such a water that Christ has ordained and commanded, and in it lies a great mystery hidden; it may well be called a Sacrament. No one should despise it; otherwise, one despises Him who commanded it. And it belongs to the believers, whom one should baptize, as He speaks: "He who
<margin>Note: Infant baptism.</margin>
believes and is baptized shall be saved." Thus one may also baptize children, for they all believe in Christ, and do not first obtain faith from the baptism itself. All believers should be baptized with common, pure water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; thus they are baptized upon the <term>satisfaction</term> <note>original: "Gnugthuung." This refers to the "satisfaction" or "atonement" of Christ—the belief that His death paid the penalty for human sin.</note> of **Jesus** Christ. If they remain in faith, they are saved through the satisfaction of **Jesus** Christ, and not through the water, which has no power or effect. Therefore, note: if one gives baptism to a believing person, and

<column-break/>

<page-num>39</page-num>
<header>of Advent.</header>

he wishes to persevere in faith, then he has been given an external sign of grace, showing that he shall be saved out of pure grace through faith, solely upon the satisfaction of **Jesus** Christ, and not through the water; for the water does not make one blessed. But if one gives baptism to an unbeliever who dies in unbelief, then one gives him a testimony that he shall be condemned—not because of the baptism or the water, which makes no one damned or blessed, but because of his unbelief, which alone condemns. We humans cannot baptize without water, for our baptizing is performed only on the body and is undertaken upon the satisfaction of **Jesus** Christ. We humans do not baptize without water, but the Holy Spirit can also baptize without water. We also cannot give Christ's flesh and blood <note>A reference to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> without bread and wine, but the Holy Spirit can feed the believers with the flesh and blood without earthly bread and wine. We take earthly things to lead us into the heavenly ones; therefore, we should not despise Holy Baptism.

# The Second Christmas Sermon

In such a quiet Sabbath <note>original: "Sabbath"; here referring to a state of internal spiritual rest and stillness of the soul.</note> the Child is seen in the manger—that is, in the heart. Thereafter, one also finds Him in the swaddling clothes—that is, in the Holy Scripture—which one can read with great joy as a testimony to these magnificent works of **GOD**. Or, if one cannot read, one hears of Him from faithful teachers in the oral office of preaching. And finally, one also recognizes **Christ** in His assumed humanity of nature. These three may often be taken as one. What is accomplished by such inward seeing, feeling, and grasping in the manger, as well as in the swaddling clothes and in His humanity, can neither be spoken nor written.
<margin>Cannot be expressed.</margin>
Whoever has it, let him thank **God** and keep it; whoever does not have it, let him hurry with the shepherds so that he too may see and attain it, and let no "beast" <note>Referring to animalistic or worldly impulses.</note> hold him back, nor any earthly worry. And although these great wonders can be neither spoken nor written, yet the mouth overflows because the heart is full, and the wondering grows ever more, and one desires to spread it and to proclaim it to others, as far as is possible.

We have today the day of John the Apostle and Evangelist, of whom Christ says to Peter: "If I will that he remain until I come, what is it to you? You follow me." And we should take that text for ourselves from John 21. But because this same John presents to us the birth of the Son of **GOD** in a special way, we wish to stay with the Feast of Christmas and consider the words read above. There are, however, two Johns mentioned in these words: one is the one who writes these words himself in the 1st and 21st chapters, whose day we observe today, and he is the Evangelist and Apostle who rested on the Lord's breast at the institution of the Supper, etc. <note>A reference to the "Beloved Disciple" leaning against Jesus during the Last Supper.</note> The other John who is mentioned here in the Gospel was a man sent from God—namely, John the Baptist, whose day we have four weeks after Pentecost. The same was a witness so that he should testify of the light, of which the Evangelist writes in this text: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with **GOD**."
<margin>John compared to an eagle.</margin>
Now this Evangelist John is compared to an eagle. This is because he swings his spirit upward into the heights to describe the beginning of all things, visible and invisible, and also to describe that the second creation <note>The "second creation" refers to the spiritual rebirth or the Incarnation.</note> was born through the preeminent Word out of the Virgin.

# Gospel on the Day of John

[John] has flown higher and has seen more sharply than the other Evangelists. He has raised himself with his internal eye from visible things to the invisible, from the temporal to the eternal, from created things to the uncreated **GOD**.

<margin>How one ought to soar into heaven.</margin>
In this way, we Christians should also learn to raise our spirits and ascend from the creatures to the eternal Master Craftsman: as if rising from the earth up to the clouds, from the clouds to the moon, from the moon to the sun, from the sun to the heights of heaven—that is, to the firmament of the stars—from the stars to the waters above the firmament, from the upper waters to the angels, from the angels to the eternal Word of which John writes here, and from the Word to the invisible, unborn Father in His rest.

All men are conceived and born through Adam’s seed, one generation from another, and according to this first birth, they are damned and lost. ## The Fourth Part

<margin>Note.</margin>Fourthly, concerning the growth and increase of the Child JESUS: *And the child grew and became strong in spirit, full of wisdom, and the grace of GOd was with Him.* <note>A quotation from Luke 2:40.</note> Whoever has, to him will be given; but whoever has not, from him shall be taken away even that which he thinks he has, etc.

Christ was a child conceived of the Holy Spirit; therefore He also grew in that which He already possessed, and increased until His perfect age. He was from heaven and grew just as other humans grow, but He grew and increased in that which He had—namely, heavenly wisdom. Although wisdom or divinity neither decreases nor increases, His body grew with its instruments <note>The author uses "instruments" to refer to the physical body and senses which serve as tools for the soul and divinity.</note>, and the wisdom or grace of GOd could reveal itself thereafter. The soul in man does not grow; it becomes neither larger nor smaller; but the body grows and increases, it is young and it is old.

We want to remind one another, however, of what circumcision was in the Old Testament until Christ. And what circumcision is and works in the New Testament, from Christ until the Last Day; for there are two kinds of circumcision: one physical, done with the hand upon the flesh, and one internal and spiritual, done without hands in the manner of the New Testament.

## The First Part.

<margin>
Why was circumcision commanded? <note>original: "Quare circumcisio mandata?"</note>
</margin>
And first, regarding the circumcision of the Old Testament, it should be known that God ordained and commanded Abraham and his seed to practice and keep these ceremonies so that He might thereby have an external, visible flock that separates itself from all heathens, peoples, and languages as a certain people for His own possession. This people hoped for the "Seed" <note>A common theological term for the coming Messiah.</note> who was to come, in whom not only the Jews but also all peoples and heathens of the earth should be circumcised. This was done so that all peoples would be moved to investigate what the cause might be for practicing such "foolish" ceremonies on the flesh of men. Thus, the ceremony of circumcision was ordained not only for the sake of the Jews (as they thought) but also for the sake of the heathens, and it was to be maintained until the coming Messiah or Savior of the world—that is, Christ—who also allowed Himself to be circumcised on the
<meta>catchword: eighth-</meta>

---

New Year's Day. 85

eighth day, as if He were a sinner. And so He abolished external circumcision and established internal circumcision through faith. Was that not a clumsy and foolish thing to all the "worldly-wise" and clever heathens—that Abraham and his people circumcised every male child in the foreskin, on the member of the body which nature wishes to have hidden and covered? But with that very act, God wished to put to shame all the wisdom and cleverness of the world, treating them like drunken, full men who thought they could find the way to eternal life on their own—yes, like blind men who did not even know if there was another life.

Thus, circumcision in the Old Testament signified that everything which is worthless or good-for-nothing must be cut away from man. <margin>1.</margin> First, lust and desire must be cut away, as they are the origin and root of all sin and idolatry—namely, one’s own will, personal opinion, and every "good intention" that a person undertakes by themselves to serve God or to find the way to their homeland. Answer: If water baptism were the new birth—that is, if faith or the new birth were worked through water baptism—then there would be an easy way to get into heaven, and one could certainly be saved without a mortified <note>original: "abgestorben," referring to the spiritual practice of "dying" to worldly desires or the "death" of the old self.</note> life, without **CHRIST’S** death, and without the killing of the sinful flesh; and all the unbaptized would have to be damned, even if they had died to themselves and the world through faith. But no sacrament or ceremony makes one saved, so that the way to heaven is not closed to anyone. However, it would be closed to many people if **GOD** had bound the new birth to the sacraments, or if the sacraments were to work the new birth within; it must come from the inner man, and not from the outer, whether it be salvation or damnation. Therefore, let those answer for it who bind their salvation to the sacraments—which even a godless person can practice, have, and use—and circumcision, as a heavy yoke, has been changed into baptism, so that we Christians might have a mild, gentle sign of grace from our mild, gentle Redeemer, to baptize the believers, and

This light or morning star is Christ, who was born not in Jerusalem, the great city, but in Bethlehem. This happens to all those who look upon the Scripture with a good heart and in the fear of God, or who allow themselves to be led by the Scripture. We see this in the Wise Men from the East, who were diligent, industrious men in the research of natural things and well-practiced in all wisdom. In their knowledge of the course of the heavens and the path of natural stars for this short mortal life, they suddenly became aware of a new star. It was large and beautiful, and though it stood there in nature, it had come beautifully beyond nature, for it did not belong to astronomy, nor was it created in the beginning with the other stars. Though it was meant to shine in a dark place until the day dawned, it will be so darkened and distorted in all the "high schools" <note>original: "hohen Schulen," referring to the universities and academic theological centers of the time</note> under heaven that one can find no light or guidance toward Christ and His life. Furthermore, such a person, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, will never again desire to go to Herod or to the high schools, but will distance himself from them as far as he can. # Gospel on the first Sunday

...[must be guarded] with spears, and so many guards walk beside you with halberds? Before Christ came into the world, and among the heathens who knew nothing of faith, it was no wonder that tyrants had to fear their subjects; but in the New Testament, now that Christ has come and is preached in the land, it is a wonder that one would not dare to trust one's own subjects. It is a sign that neither authority nor subject walks in faith, but rather against the faith. If your father and mother want to compel you to a false faith—which they might even do with good intentions—you should remain in your freedom of the inner man <note>The "inner man" refers to the soul or the spiritual self, which the author argues is independent of physical circumstances.</note> and say: "Why is it that you worry for my faith? Do you not know that I must be in that which is my Father’s?" <note>A reference to the young Jesus in Luke 2:49, explaining his presence in the Temple to his parents.</note> That is to say: you have indeed begotten me for the earth, but I have been born once more, namely from GOD, who is my Father in matters of faith, and no one on earth is. If a master or mistress wanted to compel you to a false faith, then servants and maids should say: "One must obey GOD more than men." <note>Acts 5:29</note>

Likewise, if your <term>preceptors: teachers or tutors</term>, masters, <term>doctors: highly learned scholars or theologians</term>, etc., had taught you a false way, and you became aware of the true faith, then you should leave them and say: "Our Father who art in heaven, not on earth." One must learn faith from GOD and not from men. Thus, a Christian shall believe to please no one—be they king, prince, father, mother, teacher, or preacher—but rather return to GOD and learn faith from the true Father who is in heaven. Many believe out of fear or love of man—be it authority, parents, lords, friends, or schoolmasters—and lose thereby...
