# after Epiphany.

...thereby the faith. In wanting to be obedient where they should not be, they fall into great disobedience. They do not distinguish the obedience of the outer man from the inner man; they mix one with the other, so that they often abolish and lose the obedience of the inner man through the obedience of the outer man. Or, they are obedient with the inner man by subjecting themselves to the "gods on earth" <note>A common Reformation-era metaphor for kings and magistrates.</note> and thus also fall into great disobedience. If you were in a place where one was required to go to confession and confess sins before the priest, and it were commanded of you to confess: then let the outer man confess, kneel before the priest, and confess the sins there. But guard the inner man so that he himself does not "confess"—that is, that he does not think the inner man earns anything or obtains absolution <note>The formal release from guilt or sin pronounced by a priest.</note> from the priest. Instead, let the inner man confess and acknowledge to GOD and no priest. Let the outer man bear the yoke; do not start a war over it, for you know well that the priest cannot forgive sin, and that such confession is a human invention <note>Original: "Menschen Gedichte," literally "human poetry" or "human fiction," implying it is not divinely mandated.</note> and against Christ.

Likewise, if it were commanded of you to carry the banners or to walk with the cross <note>Refers to participating in Catholic religious processions.</note>, then let that happen according to the outer man. Only see to it that the inner man is not permitted to carry the banner to earn something or to perform a "divine service" with it. Instead, let it be a cross and a yoke to you—yes, even a temptation of the devil, who attacks you thus to see whether you would become impatient and start a war, or whether you would also try to carry the banner with your inner man.

Likewise, if you are among the number of the priests and you become aware that your station is false and ungodly: let the outer man be a priest; let him [bear] the yoke or the cross...

We may, for this time, note three small points in this history <note>original: "Historia"; refers to the narrative or account of the wedding at Cana.</note>.

<margin>1.</margin> First / on the union of two spouses, that they are both one flesh, in which a divine mystery is hidden.

<margin>2.</margin> 2. On the poverty of these two little people, that Christ gladly stays with such, and not with the rich.

### The First.

Regarding the first: this wedding signifies that man and woman bind and betroth themselves to one another, and for that reason leave father and mother, so that one spouse clings to the other and they are one flesh and yet two persons. However, because they are both one flesh, they are bound together through love, so that they leave father and mother and do not hate themselves; for if the husband hated his wife, he would hate himself, that is his own flesh and blood. And if the wife hated the husband, she would hate herself, that is her own flesh and blood, and would act against that from which she came; for she is not of herself, she is from the man and out of the man. The Apostle says / <margin>Ephesians 5.</margin> You husbands, love your wives, just as CHRIST loved the congregation <note>original: "Gemeine"; used here to mean the community of believers or the Church.</note>, and gave himself for her, so that he might sanctify her and has cleansed her, that she might be pure without blemish, etc. In the same way, husbands should love their

For we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his blood; for this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This mystery is great / but I speak of Christ and his congregation. If we rightly consider these words of Paul and this mystery, it is found that according to the old birth <note>Refers to natural, physical birth into the fallen human race.</note> we are of the earth, and are not able to be married or joined to Christ our Bridegroom with the old body; but that Christ is from heaven, and we, according to the new birth <note>Refers to spiritual rebirth or regeneration.</note>, are also from heaven, and thus we are married to Christ. A father’s word should hold so much weight and be so powerful toward the son that it drives the son over many miles in obedience; and a mother’s word should be so important, strong, and effective that the child does everything in total obedience—indeed, he should sooner run through a fire than anger his father and mother. Every act of disobedience is a <term>mortal sin</term> <note>original: "Todtsünde"; a sin that leads to spiritual death</note> which is worthy of eternal death. The servants and maids who are disobedient to their masters and mistresses lose Christ, deny the faith, and rob themselves of the kingdom of heaven if they do not repent. All apprentices who are disobedient to their master craftsman and remain so, not asking for forgiveness or confessing it, etc., they lose Christ, deny the faith, and rob themselves of the kingdom of heaven. The words of superiors should be so powerful toward their subjects that they do everything required of them without contradiction, just as the soldiers did for their captain. <margin>5.</margin>
The fifth kind of faith is that an uncircumcised person becomes circumcised; for faith is the true baptism, through which a heathen becomes a Christian. For true faith is the rebirth; faith takes away sin, and not confession before a priest. Faith is a work of God within a person, therefore it works all things necessary for salvation. From this it follows that all those who do not have this saving faith—who seek to obtain and fetch forgiveness of sins through priestly absolution or the taking of the Sacrament—even if the work of God within them were as large as a <term>mustard seed</term> <note>original: "Senffkorn"; a reference to the parable in Matthew 17:20</note>, they would fetch neither faith nor salvation from the Sacrament. Their faith is a human work without power, without effect, without renewal, and without conversion. Therefore, they think to fetch faith or the forgiveness of sins from those who do not have it themselves, whom Christ had cursed. If they had faith, they would not need to "fetch" it; were their faith a work of GOD, they would not need to be strengthened by the Sacrament, for faith would be strong in itself. But because they have no faith, they want to go get it, and they find nothing; and because their faith is a human work, they want to strengthen it with sacraments. Christ did not institute faith or the Sacrament so that they should *create* faith, but rather that they should be a memorial for those who already believe.

O woe to you **mouth-Christians** <note>original: "Maul-Christen"; those whose Christianity exists only in their speech, not their spirit</note>, who think you sit in GOD’s lap with your false faith; you must be cast out into the darkness, and GOD will take people from among all heathens, nations, and languages, and seat them in His kingdom with the faithful Abraham.

# On the Fourth Sunday after Epiphany / Gospel / Matthew Chapter 8.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'J' with floral and vine-like ornamentation.</image-desc>Jesus entered into the ship, and his disciples followed him. And behold, there arose a great tempest in the sea, so that the boat was covered with waves; and he was asleep. And the disciples came to him, and awoke him, saying: **Lord**, help us, we perish. Then he said to them: You of little faith, why are you so fearful? And he stood up, and rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a great calm.

But the men marveled, and said: What kind of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' with foliage patterns.</image-desc>It is spoken by <term>Sirach</term> <note>Also known as Ecclesiasticus, a book of wisdom from the biblical Apocrypha</note> in the 34th chapter: A well-practiced man understands much, and he who has experienced much can speak of wisdom; but he who is not practiced understands little. People of the world also rightly say: what is a man worth who is unpracticed, having neither experienced nor learned anything? If this is true in temporal, worldly things, then it is also necessary in divine and heavenly things, which—

<meta>catchword: which</meta>

---

<page-num>149</page-num>
<header>after Epiphany.</header>

which concern the soul. He who has not experienced faith or wisdom, and has not practiced his prayer, is worth little and is poorly grounded. For the knowledge of Christ, or saving faith, is not a written, human science, but rather <note>original: "experientia interna"</note> an internal experience through the Cross. The Cross and tribulations test a person, refining them in faith and in the knowledge of Christ, making it certain. As the Apostle says in <term>Romans 5</term>: We glory also in tribulations, because we know that tribulation brings patience, patience brings experience, experience brings hope, and hope does not let us be put to shame. In tribulation, the Cross, necessity, anxiety, and adversity, we learn to experience and recognize two things:

1. We recognize ourselves: our faith and prayer, how unpracticed and inexperienced we are. We see that we are careless, lazy, and sleepy in the contemplation of God’s Word; that we have let others do the preaching and behaved as if it concerned others and not ourselves. We have often persuaded ourselves that we were grounded enough in our faith, in the knowledge of Christ, or in His Word. But when we lie under the Cross and come into adversity, our small, weak, and meager faith is revealed, along with our laziness and carelessness—that is what is found within us.

2. In Christ, we experience goodness, love, and faithfulness; his sweet, gentle, and light yoke; and his unshakable peace. He is the one who says: "Come unto me, and here you shall find rest for your souls." We see this in today’s text: when Christ enters a ship and his disciples follow him, they initially sail quite gently and quietly upon the sea. Christ lies down in the back of the ship and sleeps; then a great tempest rose upon the sea, so—

<meta>catchword: so</meta>

<summary>This page introduces the Gospel story of Jesus calming the storm and uses it to argue that true faith is developed through internal experience and suffering rather than just book learning. It emphasizes that trials reveal our own weaknesses while simultaneously revealing Christ's faithfulness and peace.</summary>

...so that the waves threatened to cover the ship; they fall into danger, anxiety, and the peril of death. Then they run to the Lord and speak to him: **Lord, help us, we are perishing.** He answers: **You of little faith, why are you so fearful?** You have no faith at all; I thought you stood quite well in faith and in prayer, etc. Thus, you are still unpracticed and inexperienced in this. You others have listened to preaching and seen the miracles that happened to others, but you have not improved yourselves because of them. Thus, in this distress, tribulation, and anxiety, they experience their own weakness, their unbelief, and their negligence and laziness in prayer. They have not properly practiced their faith; only now, in this danger, distress, and anxiety, are they driven and awakened to hasten to prayer and call upon Christ: "Oh Lord, wake up! Help us! We are all sinking and perishing!" 

What does the Lord do? He rebukes them for their unbelief, their laziness, and their negligence, because they did not take his many sermons to heart themselves but instead let them be said to others. He rebukes them because they never properly practiced prayer; otherwise, they could have commanded the wind and the sea themselves, if they had been practiced in faith and prayer. He stood up and rebuked the wind and the sea, and it became completely still, so that the people who were in the ship marveled among themselves: "What kind of man is this, that the wind and the sea are obedient to him?" 

In this, they recognize in Christ the love, goodness, and faithfulness toward all people, and his eternal peace. Only then do they truly recognize what it means in Matthew 11: **Come here to me, all you who are weary and burdened, I will refresh you; take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and**

<meta>Catchword: hum-</meta>

**humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is gentle, and my burden is light.** <note>original: "mein Joch ist sanfft / mein Bürd ist gering." This is a central promise of comfort in the Lutheran tradition.</note> This speech of Christ, just as it applies to physical distress and anxiety, applies even more to the distress and anxiety of the soul. The disciples do not experience this during good days, but rather in the cross, tribulation, and the peril of death. 

Thus, the simple-hearted may learn these lessons from this Gospel story:

1. That each person's station and <term>calling</term> <note>In this period, "calling" (Beruff) referred to one's God-given place in society and daily work.</note> is like a ship on the sea, especially when one follows Christ. It must be subject to turbulence, driven here and there by the winds and waves of the sea. This world is like the stormy sea; it drives, hunts, and tests Christians powerfully in their calling and station, so that they must suffer many crosses and endure and withstand distress and danger. But through this, they are tested like <term>gold</term> <note>Symbolized by ☉</note> in the <term>fire</term> <note>Symbolized by △</note>. They glory in these tribulations, for they know that tribulation brings patience, and patience brings experience, experience brings hope, and hope does not let them be put to shame. Thus they press toward God and hasten to follow Christ through <term>fire</term> <note>Symbolized by △</note> and <term>water</term> <note>Symbolized by ▽</note>, through hell and death.

2. We also learn that the Christian calling or station, when without the cross and without suffering, is initially led into laziness or security. We see this in the disciples: they follow Christ into the ship, sit down, and travel quite gently upon the sea in a quiet rest. They become inattentive and negligent; they do not think of faith or their prayers. They let the Scriptures be written for others and not for themselves; they let preaching be for other people and not for themselves. They persuade themselves that they are faithful enough and strong enough; they believe they have learned Christ well and will now stand firm. This happens to almost all beginning Christians—that in good days, they do not find much of faith or of sweetness...

Romans 5. <note>Specifically referring to Romans 5:3-5: "...we also glory in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope."</note> Likewise, the suffering of this time is not worthy of the glory that shall be revealed in us. This is just as Longinus and Megistus, courtiers of Nero <note>Likely referring to legendary figures from the apocryphal "Acts of Paul," where Nero's servants are converted by Paul’s endurance in the face of death.</note>, once spoke to Paul: "Dear Paul, tell us, where is your King who appeared to you? 5. That the unknown man, Christ Jesus, must still be revealed to the world before the Last Day. First, it is true that Christ, with his Gospel, has never been fully recognized or accepted. It is also true that he must be recognized and revealed before the destruction of the world, so that there may be one Shepherd and one fold in stillness and peace. The people in the ship did not know Christ—who he was, or if he was the Son of God—but marveled at him, saying: "Who is this man?" Since Christ was not recognized or accepted by the world even when he walked the earth in his own person, preached himself, and performed miracles,

how much less is he accepted now through his Gospel. All the universities know as little of him as the Jews did, who said he was Joseph’s son and was of the earth. And even if they say he is not of the earth but from heaven, they only do so through the <term>communication of properties</term> <note>original: "Communicatione idiomatum." A theological doctrine explaining how the human and divine attributes of Jesus are shared in one person. The author argues that scholars use this as a dry, academic label rather than a living truth.</note>; they say according to his divinity he is from heaven, but his flesh is from Adam, from the earth. The laziness of the priests and world-scholars causes Christ to remain unknown to the common man. No one knows who Christ is; he is unknown enough that <gloss>Christ is recognized by few</gloss> <note>original: "à paucis agnoscitur Christus"</note>. Now, Christ must become known and revealed with his kingdom on earth before the Last Day comes, so that he might be recognized throughout the whole world. But before this happens, a great storm must arise on the sea of this world; the water-waves must roar, and everything adverse must stand in trembling and be cleared away. Afterward, Christ will awaken and bring about a great stillness; his kingdom will dawn, he will be revealed on earth, and all who are his will know him, and find and enjoy his peace; then there will be one Shepherd and one fold. Even though it vexes the Antichrist and the Devil, it must still happen that the Antichrist and the Devil are driven out, so that Christ may be everything and all, as all the prophets have indicated.

Now let us consider the text together and hold fast to the teaching within it.

The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sows good seed on his field. In this world, one finds two kinds of kingdoms, as can be clearly seen in Daniel chapters 2 and 7 <note>The biblical book of Daniel describes a vision of four great beasts or statues representing successive world empires.</note>; one is the kingdom of the earth, ruled by the earthly, originating from the earth out of the possession of human will, and is arranged into 4 monarchies: the first was that of the Assyrians and Babylonians; the second, the Persians and Medes; the third, the Greeks under Alexander the Great; the fourth and last, the Roman Empire, divided into many kingdoms. These four monarchies comprise the kingdom of the earth, where war, quarreling, murder, strife, injustice, etc., are found; therefore they must all perish and vanish, just as the kingdoms of the Babylonians, Persians, and Greeks have vanished; and so it must also go for this last one, if we believe the prophets.

The other kingdom is not of the earth, not earthly, but its subjects are from heaven and have their citizenship in heaven; namely, the Son of Man who is in heaven. This kingdom should have had the upper hand, but the wheat is in the midst of the weeds, so that one is hardly aware of it here and there; but this spiritual kingdom from heaven, the kingdom of Christ, of which it speaks here in the parable. Currently, the members are not in one place, like Israel in Canaan; those who are subjects in this kingdom are spiritual, just as their King is heavenly. Thus they are not in one city or one country, so that one could say: the Lutherans are the kingdom of Christ, or the Papists <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics.</note> are the kingdom of Christ, or the Zwinglians <note>Followers of the Swiss reformer Huldrych Zwingli.</note>, or the Schwenkfeldians <note>Followers of Caspar Schwenkfeld, who emphasized the internal "Stillen im Lande" (quiet in the land) spiritual life over external church structures.</note> are the kingdom of Christ, or this group or that one; no, that cannot be said with truth, though every group presumes to be the kingdom of Christ; for <term>the Church is not a visible assembly in a specific place</term> <note>original Latin: *Ecclesia ist nicht Coetus visibilis in certo loco*</note>. Christ's kingdom is not pointed out by a finger in a certain people or group, but among all peoples, heathens, and languages, Christ has his own; they are scattered here and there, and the little grains of wheat must pass through the midst of the chaff.

Therefore, consider, my dear brothers, that you do not undertake to kill heretics or to sweep the church; for no one should be killed for the sake of faith. Neither do the believers act such that they brand someone a heretic and kill them for faith's sake; the sheep do not drive away the wolves, nor do they start wars with the wolves—no more than their Lamb, Christ, did. The wheat does not drive out the weeds, but lets them stand beside it in the field, if only the weeds would grant the wheat its place. The church is still in the wilderness <note>A reference to Revelation 12, where the "Woman" (the Church) flees into the wilderness to be protected from the dragon.</note> until its time; therefore the grains of wheat—that is, the believers—are scattered through all peoples, heathens, and languages,

<meta>This page continues the interpretation of the Parable of the Weeds (Matthew 13), specifically focusing on the Master's command to let the weeds and wheat grow together until the harvest. The author uses this to argue for a radical form of religious tolerance and a spiritualist understanding of faith that transcends denominational boundaries.</meta>

# Gospel on the Fifth Sunday

...master, who has forbidden the pulling up of the weeds before the harvest, and he reveals the blindness and ignorance regarding the Kingdom of Christ and of God. He shows that the Kingdom of Heaven is now in the midst of the weeds. If one wanted to kill the heretics <note>The term "heretic" (Ketzer) was used by established churches to label those with dissenting beliefs; the author argues here against the execution of such people.</note>, one would have to kill the whole world and let only the very smallest part remain alive. How many pious Christians would be swept away if one were to root out the Pope? Likewise, how many believing Christians would be uprooted if one were to kill the Lutherans? The same applies to the Zwinglians, the Picards <note>The "Picards" or "Beghards" was a name often applied to the Bohemian Brethren or other radical reformist groups.</note>, and even the Turks <note>In the 16th and 17th centuries, "Turks" was a common term for Muslims, particularly those of the Ottoman Empire.</note> themselves. For God has His own people among the Muscovites <note>People of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, referring to Eastern Orthodox Christians.</note> and Turks just as much as under the Pope and Luther. No sect hinders me or other believers, for no one can take from me the faith—that is, the Kingdom of God—in which I dwell. It does not matter if I walk among the Lutherans, if I walk among the Baptists, among the Zwinglians, or among the Turks; for I know that I am in the Kingdom of God, regardless of which people, heathens, or languages I am among. I would say that whoever does not feel as I do certainly does not yet know what the Kingdom of Heaven is, or what faith is: that it is not bound to any place, time, city, or ceremony. I keep one baptism and one Supper, wherever I may be. If I receive Communion under the Pope, I receive the true body and blood of Christ in His memory; it depends on the receiver, and not on the giver. If I receive Communion under Zwingli, I receive the true body and blood of Christ in His memory; it depends on my faith, and not on the priest's faith. Even if I were among the Turks at sea, I would have Christ's flesh and blood in me until death. Therefore, wake up, you scholars, and recognize what the Church is, and what the Kingdom of Heaven is: namely, Christ's Kingdom on earth, who sows His Word—which is Himself—into mankind,

and has set us all as good wheat. For the Word of God sown in us is the wheat, and every person fed by this wheat is the good seed, the wheat itself, so long as he remains in Christ. Nothing else is taught, preached, or sown by Christ, His apostles, or any of God's messengers than that which was implanted in our hearts during the first creation: namely, the Word, Light, and Life in all people, which also became flesh in us who wish to live and remain in His Kingdom. Life has appeared, and we humans have seen Him with our eyes, touched Him with our hands, and seen Him nailed to a tree for our sins. It is the Son of Man himself who sows His Word—that is, Himself. All Scripture and preaching conducted, read, preached, or heard according to the Spirit is exactly that which has been sown into our hearts. Therefore, it does not come in from the outside, as some say; rather, it is awakened through preaching. Whoever can give testimony through the Spirit of God regarding the word they have heard and preached, and accepts it, of them it is said: *faith comes from hearing* <note>original: "fides ex auditu"; a reference to Romans 10:17.</note>. Some take great comfort in this little saying of Paul's and think it is first carried into them from the outside. But our preaching and sowing is an external witness, an encouragement, a conviction, and an introduction. Whoever accepts this becomes a believer through hearing, because the internal and the external come together. Since we have all been set as wheat from the beginning, as good seed, so that we should be nourished and fed by it in the Kingdom of Christ or the heavenly citizenship, the servants ask: where then do so many weeds come from? # Gospel on the Fifth Sunday
### after Epiphany

->An enemy has done this, not I, says the Master of the House.<- The people 
paid no attention to the good seed, to the

can hardly perceive the wheat. The field of this world is entirely 
overrun by weeds, and it is not possible 
for men to root them out; the angels must 
do it at the appointed time. But since God 
created and placed man primarily not as a weed but as good 
seed, so that he should live in a 
kingdom on earth, etc., would it not be useful to 
root out the weeds and make a good wheat field?

<margin>NB. <note>An abbreviation for the Latin *Nota Bene*, meaning "Note well" or "Pay attention."</note></margin>Answer: It shall indeed be rooted out, and the field—
that is, this world—shall bear nothing but wheat. For

Almost all people are the weeds themselves—how should 
one weed root out another? How should the world

betray themselves, showing they are outside the sheepfold. Now 
the field must eventually be cleansed, namely at the harvest. 
Understand this thus: The harvest is the end of the fruits, 
and it may well have a triple meaning.

The Kingdom of Heaven is like a householder who went out in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard; and when he had agreed with the laborers for a <term>groschen</term> <note>A small silver coin used as a standard daily wage in the early modern period.</note> as the daily wage, he sent them into his vineyard. <margin>The Kingdom of Christ is through grace alone <note>original Latin: *Regnum Christi tantum ex gratia*</note></margin>
In this parable, Christ primarily teaches us that we cannot inherit or earn the Kingdom of God through our own merits; everything is given out of grace. We are obligated and bound to walk in the obedience of faith, to work in this vineyard for Christ's sake, and to leave and lose everything—even ourselves—without any hope of reward or repayment. And even when we have left everything and done everything, we should still say: "Ah, Lord, we have not done what we were bound to do; we are but <term>unprofitable servants</term>." <note>A reference to Luke 17:10.</note> We also see from this parable that the first and the last are equal in the eyes of God, held in the same regard. To all of us, the first as well as the last, the penny is given not out of merit, but out of grace. By this, all "pious" hypocrites and all <term>work-righteous</term> <note>original German: *Werckheiligen*; those who believe they are made holy or saved by their own good deeds rather than faith.</note> people are cast down—those who take comfort in their own righteousness, holiness, and piety, etc., which still pleases them. They hope that God must do more for them than for others, which is a wicked, devilish thing and the greatest hindrance to the Kingdom of God. For truly, what can a pot give to its potter? If you are pious, what can you give to God? If you are evil, how can you harm Him? Do you not see that He is too high for you, and that He has no need of you at all? You have need of Him. O, you cursed hypocrites and work-righteous ones, how are you so blind that you dare to speak with Peter: "Lord, we have left everything, what shall we have for it? We have done so much, suffered so much; You will have to give us more than the others who have suffered nothing

We should do everything that is commanded of us and yet not deem ourselves worthy to be obedient to such a great Lord even unto death.

The interpretation of the "hours" is varied. Some interpret these twelve hours as the history of the entire world: thus, Adam's time is the hour of the morning; the 3rd hour is the time of Noah, when God also hired His workers; the 6th and 9th hours are the times of Abraham, David, or Christ; and the 11th hour is the time of Christ, the end of the world, the evening, etc. Others wish these hours to be understood as the period from Christ’s birth until the end of the world: that Christ went out early and hired the Apostles into His vineyard in the early hour of the New Testament. Afterward, at the 3rd hour, He found others idle in the marketplace and told them to go in as well, and so on with others after them until Judgment Day. Now, if one wishes to apply this text solely to the Patriarchs, Apostles, Prophets, and teachers, etc., where one after another is called into this vineyard, one might well defend such an understanding of the hours, since one era after another has indeed provided such teachers. If one also wishes to understand this of all people in the entire world—that God has hired them all to this vineyard, just as He did the Prophets, Apostles, and teachers—then we can also interpret these twelve hours according to the age of each individual person. <margin>Parts of this Gospel. 1. <note>original: *Pater [Partes] hujus Evangelii.*</note></margin>
We may look upon three parts in this parable.

1. Upon the great goodness of GOD, that He, without respect of person, sows and plants all people equally as good seed, and allows all to be equally redeemed through His Son’s death, and seals us all equally through His almighty Spirit: thus is His Word sown in our hearts, and for that reason is also preached to us.

<margin>2.</margin>
2. We may also look upon the laziness, malice, and negligence of people, who rob themselves of the good seed and make themselves into bad seed, without the fault of GOD. For some become like the seed that falls by the wayside, some like the stony seed, some like the thorny seed; only the smallest part remains a good land.

<margin>3.</margin>
3. One [part looks] upon the strong evidence from the Word of Christ, that every human being is the seed itself; and because this parable is interpreted by Christ Himself, it is not necessary to devise a special human interpretation, but only to consider among which seed

<margin>1. The love of GOD is to be recognized.</margin>
Regarding the great faithfulness, love, and goodness of GOD toward us humans, which the simple-minded <note>Refers to the "simple" or "common" folk who need clear, uncomplicated teaching.</note> may understand and recognize from these four points.

<margin>1. In the Creation.</margin>
1. Initially, GOD created us humans good, as good seed. For even in the first creation, GOD placed His Word into the creation of man. Thus he was planted as a good tree, sown as a good seed upon a good land: for Scripture testifies thus, that God created everything good, Gen. 1. "See, there everything was very good." He spoke His word into a piece of clay <note>original: *stucke Leymen*; a reference to the creation of Adam from the dust of the earth.</note>; He sowed His Spirit in a good field. Thus in man is GOD’s Word, Spirit, Will, His seed, laws, the light and life—all of which made man into a good field or seed. For just as a farmer would not want the seed to fall on the path, or stones, or thorns during the sowing, but wants it all to fall on good land, just so little does GOD want His seed to become way-side, stony, or thorny, but rather a good land and a good seed.

<margin>2. In the Son, etc.</margin>
Afterward, for the second part: God’s love and faithfulness are known even to the simple, in that He sent His dear Son into death and had us redeemed again from the <term>inherited damage</term> <note>original: *Erbschaden*; a term for original sin or the spiritual corruption inherited from the Fall of Man.</note>. There, everything was made good, and with a gain, so that we now have no cause for complaint and may not say that all is now lost. No, indeed; we have regained everything with a profit through Christ’s death. God’s love toward us is always equal and unceasing, even if we cannot or will not always notice it. Since He then gave us His Son while we were still His enemies—who for us was hung upon the cross, killed, and has traveled to Heaven—we are thereby redeemed through death and pain, if we trust in this refuge, the Father’s Word; who then would dread dying?

...[spiritu]al fasting, where one abstains from physical food through the promptings of the Holy Spirit; this fasting is a confession and prayer in the Spirit, where one is so united and bound with **GOD** that one knows nothing of it, feeling neither hunger nor thirst because of the sweet, deep immersion <note>original: "Einsenckung"; a mystical term for the soul "sinking" into the quiet presence of God</note> in **GOD**. In this state, one does not think to earn anything by it, nor wishes to establish any form of religious service, as happens with the false ones. Those people have established orders and rules based on the example of **Christ**, **Elijah**, and **Moses** to earn something for themselves. Instead, all believers, baptized, and newborn <note>referring to those who have undergone a spiritual rebirth or "regeneration"</note> people are duty-bound and obligated to lead a moderate, sober life, not to overwhelm the body with excess food and drink. They do this through the working of faith; there, fasting, prayer, and faith are together, and that is a useful, good fasting, excellently beneficial to the body and the soul.

<margin>2. Human fasting.</margin>
The other kind of fasting, ordained by men—to abstain from certain foods at certain times—is false and Satanic. The reason: it does not proceed from faith; it is undertaken out of fear of men or out of hope for a reward, thinking that one wants to earn something before **GOD**. It feels bitter to people to fast according to such a rule, being forbidden to eat this or that. It is Satanic because the fasting is held without prayer and without faith, where fasting, faith, and prayer are separated from each other and are not essentially one. This ungodly fasting is rejected by **Christ** in Matthew 6 and by **Paul**; and the **Holy Spirit** says it Himself in our conscience that it is an abomination before **GOD** if one does not [fast] by the inspiration

<margin>The inward struggle.</margin>
"...overcomes, to him I will give the right to sit with me on my throne, just as I overcame." The cause of this inward struggle is that all believers have renounced the devil in **Baptism**; they wish to die as his enemies and never depart from **Christ** their Redeemer.

<margin>2.</margin>

Thirdly, it is because they cannot or will not come to an agreement with **Satan**. They remain children of the light and fight against the Prince of Darkness; now, light can have no fellowship at all with the evil works of darkness. Therefore, <term>Christian warfare</term> <note>original: "militia Christiana"</note> must be practiced until physical death. Such war was prefigured in the **Old Testament**, when **Israel** always had to fight against the **Canaanites** and against the surrounding **Philistines**. Whoever has a desire to go to war should remember his Baptism and the life of **Christ**; he will have enough warring and fighting against his own flesh and blood, against **Satan**, and against the world. "We do not have to fight with flesh and blood," but with the prince and the powerful—namely, with the lords of this world who rule in the darkness of this world, with the evil spirits under heaven <note>a reference to Ephesians 6:12</note>. Here the Apostle addresses not the unbelievers or the unwise, who do not need to fight at all because they have peace with the devil, but rather the believers. **Christians** have a struggle, not with "flesh and blood"—that is, not with visible, physical enemies who have flesh and blood, against whom one uses guns, swords, and long pikes, just as **Israel** had to wage war against visible, physical enemies as a figure <note>a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows a New Testament reality</note> for the New Testa-

[They] are allowed to eat with unwashed hands and thus transgress the **ordinances of the fathers**. To this, Christ answered: You transgress **God's commandment**, which is surely greater; for while you ought to provide for and honor your parents, you excuse yourselves with the offering you claim you must give to GOD. Thus, you let God’s commandments stand idle while you perform your intended sacrifice. Furthermore, JESUS said to the scribes: You hypocrites, why do you test me? What enters the mouth does not defile a person, but what comes out of the mouth defiles a person. Even if one eats with unwashed hands, it only goes into the belly and passes away; but what comes out of the mouth—such as evil thoughts, deeds, fornication, pride, and other sins—that poisons the person, etc. If something is to harm a person's salvation, it must spring forth from the heart. <note>original: "nihil externa damnant aut salvant"</note> Nothing external condemns or saves. The disciples came privately to JESUS and said: Do you know how the Pharisees were offended by your speech? From all this, we see who Christ was with, and why he departed from there and withdrew from them.

<margin>1.</margin> Namely, first, he withdrew from the highly learned of the Synagogue because they esteemed human ordinances higher than God’s commandment and God’s laws. Now, Christ is a fulfiller and a completer of divine law; they transgress it, cast it away from themselves, and concern themselves with the traditions of their 

<column-break/>

ancestors <note>The German "Altvåter" refers to the patriarchs or elders of the faith.</note> or their statutes, orders, and customs. Therefore, Christ departs from them and lets them remain blind. That these scribes only quarrel and dispute over external indifferent matters <note>The author uses "Mitteldingen," likely referring to the theological concept of "adiaphora"—actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God.</note>, ceremonies, the washing of hands, offerings, and other things that make a person neither blessed nor damned, neither sweet nor sour, and do not affect the inner person at all—whether one eats with washed or unwashed hands. Therefore, Christ leaves their borders and lets them worry about useless human things.

<margin>3.</margin> Thirdly, they are only pious in hand and pious in mouth; they speak and hear of God’s Word, but there is no fruit or power in the people. They honor GOD only with their lips; they read, sing, and gather out of habit, but their hearts remain dross. They are like tombstones that appear beautiful on the outside but are full of uncleanness within. Therefore, Christ does not wish to stay with such people; He departs from there and escapes their borders.

<margin>4.</margin>
<margin>The Father's teaching.</margin> Fourthly, they reject the **Anointing** <note>The "Anointing" refers to the inner guidance of the Holy Spirit (1 John 2:27).</note>, the inner Word, and the drawing and learning of the Father. They are not born of GOD, nor planted from the eternal, imperishable seed. They are satisfied with external hearing, with paper, with reading, and with singing; they take their pleasure in these. The inner source, from which salvation and righteousness must flow, is stifled by outward, invented worship. Christ cannot remain with such people either; he withdraws from them, as they take offense at his Word, which addresses the heart of the inner man.

<margin>The Synagogue of our time.</margin> <note>original: "Synagoga nostri temporis"</note> These reasons for his departure from the Synagogue-dwellers should be applied to the New Testament and to our current times. Here we also recognize why no truth and no Christ is to be sought or found among all the high schools <note>Universities or academies.</note> in the whole world; although no worldly-learned person can believe this, nor will any be persuaded of it.

[They] treat them like cattle—they preach to the simple man from the Catechism <note>original: "Catechismo"; a manual of basic Christian doctrine.</note>; he is expected to know it by heart along with its interpretation. They preach to him that he should hear God’s Word, come often to confession during the year, and receive the Sacrament, and that he should take comfort in the Lord Christ. <margin>4. To be taught by God. John 6:44.</margin>
Fourthly, nearly everyone takes offense at the sweet, mild, and truthful speech of Christ when He says: *You must all be taught by God; whoever does not hear it from the Father does not come to me, unless the Father draws him* <note>original: "Joh. 6. 44." Referring to John 6:44-45.</note>. They deny the Spirit, the inner Word, and nearly all sin against the third person of the Trinity <note>original: "Trinität"</note>, against the Holy Spirit. How then could Christ be with such people? Who would seek Him among such world-scholars <term>World-scholars: Academic theologians who prioritize intellectual logic over spiritual experience.</term>, other than the simple, blind person who gapes at the high schools? Therefore, I can say with truth that Christ has departed from all high schools in the whole world. He also took none of His Apostles from the synagogical highly-learned. Indeed, let someone but enter an academy <note>original: "Academia"</note> and teach the inner Word of Christ’s indwelling, and that faith cannot exist without the life of Christ—he would be received just as Christ was by the synagogical leaders in Jerusalem; indeed, truly even worse, because—

<margin>World-scholars.</margin>
—because this final world is the worst. No pious man dare lift his head in the kingdom. I speak truthful words, as true as I am a man: that Christ is not found in any high school in the whole world, nor does He allow Himself to be found by such proud world-scholars who take offense at the truth. Why then does one send our poor, innocent youth to such places where Christ, the only treasure, can neither be seen, found, nor recognized? neglect prayer for the sake of past sins, which are forgiven me by grace in Christ Jesus. Should I also wait for my own worthiness and holiness, I would become an "honor-thief," stealing from Christ His due honor and ascribing it to my own stinking works. Therefore, I say with David in Psalm 130: "Though there is much sin among us, with God there is much more grace; His hand has no limit in helping, however great the damage may be." Though my sin may have been ever so great, God's mercy is much greater in Christ Jesus (Romans 5 and 1 John 2): "Little children, if anyone sins, we have an advocate before God the Father, namely, Jesus Christ the Righteous, who is the atonement for our sin—and not only for ours, but also for the whole world." Likewise, John 3: For God so loved the world <note>original: "Sic Deus dilexit mundum"</note>, etc. Against my "holiness" or "worthiness" on the right hand, I sing with David thus (Psalm 130): "With You nothing counts but grace and favor to forgive the sin; it is in vain with our doing, even in the best life. Before You no man can boast; every man must fear and live by Your grace." <note>These are lyrics from Martin Luther's hymn "Aus tiefer Not schrei ich zu dir," a paraphrase of Psalm 130.</note> Whoever thus breaks through these trials in prayer will finally hear in their distress the sweet voice of God: "O person, your faith is great; let it be done for you as you desire."

> Thus, in such exercise we learn that trial brings patience, patience brings experience, experience brings hope, and hope does not let us be put to shame (Romans 5). And that we, in the cross and in distress, [learn to] pray

<sig>Ff</sig>
<meta>catchword: learn/</meta>

It argues that relying on one's own "stinking works" rather than Christ's grace is a form of blasphemy and that persistent faith eventually hears God's comforting response.</summary>

<margin>Faith is a touchstone of all sects.</margin>
This text is a fierce argument and dispute between two parties against each other: namely, Christ with his disciples against the Jews, and the Jews or scribes against the Lord Christ. One party declares and affirms that they are from God, are righteous and without error, but that the opposing party is of Satan, is false and full of error. This is what Christ does with his disciples against the scribes and Jews of the synagogue; the scribes and Jews do the same in return against Christ. 

But to recognize, judge, and distinguish which party is truly of God and without blame, and which party is false, of Satan, and full of error, requires an eye for it: a <term>judgment <note>original: "Judicium," referring to the faculty of spiritual discernment.</note></term> in divine understanding. Namely, holy faith, which is a <term>touchstone <note>original: "Prüffe-Stein"; historically, a dark stone used to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak they left when rubbed on it.</note></term> of all sects. It sees, recognizes, and judges all things. Now, it is indeed easy for us to believe and hold that Christ with his disciples is of God, is righteous and without error, and that his opponent is a liar and of the devil. We can even sing: *One should believe the truthful Mary alone more than the deceitful crowd of the Jews.* <note>original Latin: "Credendum est magis soli Mariae veraci quam Judaeorum turbae fallaci." This is a line from the famous Easter sequence "Victimae Paschali Laudes," referring to Mary Magdalene's testimony of the resurrection.</note> We would rather believe one person, a woman, than the great crowd of Jews. 

That is the result of the long passage of time and the reputation of the Church, and that everyone holds and believes it to be so. But had we been there and listened to such parties, we certainly would not have given our support to the single, despised Christ, but to the great mass of the scribes who studied in the synagogue, who were expected to watch over the poor people in the land so that they would not be led astray. For we would have taken offense that Christ and his disciples...

They pick up stones to throw at him, so he hides himself and goes out of the Temple. By this are understood the worldly scholars in the <term>universities <note>original: "hohen Schulen," literally "high schools," referring to the theological faculties of universities.</note></term>, who sit in the <term>consistories <note>Administrative councils or courts of the church.</note></term> and are supposed to watch over the people. They blaspheme him and revile him with their tongues—that is, with their false interpretations, glosses, commentaries, and self-authored books. They demonstrate this toward Christ’s own people; for if someone comes only in the name of Christ and preaches Christ’s teaching, life, and conduct in the synagogues and universities in an upright manner, he would truly experience the very same thing that Christ experienced from the scribes and Jewish synagogues, and even much worse. For they truly know Christ less than the Jews did; therefore they blaspheme him, revile him, and say: "Fanatics! <note>original: "Schwermer," a derogatory term used for radical reformers who claimed direct inspiration from the Spirit.</note> Enthusiasts! <note>original: "Euthusiasten."</note> Tasteless-fields!" <note>original: "Schmeckfelder," a mocking pun on the name of the reformer Caspar Schwenckfeld.</note> They write in their books thus: "We also condemn all those who speak of the **inner hearing** or the **inner Word**, who claim that one must be taught by Christ; we also condemn all who teach that Christ must dwell in us **bodily** <note>original: "Leibhafftig," referring to the indwelling of Christ's divine nature in the believer.</note>," etc. And so, when Christ takes the opposing side against them and says: "I am no fanatic, no deceiver, no false interpreter of the Scripture; I know my God who enlightens and teaches me; and if I were to say that I learned it from men and not from God, I would be a liar just as you are," then they pick up stones and want to [throw them at] him—

What, then, can such enemies of God be able to do, or what benefit can they provide, or how can they preach fruitfully?

<margin>II.</margin> Regarding the second part, namely the great power and excellent benefit that comes if one diligently hears and **keeps** God’s Word.

# Gospel on #

Christ has given and renewed [us], so that we may make ourselves children of God. To the <term>blind, proud theologian <note>A likely reference to those who focus on intellectual dogma or legalism rather than the internal experience of faith.</note></term>, this seems contrary to his teaching and his rational disputations regarding conversion and free will. For it is truly no different than: <note>original: "Omnis audiens Deum in ſe ipſo audit verbum, vitæ & vivificatur & renaſcitur"</note> **Everyone who hears God in himself hears the word of life, and is both made alive and born again.** This cannot fail for the one who persists with diligence in reflecting on such speech of Christ, not ceasing or stopping until he has found a place where he, like David, may build a city for God. As David says: "I will give no rest to my body, it shall not eat, nor sleep, nor attend to its needs, until I have found a place where God can dwell." That is to say: until I have become a dwelling or temple of God through faith in <term>silence and Sabbath <note>original: "in silentio und Sabbatho." Thus one learns to recognize the Son, who is the Light and Life of all people, who is the Word and speaks the words of life. He cannot die; He is a Lord over death, over sin, over the

# 262 Gospel on | Palm Sunday. 263

The disciples went and did as Jesus had commanded them, and brought the donkey and the colt, and laid their clothes upon them and set Him thereon. But a great multitude spread their clothes in the way. Others cut down branches from the trees and strewed them in the way; and the multitude that went before and followed after cried out and said: "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!"

The prophet Jeremiah says in the 31st chapter: "Behold, the time comes, says the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of David and with the house of Judah; not like the covenant that I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand and led them out of the land of Egypt—which covenant they did not keep, so that I had to constrain them, says the Lord—but this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel: after that time, says the Lord, I will put my Law into their hearts and write it in their minds, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God. And no one shall teach another and say: 'Know the Lord,' but they shall all know me, says the Lord, for I will forgive their iniquity. Such a covenant shall remain as long as the ☉ <note>Sun</note> and ☽ <note>Moon</note> endure. Behold, the time comes that the city of the Lord shall be built, and the gates shall never more be torn down."

<column-break/>

In this speech, the prophet encompasses all three ages of the world: the age of the Father according to the Old Testament or Covenant, where he says, "Not like the old covenant with the <term>Passover lamb <note>original: "Osterlamm." In this context, it refers to the sacrificial lamb of the Jewish Passover.</note>," following the exodus from Egypt, when I had to act with Law and constraint. The age of the Son according to the New Testament, where he says, "but a new covenant," where I will write my Law in their hearts, so that they will be my people willingly and gladly out of love and without any constraint, and I will be their God. The age of the Holy Spirit, where he says, "No one shall teach another, but they shall all know me," and the city of the Lord shall be built with its gates that shall never more be torn down or broken off.

This speech of the prophet shall serve us this time as a concept and interpretation of the sermon on this text of the entry of Christ into the city of Jerusalem on a donkey. Here we wish to consider the many-fold <term>nut <note>original: "Nuß." Continuing the metaphor from the previous page, the author refers to the "nut" as the essential spiritual truth to be extracted from the story.</note> of this entry of the Lord into the city and His entrance into the Temple. The first cause is that Christ rides into the city on a donkey, meek and poor, so that He might finally eat the Passover lamb with His disciples and establish a New Testament—a new covenant—which has nevertheless existed from the beginning of the world in the hearts of the faithful. He did this so that He might do away with the old Passover lamb of the Jews and establish a new, eternal one: namely, the institution of the <term>Lord's Supper <note>original: "Nachtmahl." Refers to the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>. For it was precisely during the eating of the Passover lamb on <term>Maundy Thursday <note>original: "grüner Donnerstag." Literally "Green Thursday," the traditional German name for the Thursday before Easter.</note> that He instituted and commanded His Supper to be eaten. Thus, the old had to pass into the new; the age of the Father with the old covenant has come into the age of the Son, and yet one remains within the other. He sent His disciples and said: "Go and prepare the Passover lamb for us, for I have heartily desired to eat this Passover lamb with you," so that the <term>New Testament <note>The author uses "New Testament" and "New Covenant" interchangeably to mean the new spiritual order established by Christ.</note> might end its outward Law, and the New might begin with the inner, living Law.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "New Covenant" established by Christ during Holy Week. It specifically links the Last Supper and the entry into Jerusalem to the transition from the Old Testament (the "Age of the Father") to the New Testament (the "Age of the Son").</meta>

# 264 Gospel on |

After they had eaten the **Passover lamb** <note>original: "Osterlamm"</note> together, he took the bread, gave thanks, and said: "This is my body." And the chalice likewise: "This is my blood; eat and drink this in memory of me." It was as if he wanted to say: until now, in the time of my Father, I have eaten the Passover lamb annually out of obligation and a lack of love, in memory of the rescue and the exodus from the land of Egypt. From now on, eat my flesh and drink my blood out of love and with a willing heart in my time, under the **New Covenant** <note>original: "neuen Bunde"</note>, so that you do not forget the eternal redemption achieved through my death, which I am about to suffer.

<margin>2.</margin> The second reason [for his entry] is that Christ rides humbly into the city of Jerusalem on a donkey so that he might seal and make powerful this eternal New Covenant—this Last Supper in which he gives us not the Passover lamb, but himself, his body and his blood—through his death, his suffering, his dying, and the shedding of his blood. For otherwise, without death, this, his **New Testament** <term>Testament <note>In this context, the word carries the dual meaning of a "last will and testament" and a "covenant" or "compact" between God and humanity.</note></term>, would not be valid. In the Old Covenant, the sealing was accomplished through the blood of oxen and calves, but the new one is sealed through Christ's blood, which we also receive in the Last Supper. As the Apostle also testifies to the **Hebrews** in the 9th chapter: "Where a testament is, there must also be the death of the one who made the testament; for a testament is only made firm through death, and otherwise has no power as long as the one who made it still lives." Therefore, even the first covenant (that is, in the time of the Father) was not established without blood, and everything was made firm and purified with blood according to the Law. Thus, death and dying are the most important part—the beginning, middle, and end of this eternal New Covenant. Whoever does not wish to die to sin with Christ cannot be worthy of the Last Supper.

Thirdly, he also rode into the city to his suffering so that he might redeem us prisoners, and

<column-break/>

# Palm Sunday. 265

and so that he might set free those of us who were bound to the bridle of the ceremonies of this Law. For without the redemption or reconciliation through the death of Christ, all people remain captive and bound by sin, by hell, by Satan, and by eternal death; and all would have remained therein if our Redeemer had not come into the world and willingly ridden to his cross, suffering, and death. Indeed, all the Jews would have eaten the Passover lamb in vain if Christ, the true Passover lamb, had not allowed himself to be killed on the wood of the Holy Cross and slaughtered for the sins of the whole world.

Fourthly, he also entered the city of Jerusalem and went into the Temple to drive out everything adverse, so that he might make us—his purchased and redeemed ones—into the **New Jerusalem** and into the true Temple. He did this so that we might be a people of God and he our God, as is said in **Jeremiah**: "They shall be my people, and I will be their God." Thus, the **Outer Jerusalem** would be brought into the **Inner Jerusalem**; namely, that our heart would become a Jerusalem, a dwelling and Temple of God according to the nature of the New Covenant. We no longer need to run here and there, seeking holy places as they did in the Old Covenant under Moses, but rather enter into the right Temple of God and pray in spirit and in truth (John 4). Although it has never been different in the hearts of all believers since the beginning of the world, it was not yet made public to the whole assembly of the Jews, as can be understood from Christ's speech to the Samaritan woman at the well, where he says: "The time is coming, and is already here, when the true worshipers will worship neither in Jerusalem nor on this mountain, but in spirit and in truth." When he says, "The time is coming, and is already here," he encompasses both Testaments—the Old within the New, and the New within the Old—as has always been...

# 266 Gospel on

...always the Father’s time is not without the Son’s, and the Son’s time is not without the Father’s; yet it is not always revealed to the entire multitude. The benefit of these four causes—or of Christ’s riding into the city of Jerusalem, where he instituted the Last Supper and suffered death, thereby redeeming us—is twofold: as temporal regarding this life, and regarding the life hereafter. The temporal benefit is that we, as the newborn, worthily take and hold the Supper in memory, just as the Jews had to keep their Passover lamb, but here it is done out of love without compulsion. In such a custom, we remember his death; that is, the consent and the renewal of our desire to remain united with Christ’s crucified body, and not to deviate from him until our own death. For the practice of the Supper requires that we die with Christ and remain united with him, and that we do not forget the new eternal covenant that stands in the midst of dying.

If the Supper is to be received worthily—that is, if it is to have power and might within us toward life and not toward damnation—then death must occur. That is, the 
<margin>False Believers</margin>
mortification of the old sinful flesh must happen within us, so that we die away from sin and do not let ourselves be satisfied with the falsehood that Christ died for us while we still wish to live in sins. We might want to **drink on his credit** <note>original: "auf seine Kreiden zechen" — a German idiom meaning to drink or live on someone else's tab or account; here, relying on Christ's grace without personal repentance.</note>; no, that would not be keeping the memory of Christ by living worthily. Just as Christ’s Testament had to be confirmed through his shedding of blood and through his death, so too must the practice of the Supper become powerful through the mortification of our sinful flesh. When we die with Christ and go into death, we receive the true body and blood of Christ unto eternal life; for the Spirit makes this food living. But if we let Christ die for us while we remain in sins,

<meta>catchword: so</meta>

---

# 267 Palm Sunday.

so we take such food of memory unto death and damnation. Therefore, one should receive this Supper worthily and not neglect it without absolute necessity for many years. For such neglect commonly happens for two reasons: either because one does not think much of the order of the New Covenant, of Christ's institution and command—believing nothing depends on it, that it is only bread and wine, and that Christ’s body and blood cannot be there since he is in heaven. Such people are wiser than Wisdom itself; they want to teach and prescribe to God how he should have given it to us—namely without bread, without wine, freely in the spirit, as he indeed gives it to all believers. Because of such annihilation or low estimation, it is neglected by some.

The others see that Christ is in earnest and that it is no joke; they neglect it because they are horrified by dying. For they must then consent to suffer with Christ, to go into death, to deny the world, and to bid farewell to all worldly lusts. They cannot practice <term>being baptized with him <note>original: "conbaptizari"</note></term>, <term>supping with him <note>original: "Concænari"</note></term>, <term>dying with him <note>original: "Commori"</note></term>, <term>suffering with him <note>original: "Compati"</note></term>, or <term>being crucified with him <note>original: "Concrucifigi"</note></term>. They bring forward **imputed righteousness** <term>imputed righteousness <note>original: "Imputativam Justitiam"; the theological concept that Christ's righteousness is credited to the believer's account.</note></term> and let it be reckoned to them; they let Christ die for them and thank him for it with their mouths—that he is so kind and has redeemed them, and that he died for them. They thank him with their mouths, but not with their hearts, nor with a repentant way of life. Otherwise, they would receive the body and blood of Christ alongside other table-companions as a memorial and remain in the New Covenant, in the New Testament. Let this be said of the first benefit in this time: namely, that we newborn people worthily receive the Supper in memory of his death, to suffer and die with Christ, and thus to remain in the New Covenant, of which God spoke through the Prophet Jeremiah.

The second benefit of the Supper <note>The author uses "Nachtmahl," literally "night-meal," to refer to the Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> concerns the Resurrection: that through Christ’s flesh and blood we have become a good seed, destined to rise in an eternal, unbreakable, and glorified body. In this state, we shall dwell in God and God in us for eternity. No creature can fully measure or express this benefit of the New Testament throughout all eternity. The era of the Holy Spirit is also encompassed in the cited passage from Jeremiah and prefigured in this text. For Christ’s entry on a donkey—gentle, poor, and despised by the world, yet highly honored and praised by the innocent—is a prophecy of the New Testament, of the time of the Son, and also of the time of the Holy Spirit. 

It speaks of the Antichrist, of the false prophets, and of the false teachers who have come and continue to come in Christ’s name. They do not come on a donkey like Christ, nor on foot like Peter, but in carriages and on steeds, on <term>nags</term> <note>original: "Caballen," a word for horses derived from Latin, here used to imply worldly pride or ostentation</note>. It is as if I knew of future things but did not wish to speak of them aloud, choosing instead to depict them through an image, or write a comedy, or perform a tragedy to show how things would unfold. This is exactly what Christ does with his entry into the city of Jerusalem on a donkey, and with his entrance into the Temple, from which he violently drives out the buyers and sellers. He rides into the city humbly—gentle, poor, and despised—toward his agony, toward suffering and death, seated upon a donkey. That is to say, he rides upon the most scorned of animals, as if Christ wished to say: 

"See that I come in poverty, in lowliness, in contempt, and in gentleness; but after me, my adversary, the Antichrist, shall rise up. The swarm of false teachers, etc., shall enter the city

They will not come from humble places like the fisherman's net, but from the synagogues and from the <term>high schools</term> <note>original: "hohen Schulen," referring to the prestigious universities of the era</note>. The poor will not show them honor or serve them, but only the rich and the powerful. The children, who belong to the Kingdom of God, will not cry out to them; instead, the learned and the wealthy will write for him (the Antichrist) <term>funeral dirges</term> <note>original: "Epicedia"</note>, <term>poems</term> <note>original: "Carmina"</note>, and letters of praise that are not fitting for the Kingdom of God. 

They will not eat from the Gospel as Peter did—receiving whatever daily food was set before them—but they will make a business out of my Gospel. They will extract great income, great <term>prebends</term> <note>original: "Pfründen," an ecclesiastical post that provided a guaranteed income from land or tithes</note>, and tithes from it, gathering vast estates and riches. They will not be ministers or servants, but masters, setting themselves up as the heads of all worldly people." 

When the despised common people and the children raised a cry of praise during Christ’s entry on the donkey, the scribes said in wonder: "Do you not hear what these are saying? Docter," a scholar who has attained a formal doctorate in theology</note>." It was as if honor should only be shown to the rich and never to the godly poor. The fact that Christ also teaches in the Temple itself / heals the blind and the lame in the Temple / after He previously drove out all buyers and sellers with wrath and storm / and overturned the chairs of the dove-merchants / teaches us three things through this. 1.
